The first season of Heroes is almost perfect – here’s why

New Scientist September 25, 2026

You rarely appreciate the significance of a moment while you are still living through it. But that is exactly what happened to me, 20 years ago this month, when a show called Heroes first aired.

As you may have gathered from the title, it followed ordinary people whose genes have blessed (or cursed) them with extraordinary abilities, from time travel to telepathy. Made in the wake of the Human Genome Project, it was an elaborately plotted mystery, blending comic book aesthetics with a glancing interest in evolution. And for the past two decades, it has had the dubious honour of becoming a byword for failure: after a stellar first season, Heroes limped its way through three more outings of questionable quality.

The minute I saw Heroes, I knew I was changed. It was the first TV series to set a fire in my head, at age 10. If I wasn’t watching it, I was talking about it; if I wasn’t talking about it, I was thinking about it. Chances are I was probably dreaming about it, too. But the extent of my obsession, combined with that notorious drop-off in quality, has stopped me from rewatching it or its spin-off, Heroes Reborn, in the years since.

Advertisement

The 4 best science-fiction shows of 2026 so far

That changed last month with the sad news that Hayden Panettiere, who played the show’s most iconic character, Claire Bennet, had died. Since then, I have been revisiting that almost-perfect first season – and you should do the same.

Even before its narrative spiralled out of control, Heroes had a sprawling ensemble of leads. Claire, a 16-year-old cheerleader living in Texas, was the most consequential. Her body rapidly regenerates its cells when injured, making her practically indestructible – and attracting the attention of Sylar, a superpowered serial killer. Meanwhile, geneticist Mohinder Suresh seeks to complete his late father’s work by contacting similarly gifted individuals, such as Peter Petrelli, a hospice nurse who dreams of flying, and Isaac Mendez, who can paint the future when under the influence of heroin.

Heroes, like Isaac, had a knack for striking images. Its first season is full of them: a cracked pair of horn-rimmed glasses; an office worker from Tokyo teleporting to Times Square in New York; a nuclear blast that Claire, somehow, can help prevent. “Save the cheerleader, save the world,” time traveller Hiro Nakamura tells Peter. This uncanny ability to distil essence and theme into potent symbols or phrases was the series’ own superpower. Not to mention the music: a whirling updraft of drones and chimes, featuring ethereal vocals from L. Shankar, it became a landmark score in television history.

Fabulous time travel novel is part-thriller and part-romance

It’s easy to dismiss Heroes as a Lost-alike: it was perhaps the best in a flurry of shows trying to emulate that legendary series, right down to its characteristic blend of science fiction and mysticism. But like Lost, Heroes explains a lot about what high-concept TV has become today – and has admirable qualities that its successors are thoroughly lacking.

It is a wholly original idea from creator Tim Kring, albeit one inflected with the tropes of classic comic books. It is also stuffed with action – certain plotlines, like psychic cop Matt Parkman’s collaboration with the FBI in the hunt for Sylar, could have been a show all on their own. And it proves that a show that captures true brilliance, however infrequently, will always be worth watching.

So I implore you to watch (or rewatch) the first season of Heroes. You may be averse to starting a series known to nosedive, but, as I have explained to many sceptical friends over the years, it is worth the hurt. And upon rewatching with an adult’s eyes, I have appreciated just how special Panettiere was as Claire. Her performance deserves to be remembered as one of the best of the 2000s.

Election 2026: Act wants to deploy ‘noise cameras’ to catch loud cars, boy racers

New Zealand Herald September 25, 2026

Act's James Christmas (inset) announced the policy for the David Seymour-led party.

The Act Party is campaigning on deploying a “fleet of relocatable noise cameras” to catch “excessively noisy vehicles” in the hope of bringing “peace to communities”.

The policy, revealed on Saturday, appears to be intended to help Act’s James Christmas campaign in the east Auckland electorate of Tāmaki, with the party saying the initial rollout of 20 relocatable noise cameras would partially start in that area.

Act currently holds Tāmaki, having won it off National in 2023, but its incumbent MP, Brooke van Velden, is stepping down. Christmas, a former National Party candidate now standing for Act, will compete against National’s Mahesh Muralidhar and Labour’s Max Harris, among others.

In a press release, Christmas said he had heard from locals that they wanted noisy vehicles addressed.

“I can see the attraction for boy racers to come to Tāmaki, but it’s not fair on the families and working people who have their life disrupted just because they live in a great location with nice streets,” he said.

“These kinds of disturbances are already illegal, but effective enforcement can depend on a police officer happening to be in the right place at the right time. By the time a person makes a complaint and an officer shows up on the scene, the vehicle could be long gone.”

Act is promising to introduce relocatable noise cameras which can be deployed in communities “suffering persistent problems with excessively noisy vehicles”.

“Modern noise cameras combine microphones, video and number plate recognition. They measure the sound generated by passing vehicles, identify which vehicle produced it, and record the evidence needed for enforcement,” the party’s policy says.

“Instead of requiring a police officer to personally witness an offence, excessively noisy vehicles can be detected as they pass and infringement fees issued in the same way as speed cameras.”

These would be “targeted at identified hotspots”, with the New Zealand Transport Agency (NZTA) able to relocate them “as problems emerge rather than allowing drivers to simply learn the location of a permanent camera and avoid it”.

The party pointed to the cameras’ use internationally, as well as a temporary local use in Tauranga in 2013 to detect noisy truck engine braking.

The Land Transport (Road User) Rule 2004 already prohibits excessive noise, but Act says it’s currently a “largely subjective test, which is difficult to enforce automatically”.

For example, the current rule allows for a consideration of a range of circumstances, including the time of day, locality, and the “likelihood of annoyance”.

Act would introduce a specific noise limit for the cameras to measure, with its starting point being 86 decibels on roads with speed limits of 50km/h or less, and 90 decibels between 50km/h and 70km/h. This would be subject to consultation and technical testing.

The party would also make necessary legal changes so “evidence from approved noise cameras can be used to issue infringement notices”. These would be in place by the end of 2027, Act says.

The infringement fee for operating a vehicle that creates excessive noise would be increased from $50 to $300, with the maximum court fine increasing from $1000 to $3000.

“Parliament has already legislated those penalties for the separate offence of creating excessive noise within or on a vehicle, which can include noise from car stereos and sirens.

“From 9 January 2027, that offence will carry a $300 infringement fee and a maximum court fine of $3000. No equivalent increase was made to the offence covering excessive noise produced by the operation of the vehicle itself, including excessive engine and exhaust noise.”

An infringement fee would only be issued where it can be established the noise limit was exceeded, and the sound was attributed to the identified vehicle. Data collected by the camera would be subject to “strict retention and deletion requirements”, and those issued with a notice would be entitled to request a copy of the evidence.

Act would allocate $2 million for the initial rollout of 20 noise cameras starting in Tāmaki and other hotspots, a “conservative” costing it’s based on international and local experience.

“Hard-working Kiwis shouldn’t be punished by people who can’t take personal responsibility for their noise. Noise cameras enable evidence of offending to be collected the moment the offence occurs,” said Christmas.

“Pairing technology with clear standards and real consequences will give residents the peace and quiet they deserve and ensure the comfort of many isn’t sacrificed for the noise of a few.”

Jamie Ensor is the NZ Herald’s chief political reporter, based in the press gallery at Parliament. He was previously a TV reporter and digital producer in the Newshub press gallery office. He was a finalist in 2025 for Political Journalist of the Year at the Voyager Media Awards.

Greenpeace occupies Government research ship in Wellington over deep-sea mining survey

New Zealand Herald September 25, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Greenpeace activists have boarded a New Zealand Government research vessel in Wellington this morning.

They are protesting its role in surveying the Pacific seafloor for a US company planning to begin deep-sea mining as soon as 2027.

The protesters say the ship, the Tangaroa, has just returned from exploration work for Glomar, which is seeking to fast-track mining in the Pacific.

One activist dressed as US President Donald Trump flew an American flag from the Earth Sciences vessel, while another held a banner reading: “Don’t Mine the Moana”.

The protest claims to highlight the role New Zealand is playing in Trump’s attempts to bypass international law and expedite deep-sea mining in the Pacific, despite international resistance to the practice.

Activists sent a clear message during the protest: New Zealand must not be complicit in Trump’s minerals grab.

Greenpeace Aotearoa campaigner Juressa Lee said it was disturbing to see the vessel, which is owned by the New Zealand Government, being used to further “American imperialism” in the Pacific.

“If deep-sea mining is allowed to go ahead it will strip the seafloor, risking irreversible damage to the ocean we all rely on, to supply minerals for Trump’s war machine,” Lee said.

“Pacific peoples are at the frontline of this fight, and deep-sea mining puts their way of life and cultural heritage at risk. It must not be allowed to start.

“While the rest of the world is still debating if deep-sea mining should even be allowed to go ahead, Trump has gone rogue.

“He’s decided that the US will just start mining regardless of international laws, and the rights and interests of the communities who rely on the ocean.

“New Zealand must not be complicit in this.”

The Tangaroa has just returned from the Clarion-Clipperton Zone in the international waters of the Pacific, where it surveyed deep-sea minerals, Greenpeace said.

The research was on behalf of UK Seabed Resources Ltd (UKSR), a wholly owned subsidiary of the US Glomar Minerals Inc, which has made clear it intends to begin commercial exploitation of the seafloor next year.

Glomar has said the mineral nodule sampling carried out aboard the Tangaroa will help secure critical mineral supply chains for the US.

Trump issued an executive order in April last year to fast-track commercial deep-sea mining in US and international waters.

This year, the US Government launched Project Vault, an initiative to secure a global supply chain and stockpile a reserve of minerals for military and industrial purposes.

The US administration is preparing to issue unilateral commercial permits for seafloor minerals.

The move would bypass the International Seabed Authority, where UN member states are negotiating the regulations that will guide deep-sea mining.

Glomar chief executive Chris Williams has publicly stated that seabed mining “is likely to proceed regardless” of international negotiations.

Using data gathered by the Tangaroa, Greenpeace said Glomar appears set to apply for a US commercial exploitation permit.

The Pacific region overwhelmingly rejects deep-sea mining, with 46 countries worldwide, including New Zealand, supporting an international moratorium.

Lee said the New Zealand Government appeared to be aligning itself with Trump’s “imperialist extractive agenda”, rather than standing with its Pacific neighbours.

The Tangaroa is no stranger to protest.

In 2015, Greenpeace activists occupied the vessel in protest at its use by the international oil industry to survey the waters of Aotearoa for deep-sea oil drilling.

“We have a long history of taking action when our Government has chosen to back international polluters over our oceans,” Lee said.

“Fair warning to them, we will not stand by while they make us complicit in US imperialism and this new wave of colonial extraction.”

More than 100,000 New Zealanders have signed an open letter to Foreign Affairs Minister Winston Peters calling for him to support a global ban on deep-sea mining, joining millions around the world who oppose it.

In 2022, the Government announced support for a conditional global moratorium on deep-sea mining.

Earth Sciences NZ and the Police have been approached for comment.

New Zealand Herald September 25, 2026

Dr Oliver Hartwich of The NZ Initiative says too many of the country’s business leaders are living in a "climate of fear".

Oliver Hartwich has put his finger on something rather uncomfortable.

The New Zealand Initiative director says too many of the country’s business leaders are living in a “climate of fear” – worried that speaking publicly against election policies which are anti-business and market interventionist could invite political retaliation.

In an open letter signed by 51 mainly NZ Initiative members, Hartwich argued New Zealand cannot attract the investment it needs if investors believe property rights, contracts and long-term business decisions can be overridden by political expediency.

He has a point.

But having subsequently spoken to a number of chief executives who were approached to sign the Initiative’s open letter on this score, I am not convinced the explanation is quite as simple as fear. Several told me, in effect: I may agree with the principle. But I don’t necessarily want to put my name to this particular political intervention.

Some are plainly concerned about being singled out by politicians who may later regulate their businesses. Others have a more prosaic reason for staying silent: they want to see what policies survive the election and, crucially, the coalition negotiations that follow it.

Others too, sit as Crown-appointed directors to listed companies – such as Meridian Energy, Genesis Energy and Mercury NZ – where public comment on the politically charged issue of separating the gentailers’ generation and retail arms could be seen to compromise their political neutrality during an election. Emphasis on “could”.

Take New Zealand First’s proposal to buy back BNZ from Australia’s National Australia Bank and merge it with Kiwibank to create a new Crown-owned National Bank of New Zealand.

It is a dramatic proposal. NZ First says the new bank would be commercially run and funded through a mixture of sovereign banking bonds, Crown debt, investment capital and Kiwibank’s existing capital.

But National has already rejected the idea. Cabinet Minister Chris Bishop said he’d seen estimates suggesting it would cost between $24 billion and $30b to buy back the bank (which NZ First disputes), with much of the cost paid through borrowing. Act is also opposed.

So why would a major business leader put their name to a public campaign against a policy that may never survive the coalition bargaining process?

There is another reason for caution.

New Zealand does need a more competitive banking system. The Commerce Commission’s 2024 market study found that ANZ, ASB, BNZ and Westpac did not face strong competition and described the market as a stable, highly profitable two-tier oligopoly.

It recommended measures to encourage greater competition, including a stronger Kiwibank and open banking.

So defending private property rights cannot become a convenient slogan for defending incumbent market power.

Of course, Governments should intervene in markets where there is compelling evidence of market failure, abuse of market power or a clear public interest.

The question is whether Governments should start rewriting the rules of private ownership and existing contracts because an intervention sounds attractive during an election campaign, which is the guts of Hartwich’s letter.

Competition law exists precisely because the market does not always police itself – the supermarkets are arguably a case in point.

National has said it would split Foodstuffs into New World and Pak’nSave; Labour would require Woolworths and Foodstuffs to operate their wholesale supply businesses independently from their retail stores, and the Greens would break up the “duopoly” requiring at least 120 stores and the distribution centre capacity to be sold into public ownership to form KiwiMart, a publicly owned supermarket chain with the mandate to prioritise affordability.

The public relations fightback is well underway.

But is there an issue?

The Commerce Commission last month signalled it would take legal action against Foodstuffs South Island alleging anti-competitive behaviour.

“The conduct we allege occurred deprives Kiwis of the best possible prices when shopping at their local supermarket and limits competition,” commission chair Dr John Small said.

“Under the franchise model, individual South Island Pak’nSave supermarkets are supposed to be able to compete on pricing, discounts and promotions.”

Instead, the commission alleges Foodstuffs South Island applied guidelines and rules that stopped independently owned and operated supermarkets from offering certain discounts unless they received prior approval.

The commission will argue that the alleged conduct constitutes resale price maintenance, which is prohibited under section 37 of the Commerce Act.

Resale price maintenance prevents retailers from setting their prices below certain levels. The commission says such conduct can limit competition and lead to higher prices.

These are allegations that will ultimately have to be tested through the legal process. But the case raises a broader question about the balance between central control and genuine independence within a franchise model.

Then there are the gentailers.

There is a cold, hard fiscal reason for the Government to think twice before dismantling the gentailers as business organisations including the Auckland Business Chamber have advocated.

Its 51% holdings in Mercury, Meridian and Genesis generated roughly $599.5 million in dividends in the year to June 2026.

There is of course a policy argument for greater competition, but structural separation has significant implications for investment and the electricity system.

In my view, there is an even bigger question: how comfortable should taxpayers be with a Government simultaneously acting as policymaker, regulator and majority shareholder?

That is not an argument for leaving business regulation unchecked. Quite the opposite. Competition law exists precisely because the market does not always police itself.

With retirement villages being forced to change contracts – another Initiative bugbear – a different and more fundamental question about certainty of contract is raised.

The counterview is that these are older New Zealanders who may have put virtually all their housing wealth into a retirement village and then discovered that getting their capital back can take many months.

Why shouldn’t Parliament be able to intervene where the regulatory framework has demonstrably produced an imbalance between residents and operators?

Retrospectively, cancelling lawful mining approvals raises an even sharper issue of sovereign risk. A mining permit gives an investor legal rights under a regulatory framework; but it doesn’t give the investor a permanent guarantee that Parliament can never change that framework – this is unfortunate but a fact.

There is a strong argument that New Zealand needs business leaders prepared to speak more openly about productivity, regulation, infrastructure, tax, investment and the long-term economic direction of the country.

We don’t need a business community that becomes so risk-averse that it no longer participates robustly in public debate.

But we also need politicians mature enough to hear criticism without treating the critic as the enemy.

On that score, the evidence is not yet overwhelming.

Whenua 2.0: Updated map, new histories showing Māori-Pākeha land deals in New Zealand

New Zealand Herald September 25, 2026

Wherever you live in New Zealand, there’s a story – but most of us have no idea what it is. Now we can find out. Two years after the Herald launched Whenua: Our land, our history, data editor Chris Knox updates the map of Aotearoa with official historical accounts and asks historian Rachel Buchanan what these Treaty settlement documents tell us about our national story.

If you’ve ever wondered about the history behind your home, town or suburb, you can now find it on a map covering most of New Zealand.

The stories behind each place – searchable on our updated Whenua map below – come from more than 80 historical accounts agreed between the Government and iwi under Treaty of Waitangi settlements in the last 30 years.

Between them, these historical records cover most of the country, except for a large portion of Northland, an area of Rangitīkei and part of East Cape, where there are still no settlements. In other areas, not every iwi with a historical interest has settled, but you can still see the accounts from tribes that have reached agreements.

To see a place’s land history, click on a location on the map or enter a place name in the search bar. (The accounts are extracted from the original documents as close to verbatim as possible.)

The stories on the map show how the Crown often purchased land for a pittance and ignored its legal obligations afterwards.

For example, if you live in the central suburbs of Auckland, such as Mt Eden, Mt Albert or Pt Chevalier, you can see how the Crown bought – and rapidly resold – those 5260ha (13,000 acres) of land from Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei for £200, four horses, 30 blankets, 10 cloaks, one tent and a desk.

Wellingtonians may be surprised to learn that prime land in the city was sold to prospective settlers in London by the New Zealand Company before it had even arrived in New Zealand.

In the South Island, Ngāi Tahu was protesting that the Crown wasn’t keeping its side of the bargain from as early as the 1840s.

And in Bay of Plenty, two men who led a military campaign that confiscated 991,148ha (245,000 acres) of land were appointed to rule on the legality of the seizure – they found it valid.

A common theme is that the Crown failed to uphold its end of the deal. For instance, the 2428ha (6000-acre) Kohimarama block in Auckland was purchased for £100, a boat, livestock, clothing, tools and dry goods. Ngāti Paoa testified that they were promised land at Saint Georges Bay as part of the purchase. The land was never set aside.

These accounts, agreed between individual iwi and the Government, have formed part of our official history since the treaty settlement process began in the 1990s.

Yet they haven’t filtered down into popular consciousness. In her account of Parihaka, Ko Taranaki Te Maunga, historian Rachel Buchanan wondered why.

Explaining how the process works, she wrote: “Employees of the Crown work with iwi employees [actually, more likely iwi volunteers] to research and write deeds of settlement, including negotiated historical accounts.

“The accounts are peer-reviewed by independent eminent historians.

“The deeds are signed and published on the Office of Treaty Settlements’ website ... and then what? ... Do schools teach them? Do textbooks refer to them?”

Buchanan, who is a member of Te Pouhere Kōrero Māori Historians Network, told the Herald the accounts were “most certainly worthy of a lot more attention and celebration” as they corrected a one-sided view of New Zealand history.

She described them as “as negotiated histories that draw on iwi understandings that can remain obscured or ignored in mainstream accounts”.

The accounts were not the way history was normally recorded, firstly because they were legal documents, Buchanan said.

“Each paragraph is numbered like a bit of legislation, and you don’t find that in any history book.

“That’s because they are actually produced through argument or debate and then they’re agreed upon.”

In the Taranaki and Parihaka agreements, she remembered “a really intense debate” over whether the word rape should be used – eventually it was.

“It is so unusual for history to be made in that way, but it reflects how things are done on the marae.”

The accounts range from the 69-line Waikato-Tainui account which begins with, “1863-1864 the Crown engaged in a war against Maaori [sic] in the Waikato [sic], causing suffering to the people there”, to more than 3000 lines for their Ngāti Maniapoto neighbours.

They paint a picture of a nation built on a slippery relationship with due process and contracts, with little to no respect for Māori ownership.

A common refrain in the historical account is problems arising from the “10-owner rule”. Māori traditional ownership of land was communal, but land-hungry settlers found this frustrating, as they often didn’t know who to deal with.

The 10-owner rule was the start of the Crown’s attempt to fit Māori land into the European land system. The Native Lands Act 1865, set up to create legal titles for Māori, only allowed a maximum of 10 owners for any given block of land. Often this meant the recorded owners were only a subset of those connected with the land.

Ngāti Tūwharetoa’s account says the iwi later “petitioned for the cancellation of their 10-owner title ‘because it is wrong that the Crown grant should have effect over the land of all the people, men, women, and children, we strongly object to that system’.”

“They appealed to have all the owners included on the title for the block, but were unsuccessful.”

In other cases, those who were listed as owners had little or no connection with the land. The Ahuriri Hapū account for the modern-day Napier area states, “In 1891, Pāora Kaiwhata recalled that at the first hearings, ‘The judges told us to go outside and choose 10 men for each block of land, and that the 10 would act for the people’.”

Surveying was also used by the Crown to encourage or force the sale of land. The Tūhoe account records, “the survey of Tahora 2 was conducted in secret, without authorisation and contrary to survey regulations. It was then approved by the Surveyor General, despite significant opposition from Tūhoe and other right holders. The unwanted survey cost the owners 16,658 acres [6741ha] of the block”.

The Crown often did not hold up its side of the bargain, particularly over promises to set aside land and build roads, schools and hospitals.

The Tūhoe account reveals that an important factor in the tribe’s original agreement was the promise of roads for the remote, bush-covered hills of Te Urewera in the eastern North Island. But the Government did not complete the roads, even though Tūhoe had contributed 16,187ha (40,000 acres) of land valued at £20,000, about $2.4 million today, for this purpose.

In Auckland, both Bishop George Selwyn and Governor George Grey recorded the Crown’s failure to carry out its obligations. Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei’s account records: “The Government’s failure to set aside money for the endowment fund was criticised by Bishop Selwyn, who stated: ‘By this fund, we hoped that schools, hospitals, hostelries, would be built; that every useful art would be taught; every habit of civilization [sic] introduced; and the whole social character of the people changed for the better ... I am sorry to be obliged to state that not one of these objects has been accomplished, or rather that not one has been attempted’.”

The same account also records that another “fund was not drawn upon until 1862, when part of it was used to build a bridge between Ōrākei and Remuera [which was also of general benefit to all Auckland residents]”.

About 15% of the North Island was confiscated from iwi who were “in rebellion” against the Crown. Some of this land was later returned when the confiscations were found to be excessive or taken from iwi who were not involved in the conflict, but the process of returning the land often created more problems.

Ngāti Awa’s account records that the Crown confiscated 99,148ha (245,000 acres) from the tribe, some from hapū who had no involvement in the conflict. A court was set up to compensate anyone who had “suffered land confiscation” when they hadn’t “been in ‘rebellion’”, but the two judges had both played important military roles on the Crown’s side of the conflict. Unsurprisingly, they found most of the confiscations were valid – a further injustice eventually acknowledged by the Crown in the settlement agreement almost 150 years later.

Similarly, Ngāti Tūwharetoa lost its Tarawera block (about 31,000ha or 76,700 acres) and the Tataraakina block (about 15,000ha or 37,000 acres) in the 1867 Mōhaka-Waikare confiscation but never got them back.

The central North Island tribe’s account reads: “Under the terms of the 1870 deed, these blocks were awarded to a small number of individuals from another iwi.”

Buchanan said the historical accounts were valuable as a snapshot in time but it was also helpful to look through a Māori lens, which viewed history as always evolving and changing.

“If you wrote a historical account now of the region in Wellington central, maybe there’d be some different observations,” she said.

“It’s something close to us all and I think that’s important for everyone. Whether you’re Māori, Pākehā or have a combination of everything – or something completely different – it’s an invitation to think about history as something living.”

Chris Knox is a scientist turned data-journalist who investigates the stories behind the numbers and creates interactives for Herald readers to explore them.

Hawke’s Bay vineyard lit up with 600 candles - no, it’s not an art show

New Zealand Herald September 25, 2026

The Smith and Sheth vineyard lit up with candles to prevent frost damage. Photo / Richard Brimer Photography

A Hawke’s Bay vineyard is using a relatively rare - but spectacular - technique to avoid frost damage.

A Smith and Sheth vineyard in Omahu, near Hastings, was lit up with 600 candles on Friday morning to fight a potentially harsh frost.

Professional photographer Richard Brimer has been trying to get a snap of the vineyard lit up for a couple of years, and was on hand to capture the remarkable sight.

Common ways to fight frosts include frost fans, spraying water over crops, or even deploying helicopters over orchards and vineyards.

Nick Paulin, national viticulturalist at Aotearoa NZ Fine Wine Estates, the parent group of wine company Smith and Sheth, said candles were more common in Europe to fight frosts.

“Those candles we actually imported from France.”

He said the main reason they used them was the shape of the 3ha Omahu vineyard.

“It’s a really odd-shaped block. It is a long rectangle.

“So to cover it with wind machines is not cost-effective, like we’d have to put in two wind machines for [only] 3ha to cover it.”

He said they did not have access to large amounts of water either, so could not use water to avoid frost damage.

He said the candles, which they purchased in 2022, were not common because they were so labour intensive.

It took three staff about 45 minutes to light all 600 candles, during the middle of the night.

“No one is going to put these things out on 100ha.”

The candles themselves are made of plant-based wax with a cardboard wick, and are moved around in steel buckets, and can be stored away when not required.

Paulin said the vineyard had alarms that trigger when the temperature drops to 1.5C, and staff are kept on standby.

If temperatures reach zero, it can seriously damage the crops, so prevention is required.

MetService recorded the temperature in Hastings dropped to 0.5C on Friday morning, and 1.3C in Napier.

The Smith and Sheth cellar door is located in Havelock North village.

Two people were so concerned by the sound of helicopters flying over Hawke’s Bay early on Friday morning that they called the police.

A police spokesman said reports of the helicopters came in from Hillary Cres in Maraenui at 12.30am and Ulyatt Rd in Meeanee at 2.20am.

In both cases, police made inquiries and determined the noise was from helicopters working to keep frost off fruiting plants, the spokesman said.

It was a busy night for orchardists, with this time of year crucial for keeping vulnerable fruit from getting frost damage.

Muay Thai brain injury survivor Isaac Chan plans charity run across New Zealand

New Zealand Herald September 25, 2026

Isaac Chan is determined to run the length of New Zealand a year on from receiving lifesaving neurosurgery after suffering a traumatic brain injury in his first Muay Thai fight.

The 25-year-old, Auckland-based doctor suffered bilateral subdural haemorrhages, which were slow bleeds on the outside of both sides of his brain, but he wasn’t aware of the extent of his injuries immediately.

“It was my first amateur Muay Thai fight,” said Chan.

“I came up against a very very good, very strong opponent. Had a really hard, scrappy fight and he landed quite a flush head kick at the end of the second round.

“Knocked me down, got back up, kept fighting, finished the fight. And it was nothing too acute really. I felt like I’d been knocked around a little bit.

“But as I said with the injury that I had, it wasn’t until quite a while later that I found out the extent of it.”

Symptoms included dizziness and headaches, but he felt it could have been an ear infection before the pain became so bad he had to admit himself to hospital, where they scanned his brain and discovered the bleeding.

“I was at home in Tauranga when I found out. I got flown up to Auckland to have neurosurgery, an operation which released all of the blood out from that area.

“And then from there it was just a slow and quite long and really difficult recovery.

“I had to start from, not quite square one, but I had to start from basics and I couldn’t do things like work and I couldn’t exercise.”

Chan said despite being a doctor, he found the entire experience isolating, scary and uncertain, with the mental side of recovery one of the toughest challenges.

“I was at home. I couldn’t do really anything physically for a while. I tried to keep busy with things like reading and just keeping my mind active.

“I guess recovery for me is also where I went to mentally and that was a really quite difficult and dark place.

“Having what felt like everything taken away and then facing the uncertainty of having a brain injury and what that looks like, that was a huge part of my recovery and I really didn’t know at the time that there’s charities like Brain Injury New Zealand and those sorts of things in place to help people through that sort of part of their recovery.”

Chan is attempting to run from Bluff to Cape Rēinga in January and hopes to raise $100,000 for Brain Injury New Zealand while creating awareness around what those with similar injuries might be going through.

“It’s really just the uncertainty and the unknown that’s the big thing for me.

“And that’s that’s what I want to help help raise the discourse around and help people that were in my position and that are feeling uncertain and don’t know what’s going on, just to have a little bit of hope and know that recovery is not linear and you can you can still go on to do great things.”

Chan said returning to work was a good feeling but running had been a particularly important outlet for him since the brain bleed.

“That started off being the only way that I could get back into things and physical activity.

“I started walking and started jogging and started running. And from that it’s grown into more of a tool that I can use to help do what I want to do and help push myself.

“I’m not fighting Muay Thai anymore after something like that and [running’s] much of the same really. There’s no one out when you’re in the ring, there’s no one out there fighting for you, and similar when you’re out on your runs, there’s no one out there running for you.

“So I think it’s for me it’s a really important tool just to push myself and help myself grow.”

The 25-year-old would slowly increase the distance he was running every time he went out and with his aim of running the length of New Zealand, he hopes to run a marathon a day.

“Stacking up 42km every day, I think would take about 60 days roughly on some rough math, but I think a marathon a day is the target.”

Chan plans to keep people updated on his progress on his “Run it back NZ” social media pages and show people who suffer brain injuries can still accomplish major achievements.

“I want to show myself that I can do something like this and it’s about taking accountability for what’s happened and wanting to make something cool from this experience that I was sort of agonising over for a long time and felt quite bitter and angry about.

“But then more than what I’m saying, it’s about helping and showing other people what you can do and doing it all in the name of a really good charity.”

He was also clear he won’t be making a return to the fighting ring.

“There’s always a desire and I’d love to do something like that, but I think protecting myself and after what’s happened I’ve got a different calling.

“As my coach said, I don’t have to be in the ring fighting anymore, so no more fights.”

More than 3300 bowel cancers detected after 3 million screening kits distributed

New Zealand Herald September 25, 2026

More than 40% of cancers detected through the national screening programme have been found at an early stage. Stock photo / 123RF

More than 3300 bowel cancers have been detected through New Zealand’s national screening programme after three million testing kits were distributed.

Health Minister Simeon Brown said more than 40% of the cancers had been detected early, when they could often be successfully treated.

The National Bowel Screening Programme began in 2017 and offers free screening to eligible New Zealanders.

The Government began lowering the starting age for screening from 60 to 58 last year, with the change being progressively introduced around the country.

Brown said 96% of newly eligible 58 and 59-year-olds had been invited to take part in districts included in the first stage of the rollout, which began in October 2025.

More than half of those newly eligible in the second group of districts had been invited since that rollout began on March 23.

So far, 1320 people have returned positive screening results under the expanded eligibility and 37 cancers have been detected.

“Every one of those 37 people would have had to wait another two years for a screening kit under the old age limit,” Brown said.

“Instead, their cancer has been found sooner, giving them the best possible chance of successful treatment.”

Budget 2026 included funding to lower the screening age again, from 58 to 56.

The Government estimates the change will make more than 200,000 additional New Zealanders eligible for free screening.

It is projected to prevent 638 cases of bowel cancer and save 522 lives over the next 25 years.

The Government ultimately intends to bring New Zealand’s eligibility in line with Australia.

In Australia, people aged 45 to 74 are eligible for screening every two years.

Those aged 45 to 49 can request their first free kit, while people aged 50 to 74 are automatically mailed one every two years.

A home test known as the FIT for symptomatic pathway rolled out nationwide in July for people experiencing possible bowel cancer symptoms.

Brown said the test was designed to help clinicians determine which patients most urgently needed colonoscopies, while freeing up specialist capacity as screening eligibility expanded.

“We are committed to lowering the bowel screening age to match Australia, and we will keep going as quickly and as safely as we can.”

New Zealand has comparatively high rates of bowel cancer internationally.

Ministry of Health advice last year described it as the country’s second-highest cause of cancer death, behind lung cancer.

Figures also show bowel cancer is now the leading cause of cancer-related death among New Zealanders under 50.

Dune 3 will be a hit, but there’s one mad version we’ll never get to see

Sydney Morning Herald September 26, 2026

Even the dreams of top directors get left on the cutting room floor. In some cases, it’s a blessing.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

This year’s much-anticipated touchdown of Denis Villeneuve’s third Dune film coincides with the 50th anniversary of the most valiant yet doomed attempt to bring Frank Herbert’s science-fiction epic to the screen. This earlier quixotic quest eclipsed even the interstellar ambitions of Villeneuve and his team.

In the 1970s, Chilean-French auteur Alejandro Jodorowsky embarked on an unhinged mission to shoot a Dune film equivalent to an acid trip. His assembled cast included Orson Welles, Gloria Swanson and Mick Jagger; Pink Floyd were on soundtrack duties; French illustrator Moebius and artist H. R. Giger (of Alien fame) designed the psychedelic visuals. Even surrealist grandmaster Salvador Dali signed on, demanding an hourly rate of $100,000. Jodorowsky’s script was 14 hours long, and the production “bible” he created stretched to almost 300 pages (a rare copy sold for $4.3 million – 110 times the expected figure – at Christie’s in 2021).

The film was too ludicrous to manifest in reality but it did spawn Jodorowsky’s Dune (2013), a wildly entertaining documentary tracing the making of a film that wasn’t made. Has there ever been another unrealised pipe dream so tantalising in its promise that other films have been made about it?

As it happens, yes. Jon Schnepp’s The Death of ‘Superman Lives’: What Happened? (2015) offers a glimpse of the monstrosity that might have been had Tim Burton directed his Superman movie with Nicolas Cage as the Man of Steel. Christopher Walken, Courteney Cox and Sandra Bullock were picked for supporting roles, the script was penned by Kevin Smith (Mallrats) and the whole fiasco was produced by Jon Peters, a former hairdresser who insisted that his Man of Steel wasn’t allowed to fly or wear the red-and-blue outfit, and that the film end with Superman fighting a giant spider.

These non-existent movies are just two of the countless unrealised projects that are like cinema’s dark matter: you’ll never see them but their sheer volume holds everything else together. Miles Davis is alleged to have said that great music is about the notes you don’t play; the films a director doesn’t make might be as important as those they do.

For most of his life Stanley Kubrick maintained an obsessive drive to create a film about Napoleon, even enlisting the support of 50,000 members of the Romanian People’s Army to re-enact battles. It wasn’t to be.

For every Basic Instinct or Starship Troopers Paul Verhoeven has directed, there are dozens of films he’s had to abandon: Tom Cruise as Houdini, the early years of Adolf Hitler, a take on the life of Jesus.

And who wouldn’t pay to see Luca Guadagnino’s American Psycho? Darren Aronofsky’s RoboCop? John Carpenter’s Top Gun, Fatal Attraction or Santa Claus: the Movie?

In an alternate timeline all of these exist. But history is haunted by the spectres of films that don’t. Some are the victims of overreaching ambition, while others are vanity projects best left unrealised. A depressing number find themselves wallowing in “development hell”, the industry term for productions that sink into an eternal cycle of script rewrites, studio changes and funding sinkholes.

Jon Peters – the aforementioned hairdresser-turned-producer (and one-time Barbra Streisand squeeze) – is the kind of colourful Hollywood character who can pave the way to development hell. After he attained the rights to Neil Gaiman’s classic Sandman series, he offered up what the author described as “quite easily the worst script I’ve ever read”. Again, there was the inexplicable inclusion of a giant spider (a dream Peters finally realised on 1999’s Wild Wild West, a film critics lambasted).

Some of the greatest hits (or likely misses) we can only imagine: Stanley Kubrick’s Lord of the Rings with Paul McCartney as Frodo and John Lennon as Gollum; Sofia Coppola’s The Little Mermaid, reportedly too dark and risky to finance; indie darling Lynne Ramsay’s unlikely foray into western territory on Jane Got a Gun, which was completed to lukewarm reviews by Gavin O’Connor; Spike Lee’s remake of Bruce Lee’s Enter the Dragon with comedian Ken Jeong in the kung fu king’s role; disaster master Roland Emmerich’s entry in the James Bond franchise.

The list of off-kilter choices to direct Return of the Jedi is enough to induce whiplash. Terry Gilliam would likely have spun off the series in an odd direction but just imagine what Davids Lynch or Cronenberg would have done had they said yes to the job.

And picture the iconic Wolverine played not by Hugh Jackman but by the notably less ripped Bob Hoskins, who was originally slated for the role in the first X-Men adaptation, then to be directed by Kathryn Bigelow.

Bigelow’s own filmography illustrates how the films that don’t get made are as illustrative as those that do. In the 1990s she headed up a string of genre classics, from erotic thriller Blue Steel to surfer heist caper Point Break. Post-9/11, though, she took a hard shift towards serious, politically provocative films such as The Hurt Locker and Zero Dark Thirty. Her catalogue of unrealised projects since that point drives home this career turn, full of titles such as Held by the Taliban, Mogadishu Minnesota and The True American.

Australian directors might struggle to get projects up here but the difficulty can scale up exponentially when they arrive in Tinseltown. Jocelyn Moorhouse’s adaptation of Murray Bail’s Eucalyptus was production-ready in 2005, featuring a dream team of Nicole Kidman and Russell Crowe, before Fox Searchlight canned the project.

Fellow Australian Peter Weir’s filmography may include Picnic at Hanging Rock, Dead Poets Society, The Truman Show, Witness and Green Card but many subsequent projects failed to gain traction and he eventually announced he was quitting the game.

Development hell is a place particular to big-name filmmakers, simply by virtue of their clout. Studios won’t pander to an up-and-comer whose ideas don’t wash but when a Kubrick or a Spielberg has a passion project, they’re not so easily dismissed. Ordering endless rounds of casting changes and screenplay revisions is a way to keep the big earners appeased without actually committing to their financially dubious hobby horses.

And sometimes the bean counters aren’t the villains of the story. Quentin Tarantino’s Star Trek, set in 1930s Chicago? Hard pass. Sylvester Stallone’s film about Edgar Allan Poe with himself in the lead? Nevermore! Francis Ford Coppola’s Megalopolis spent almost half a century in development hell; he ultimately financed the production himself, the result a sprawling mess that earned less than 10 per cent of its $120 million production budget.

Sometimes a dream is better left that way. Zack Snyder’s bombastic Hollywood fare – 300, Man of Steel, Justice League – has been box-office dynamite but after decades in development hell he finally self-produced his dream project, The Last Photograph. It debuted at the recent Toronto International Film Festival, with critics dubbing it “supremely indulgent auteur gunk”, “boring, bloated, brutally violent” and “an utter disgrace from start to finish … Snyder at his most unfiltered, with no studio intervention”. It’s about the notes you don’t play, Mr Snyder, and the giant spiders you keep to yourself.

It’s one thing for a passion project to go unrealised but another level of heartbreak awaits filmmakers who complete a work only for it never to see the light of day.

Coyote vs. Acme, completed in 2023, rated well with test audiences before Warner Bros Discovery decided to shelve it as a $30 million tax write-off. It took a concerted campaign by indie distributor Ketchup Entertainment (and a $50 million price tag) for the film to finally make it to screens. As of writing, it holds a 96 per cent score on review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes.

Few similar tales achieve such a happy ending. The DC superhero flick Batgirl featured a stacked cast including Leslie Grace (In the Heights), J. K. Simmons, Brendan Fraser and Michael Keaton returning to the suit he first squeezed into for Tim Burton’s 1989 Batman. The film was close to completion when Warner Bros Discovery cancelled its release and wrote off another $90 million tax-wise.

Other films have been consigned to the vaults for less financial reasons. The most famous is probably Jerry Lewis’ The Day the Clown Cried, in which a clown sent to a Nazi concentration camp attempts to offer hope to the children imprisoned there. After viewing a rough cut the co-writer declared it was unfit for public viewing and denied all rights for release.

James Franco’s The Long Home was completed in 2016, with a cast including Josh Hutcherson, Courtney Love, Ashton Kutcher and Josh Hartnett. Allegations of inappropriate sexual behaviour by Franco during the shoot, however, ensured that the finished film has never been publicly screened.

In 2009 Tony Kaye (American History X) completed a rough cut of post-Hurricane Katrina crime drama Black Water Transit but the work became a hot potato in a series of legal disputes that culminated in one of the film’s producers being sentenced to eight years in prison for fraud.

Some nearly finished films have been denied the fairytale rescue Coyote vs. Acme has enjoyed. The 2025 musical comedy-drama Golden had some serious talent flex: Michel Gondry directing, Pharrell Williams as co-producer and composer, and an all-star line-up including Janelle Monae, Missy Elliott and Andre 3000, but Universal Studios cancelled the film before it was released.

Coyote vs. Acme is in cinemas now.

Rock and roll, fantasy and Silicon Valley fascism: 10 new books

Sydney Morning Herald September 26, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

This week’s fiction includes a moving work set in the aftermath of the American Civil War to a world filled with magical animals, while non-fiction ranges across the local rock scene, the heroes and villains of history and WWII fighter pilots.

The Newer World by Sebastian Barry (Allen & Unwin $34.99)

Some may quibble that as a white Irishman, Sebastian Barry ought not to have the authorial right to adopt the voice of Tennyson Bouguereau, a black man navigating the messy aftermath of the Civil War. But if anyone can perform this act of cultural ventriloquism well, it’s Barry. The Newer World navigates the world of Tennyson, who, alongside his twin sister, was born into slavery but eventually freed, only to discover that freedom is not necessarily equivalent to acceptance in the deep American South. The newer world is not that much shinier than the old one. From rural Tennessee to Nashville, where Tennyson, with his beautiful voice, is given a chance to join a choir, and then to England when he goes on tour, and then back to America, Barry recreates the 19th-century period with vividness and colour. Written in the first person, this historical fiction is elegantly wrought. Like his poetic namesake, Tennyson’s descriptive mannerisms are filled with rhythmic, lyrical touches that can seem grandiose at times. But the narrative balances racism and trauma with hope and transformation.

Strange Familiars by Keshe Chow (Hachette, $34.99)

Two academic rivals at a College of Magical Veterinary Sciences battle it out: in the one corner is earnest and hard-working Gwendolynne Chan, and facing her is rich nepo baby Harrisford Briggs. The reader will be forgiving for thinking the novel will focus on cutesy and strange animals doing fantastic tricks before they become injured, but Keshe Chow leads the narrative elsewhere. Set in an alternate London, her world-building involves the pair trying to figure out why there’s excessive magic that turns the animal-familiars feral and also causes explosions in the city. They have to join forces to stop the surges. Strange Familiars is told through alternate viewpoints of the protagonists as they investigate competing organisations that distribute and oppose the global supply of magic. The enemy-to-lovers trope is predictable, with Chow at full rein in exploring the romantasy genre. It’s a fun read – the first instalment of a series of two, and Percy, Gwen’s snarky telepathic cat, is a joyful addition. If only there were more magical animals in the mix.

Female Life on Planet Earth by Laleh Khadivi (Oneworld, $32.99)

Set in Los Angeles, this novel is about secret lives and the relationships between mothers and daughters. It focuses on the year Heti spends after the death of her mother, Anahita. While she plans a large-scale mourning anniversary at the urging of her bossy traditionalist aunt, Heti receives a mysterious package containing photos of a younger Anahita, enveloped in a black veil and carrying a machine gun. The mother Heti knew and loved was sweet and nurturing – who was this fighter in combat mode? What follows is a series of conversational vignettes with strangers about what it means to be a woman. But too much time and energy are spent on such peripheral musings, with comparatively scant details about Anahita’s past only allowed to surface toward the end. Though the book obviously references revolutionary Iran, it’s odd that Laleh Khadivi refrains from mentioning the country. Perhaps she’s aiming for universality of themes about war, religious fanaticism, persecution, womanhood, diaspora, and immigration, but depersonalising the context does a disservice to the narrative.

Midwest by Caitlin Maling (Upswell, $27.99)

In this suite of poems, Caitlin Maling roams the coastal waters of Western Australia with a keen eye. Mailing grew up in and around Fremantle, and her love of the vistas around this port city is evident. Midwest, her sixth poetry collection, continues her exploration of the natural world, especially its watery depths and the animals that live or at least struggle to survive within or near the sea. As the Tour Guide at the Ocean Park Marina and Aquarium puts it, “Everything you see is food, sex or death.” Whether it’s sea eagles nesting, parrotfish pecking at coral, sea snakes copulating or crabs being cracked open to eat, Maling’s words are visceral and sometimes startling. There are shipwrecks, salmon farming and single-celled organisms called stromatolites among the mix. Among her descriptions of the birds and beasts, she also writes about motherhood and her young son. Sometimes Maling’s metaphorical reach will make you stop and consider the world anew – she describes rock as “breaking out of the earth like bones” and an octopus’ nodules like “Mardi Gras beads, but finer filigree.”

Gone Guru by Nadine Browne (Fremantle Press, $34.99)

Noni has flown into New York from WA and barely settled in her Harlem apartment when she discovers that her new flatmate, Vincent, a self-styled transcendental meditation guru with millions of followers and millions in a trust fund, has disappeared. Maybe he’s too busy trying to find himself? Though Noni has distractions of her own – she’s failing to combat imposter syndrome at a prestigious writing program – she becomes invested in finding him. Noni’s trying to think of a story for her class while navigating the strangeness of a new city; the missing Vincent may just be the catalyst she needs. Gone Guru is an auto-fiction, with Nadine Browne drawing on her own experiences. Partly a sleuthing story, with the clamour, colour, vibrancy, and characters of New York as a background, and partly an exploration into the challenges of being a creative writer (particularly with someone as intimidating as Joyce Carol Oates as a teacher), the book is an enjoyable and funny romp that surveys serious issues (race, class, identity, literature, culture) with a light touch.

A History of the World in 51 Heroes and Villains by Tom Holland & Dominic Sandbrook (Bloomsbury, $36.99)

History is, of course, about far more than heroes and villains, but they can be a lot of fun, as The Rest is History podcast team demonstrates in this collection of cameos. And they’re not all human, either. Like Wojtek, the Syrian brown bear adopted by the Polish army in exile during WWII, who lugged heavy crates of munitions up the slopes of Monte Cassino, Italy, during the Allied advance and made a highly valued contribution to the war effort. Much loved by the troops, and with a penchant for cigarettes and stealing women’s underwear, Wojtek eventually died in the Edinburgh Zoo, an undisputed hero with his own statue. Some of the other figures, however, aren’t so clear-cut. The mad monk, Savonarola, for example, lauded by some as a Reformationist hero combating excessive wealth and corruption, and reviled by others as a murdering, puritanical fruitcake. Then there are the mysteries, like Elizabeth 1. Was she really a virgin, or just good at “branding”? Incorporated into a tale that stretches from Roman times (Boadicea gets a guernsey) to the 20th century are potted biographies of the likes of US-born photographer, war correspondent and former model Lee Miller, who famously soaked herself in Hitler’s bath. Reading this is a bit like opening a packet of potato chips; once you start it’s really difficult to stop.

In the Realm of the Last Man by Francis Fukuyama (Profile, $45)

Francis Fukuyama is best known for 1989 essay The End of History, which, he argues in this combination of memoir and dissertation, was wrongly interpreted as a piece of neo-conservative triumphalism – at the same time, stating that he was part of the neo-conservative clique that included the likes of Irving Kristol. Since then, he’s changed his mind, left old alignments behind, and moved closer to the left. What happened? Two things: the Iraq invasion of 2003, which he opposed after concluding that the post-war period of reconstruction would be a disaster, and the GFC that followed not long after, and which led him to question and reject the twin neo-conservative precepts of largely unfettered marketplace capitalism and a strictly limited government role. He might still talk of “history” in quasi metaphysical, qualified Hegelian terms, but his engaging, plain-speaking essays demonstrate that the mind (not just history) is constantly evolving, that someone can break free of outmoded beliefs and world views to see things anew.

The Nerd Reich by Gil Duran (Simon & Schuster, $36.99)

Once upon a time, Silicon Valley was the home of nerdy, vaguely left-leaning liberals. All that has changed. These days it sits at Trump’s table and with sinister intentions. When Elon Musk waved a chainsaw around at a Conservative convention just after Trump’s second coming (the chainsaw symbolising ruthless cuts to government and bureaucracy), the New Yorker announced Techno Fascism comes to America. Journalist and political advisor Duran traces its rise from the late 1990s to the present day. And he paints a truly alarming picture of the world’s most obscenely wealthy men being invited into the Trump administration on a mass scale. These techno-oligarchs, he argues, aren’t content to work within the democratic system – they hate it, want to destroy and replace governments and countries with corporate city states. To counter it, he says, we need to “rethink our relationship with technology, which means rethinking what it means to be human”. Welcome to the new fascism and the “Nerd Reich”, funded by cryptocurrency, enabled by AI and run by oligarchs with deep-seated, anti-democratic, global ambitions.

It’s Not for You by Kelly-Dawn Hellmrich (Penguin, $36.99)

I confess I’d never heard of the band Camp Cope before – but I did bow out of the music scene in the late 1970s. All the same, I can recognise, in Kelly-Dawn Hellmrich’s combination of memoir and interviews with fellow women and gender diverse musos, the nitty-gritty of band life. Whether she’s recalling seeing Sarah Blasko in a Sydney café at 18 and interviewing her years later, watching a bouncer in Launceston beat the daylights out of a drunken kid (then make a pass at her), recognising the indigenous blood that flows through her, being told her bass playing wasn’t up to scratch or talking to veteran Marcia Hines about the early days, the key theme of being a woman (or just different) in what has always been a very blokey game, is authentically rendered, often with subtle poignancy that underpins the anger. Among other things, her description of being in a Collingwood share house and being asked to join Camp Cope is understated, immediate, and like the book itself, has the ring of the real thing.

Whispering Death by Patricia Skehan (Hachette, $34.99)

The eponymous death whisperer is the WWII Beaufighter, whose twin engines were so quiet they could sneak up on the enemy and not be heard until they were overhead – too late. In 2012, a former pilot from a Beaufighter squadron called the Green Ghosts (who served in the Pacific) approached Patricia Skehan with boxes of documents and a request that she write their story. Who could refuse? She chronicles the tales of the crews, incorporating their diaries (along with archival material) so that the story is often told in the first person. Mentioned also are the code-breakers (mostly women) who supplied such vital information – especially, using captured files, the de-cyphering of the supposedly unbreakable Japanese code. One for WW2 buffs.

What else is happening in the book world?

Three shots, a shopping trip and 14,000 hours of CCTV: The case against Beau Lamarre-Condon

Sydney Morning Herald September 26, 2026

This is what the jury has seen and heard in the trial of the former police officer accused of murdering Sydney couple Jesse Baird and Luke Davies.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

It was a seemingly unremarkable scene. Shortly after 9am on Monday, February 19, 2024, a man dressed as an Uber Eats rider, motorcycle helmet on and paper bag in hand, appears on a street in Paddington in Sydney’s eastern suburbs.

Within an hour, three gunshots will ring out in a terrace house nearby. The apparent delivery rider, captured in CCTV footage of the street, was the then-NSW police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon, a Supreme Court jury has heard. He was also the alleged gunman.

The Crown alleges that Lamarre-Condon stood in his disguise on the street for about 20 minutes, “steeling himself for what he was about to do”.

Shortly before 10am, it alleged, he used his police-issued Glock pistol to kill Sydney couple Jesse Baird, 26, and Luke Davies, 29, in Baird’s share house, before cleaning the scene and disposing of their bodies in surfboard bags.

Lamarre-Condon, 31, a former senior constable, has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder. His criminal trial started in Sydney on Monday and is expected to run for up to 12 weeks.

The prosecution case is that Lamarre-Condon murdered Baird, a former Network Ten producer and presenter, after developing an “obsessive and jealous infatuation” with him that escalated when Baird ended their casual relationship in November 2023.

Davies, a Qantas flight attendant, was Baird’s new boyfriend. The court heard the two men were “smitten”. “It was the real deal,” a friend told the court.

The murder of Baird was premeditated, according to the opening address by Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC. The accused’s preparatory steps allegedly included buying a surfboard bag two days before the killing to store his body.

The prosecution alleged that the murder of Davies was not planned but that Lamarre-Condon shot him to eliminate a witness to his crime.

At 9.49am and 33 seconds, the prosecution said, the first gunshot was heard in CCTV footage from a neighbouring property, followed by another 4 seconds later.

At 9.50am and 28 seconds, the third shot was heard.

The defence does not dispute that the then-police officer was wearing the Uber Eats disguise, or that he was at the home when the men died from gunshot wounds.

The defence case is that he went to Baird’s home to collect some of his belongings after the break-up, but he expected nobody would be home.

He “disguised himself … so he could masquerade as a delivery person if anybody unexpectedly opened the door”, his barrister, John Stratton, SC, said in an opening address to the jury.

The Crown alleges that Lamarre-Condon shot Baird twice in the kitchen of the home, including an execution-style shot through the temple, and shot Davies through the door of the bedroom after he called Triple Zero.

The defence case is that the then-police officer, still in disguise, was surprised by Baird once he entered the home after nobody answered his knock.

The two men struggled, the defence says, and the accused’s gun went off twice, fatally wounding Baird. The gun was flung into the loungeroom.

Lamarre-Condon picked up a mobile phone and started calling Triple Zero, the defence says. Davies was holding a knife and also grabbed the gun, according to the defence, and shot himself accidentally in a second struggle.

The Crown case is that Lamarre-Condon engaged in a series of obsessive behaviours in the months before killing Baird, including using his position as a police officer to obtain footage of Baird on a date with another man in May 2023.

The court has heard that Baird broke up with Lamarre-Condon for the first time in April 2023, and the accused was disappointed that he did not want a serious relationship. The two men resumed seeing each other briefly in late 2023 before Baird ended it permanently in November.

Lamarre-Condon is charged with breaking into Baird’s home in August 2023, after the first break-up, and stealing Baird’s wallet and phone.

He has pleaded not guilty to aggravated break and enter. The defence case is that he used a key Baird had given him to enter the home.

Baird reported the alleged break-in at the time and said he had woken shortly before midnight to a man standing over his bed. Investigating police took a photo of a bobby pin in the lock of Baird’s home, tendered in evidence in the trial.

During the first week of evidence, the court heard from a series of witnesses about Lamarre-Condon’s posts on social media about Baird.

One professional acquaintance testified that Lamarre-Condon told her he would post photos on Instagram that were not visible to Baird but could be seen by a select audience of potential romantic rivals.

The images gave the impression that he was in a relationship with Baird.

The posts were designed to send the message that he and Baird were “together and to back off, basically”, the witness said.

She said Lamarre-Condon had posted a photo of a bouquet of flowers with a caption designed to suggest Baird had sent them to him while he was in Melbourne.

“I said: ‘That’s crazy,’” she told the court. “He said: ‘It works.’”

Text messages tendered in court show Lamarre-Condon claimed the flowers were a gift for his mother from his stepfather when Baird asked him for an explanation.

Another witness gave evidence on Friday that Lamarre-Condon admitted to her that he had “staged the photo” of the flowers. She said he also used her phone to pose as her to send Baird a message on Instagram after their break-up that claimed, falsely, that he had cancer.

Baird broke up with Lamarre-Condon permanently after the Instagram post about the flowers, the court heard. “I would appreciate it if you could refrain from contacting me,” he said in a text message tendered in court.

On Friday, a close friend of Lamarre-Condon said he had asked her over for dinner in May 2023: “What would you do if I told you I killed somebody? Would you help me hide the body?”

She said she froze and replied: “No, because I don’t want their ghost to haunt me.”

She said Lamarre-Condon “kind of laughed it off” and said, “Don’t worry, I didn’t do that, but I did do something crazy”.

Furthermore, she testified that Lamarre-Condon told her that he had been watching Baird from outside his house, using his mother’s car and wearing a black hoodie.

“In that time he’d seen Jesse have sex with other men,” she said he told her.

She said the accused also claimed that he saw Baird over the back fence taking photos with friends with a Polaroid camera he had given him.

Lamarre-Condon told her he kept watching until Baird left the home and saw where he left his key.

“He [said he] went and got the key and unlocked the door, broke into the house, he stole the Polaroid camera, he ate Jesse’s Easter egg, and he said that there was something else that he did, but he wouldn’t tell me what it was, which concerned me,” she said.

The Crown has played the jury a series of compilations of 14,000 hours of CCTV footage from 200 locations, including from a sports store in Westfield Miranda where the accused bought a large surfboard cover with a friend on February 17, 2024, two days before the alleged murders.

The Crown has foreshadowed that the court will hear evidence that Lamarre-Condon asked whether his friend would fit inside the surfboard bag.

The friend allegedly replied “probably not”, according to the prosecution’s opening address to the jury, and the accused said: “I’ll grab this one instead, it should be big enough.” His friend is not accused of wrongdoing.

The Crown alleges that Lamarre-Condon bought a second surfboard bag on February 19 after the alleged murders, for Davies’ body, and two more on February 21 when he discovered the first two bags were too small.

The defence case is that Lamarre-Condon panicked and dumped the men’s bodies in the bags in Bungonia, near Goulburn.

“He was a police officer, and he knew this looked bad,” his barrister, Stratton, said in his opening address.

Stratton submitted that the accused’s actions after the men died – leaving the bodies near a Greek monastery, after a failed attempt to sink them in a dam – were “not the actions of a man who believed that he was guilty of murder”.

Rather, they were the actions of a man who had “panicked considerably, who knew the gravity of the situation that he was in and how it might be perceived and was overawed by it”.

The trial continues.
