Life inside the world’s most famous private school

Sydney Morning Herald September 26, 2026

Tailcoats, tuck shops, dames and divs: what can Prince George expect at Eton College?

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Coming off the motorway out of Slough, Archie* marvelled at the miles and miles of playing fields whizzing past on the left. “I don’t think I’d ever seen that many pitches in my life,” he said. A sports-mad, nervous 13-year-old, he took in this expanse of emerald green that was to be his making over the next five years: a whirlwind of rugby, football, “field game” and “wall game” (more on which later). As he zoomed over Windsor Bridge, his new world unfurled before him: Chapel, the red brick wall and College. Eton College, to be precise.

“I had a lot of adrenaline. My heart was going crazy. I was terrified,” says Archie, a recent Old Etonian (OE), now aged 23, of his first day at the world’s most hallowed private school.

The Berkshire campus is, after all, a rarefied bubble of educational privilege, typified by its grown-up-looking boys in tailcoats. Founded in 1440 by King Henry VI, today it hosts 1345 boarding boys aged 13-18, for a fee of £21,891 ($41,200) per term, with three terms per academic year. Around 20 per cent of the pupils are on up to 100 per cent bursaries, and “probably about 40 per cent come from families for whom the word ‘school’ means Eton,” says insider Michael* – a current Eton parent and OE who knows the school inside and out. “But the mix is far wider and more international than ever it was.”

When you’re not sixth generation (and maybe even when you are), nerves are par for the course. But first-generation Archie attests, on arrival, that he was thrown instantly into a game of football and came out muddy, tomato-red and buzzing.

And now, school’s back. Last month, 250 apprehensive first years began their scholastic careers. Among their number are illustrious names from many nations. But one in particular is historic: Prince George, heir to the British throne. He is following in the footsteps of his father, the Prince of Wales, and no fewer than 20 UK prime ministers. Aside from political beasts (Boris Johnson, David Cameron, Harold Macmillan), there have been literary greats such as George Orwell, tech giants, Olympic stars and grand aristocratic names.

“The reason I think Prince George’s parents particularly liked Eton,” says Michael, “is that Prince William, when he was there, felt he could be very much himself. [Because of that] he made so many friends that have stayed with him. [For George, like William] there will be no special treatment: he’ll just be a normal boy.”

Indeed, being a well-connected scion or an heir – even to the throne – does not entitle you to popularity at Eton. In order to become a BNOC (big name on campus), you have to have something more than a rich or royal father. No one cares who your parents are, because almost everybody’s parents are someone. One has to earn their place at the top; and that is a question of character.

“The BNOCs were never the people with a famous parent,” says Archie. “It would be people who established themselves as such. It’s the people who see themselves as the bigger characters.” Quite often, he explains, the best sportspeople were also incredible academically, which helped their reputation.

Regardless, “Prince George will receive not just the finest education in the world, but possibly the broadest,” explains Tori Cadogan, editor of Tatler’s prestigious annual Schools Guide. “Of course, academics are excellent, with 78.2 per cent of A-levels achieving A-A* in 2025 resulting in 52 Oxbridge offers. But it’s the co-curricular, with their outstanding facilities that really sets Eton apart.

“For the famously sporty Wales family, Prince George is in the perfect place,” Cadogan continues. After all, the Prince and Princess of Wales are known sports lovers, and as a primary school student George has been said to be just as keen, participating in triathlon, football, rugby and field hockey.

“The fabulous new indoor sports centre, known as Coleman’s, has recently opened, featuring a six-court sports hall, eight squash courts, an athletic development suite, a climbing wall, and enhanced training and wellness facilities,” Cadogan adds. “This is along with the new Athens Centre, housing the incredible swimming pool and indoor basketball court.” Not to mention the 38 football and rugby pitches, 19 cricket pitches, 56 tennis courts, a nine-hole golf course and two-kilometre Olympic rowing lake at Dorney. It’s Disneyland for sportsmen.

What else awaits George and his peers on campus? First years move into F Block – which is not a singular block, but refers to groups of 10 new pupils spread out in each of the 25 boarding houses across campus – a day before their seniors return. Each house has a historic name (such as Godolphin, Villiers and Walpole), rendered somewhat useless by the fact they are referred to contemporaneously by the initials of their master. One of Eton’s many idiosyncrasies.

Each house also has a dame, Eton’s version of a matron, usually the wife of the house master. She is – among many other things, I’m told – often the arbiter for the appropriateness of posters in dorm rooms. Football team or girls in tennis gear are usually OK. Nudity or vulgarity, not.

On day one, students move into their rooms (Etonians are afforded the luxury of a single room to themselves from the start), where beds have custom long and skinny mattresses, and are welcomed by a tea party thrown by their housemaster and dame.

“It’s the first time where people can eye each other up and see what the other nine are like,” says Michael. “You always get a very interesting mix of parents, some of whom know the place quite well, and some for whom it’s all new.” This has been the birthplace of many future power bromances – and surely where George will find his first tribe away from home.

Day two begins with guided visits. Eton, like a village, sprawls over half a mile (800 metres), with lessons (“divs”) in buildings as far as 10 minutes apart. “Etonians tend to walk about 15 per cent faster than anyone else you’ll ever go on a walk with again,” says my insider. The youngsters will have to watch out, too: Judy’s Passage, which runs through the centre of the college, becomes an unruly ruckus between divs, as time is spare and the older boys “tend to throw their weight around”, says Archie. The young ones may have to duck and dive out of the way.

George will soon become familiar with things like “Burning Bush” – the Victorian street lamp in Eton town where everyone meets up. The high street is “fabulously old-fashioned”, says Archie. Very important are the two tuck shops, Rowlands and Tudor Stores. “Rowlands sells chips, ice-creams, sweets and sandwiches. And Tudor Stores, on the edge of the high street, is considered to have the best ice-cream in the school,” says Michael.

The F-blockers will already be familiar with any one of its tailors (Tom Brown, Welsh & Jefferies, New & Lingwood, Billings & Edmonds), where they will have recently been measured for two sets of tails, waistcoats and trousers. “It’s very untouched, very old-school, but it’s not a Savile Row experience,” says Archie. “It’s like you walking into a dry cleaners, but every single thing on the shelf is tailcoats, because all the tailors also handle the cleaning. There’s no cigar lounge in the corner.”

That evening, they will learn how to apply the stiff collars with studs, as taught by the dame. “It normally takes about three attempts to learn how to do it, then after that it becomes second nature, and you can do it in three seconds flat,” says Michael.

By the third day, George and his contemporaries head to College, the oldest part of the school, where the Provost, Nicholas Coleridge (descendant of Samuel Taylor), ultra charming and ultra connected after decades in leadership at Condé Nast, gives a speech. I’m told last year he advised “finding two or three things that you particularly enjoy doing and doing them”. And goodness do they have choice: sports, theatre, painting, drawing, debating, student journalism, theology …

There are some early trials, too – including a mandatory singing test for Eton’s three world-class choirs. “Some boys are very keen to get in and some are very un-keen to be chosen, so they sing badly on purpose,” chuckles Michael. And in classes, which start around day three for the youngsters, the masters (or “beaks”) treat pupils in a very adult way: “You feel like they’re talking to an equal even though they have, like, three PhDs,” says Archie. It is perhaps one of the reasons the OEs leave with such applicable confidence.

Soon, the rhythm of the day will kick in. An alarm bell rings throughout the house every five minutes from 7.15am to 7.30am, by which time everyone must be at breakfast, which, on a normal day, is cereal, toast, eggs, beans and bacon, and on Sundays is a full-English-style fry-up. Breakfast is followed by Lower Chapel for the first two years, then they move into the famous big Eton Chapel. It’s a 10-minute morning service, with one hymn and a prayer: “Usually 19 out of 20 boys are sitting alert and to some extent listening, then the 20th has his head resting on a hymn book, and clearly half-asleep,” says the insider. But all agree, even for the non-religious, it is the tradition most missed on departure.

Five 40-minute-long divs in the morning are split by Chambers (elevenses – “A morning snack of cheese on toast or a sausage roll,” says Archie. “Occasionally, we’d get a slice of square pizza”) and followed in the first two terms by two hours of intense sport. First years in their first term must choose either rugby or football, but as they get older, more choice opens up. There are two more divs before EW (extra work) and then dinner; for some, in house, and for others, in a communal canteen. “Everyone would pile in and suddenly the noise was a million decibels,” says Archie. ”Then it falls dead silent and the housemaster gives grace.”

A hearty meal has been well-earned by this point, which is why, according to one OE, scandal arose one Friday when a new chef decided to do “healthy” fish ‘n’ chips. “There was outrage,” says the OE. “We’re used to having a big battered cod, big chunky chips, mushy peas, just slopping on a plate. And then you come in and it’s this little pale, white, uncouth boiled cod and new potatoes … We started a food committee after that.”

George might also find himself pulling into the illicit world of snack trading. As one insider told me: “A healthy supply of tuck equalled trading power. One student had a fake can of Heinz baked beans that the bottom came out of, and kept the keys in there for his tuck box. He’d exchange a bar of chocolate to make his bed; four slices of toast to take his tails to the cleaning rack.”

And of course, Eton would not be Eton without its unique sports – wall game and field game, early iterations of rugby and football. “Some people think it’s a very good game, but it must be said it never caught on at any other schools,” says the Eton insider. Nevertheless, for those in a sporty house, winning the annual Ties championship in either sport is the pinnacle of success. For others, it will be top grades and others again learning the ability to debate like a great.

“It is a very great privilege to attend such a physically beautiful school,” concludes Michael. “It’s got something slightly more sophisticated in the air, and that often rubs off on a number of the boys.” And, indeed, not one but now two future kings.

* Names have been changed.

She’s loved by millions of Australians but in her darkest moment, Magda Szubanski chose to be on her own

Sydney Morning Herald September 26, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

For four decades, Magda Szubanski has made us laugh. She’s as much a public figure, whose various comedic facets range from the purse-lipped Chenille, the chain-smoking Lynne Postlethwaite or the forlorn Sharon Strzelecki, as she is a familiar and beloved extension of our collective family.

But the very funny world of Magda Szubanski became very serious on May 5, 2025. “I remember the date, I’ll never forget it,” Szubanski says. “I know this sounds bizarre, but I felt relief because I had been so unwell. I think I was in a state of shock for about two months. I cried, also. I was just all over the place emotionally.”

Less than a month later, she went public with her diagnosis of a rare, aggressive blood cancer. “I won’t sugar-coat it: it’s rough,” she wrote at the time. “But I’m hopeful. I’m being lovingly cared for by friends and family, my medical team is brilliant, and I’ve never felt more held by the people around me.”

Flash forward to the present and Szubanski, 65, is in “deep remission”, has a new book, I Can’t Tell You But I Will, coming out and sits down to speak to Good Weekend with an enthusiasm and ebullience which is familiar to us all. She’s here and pulling no punches.

The public response to the diagnosis was, in many ways, testament to the significance of the contribution she has made to our cultural lives. There was genuine affection for her, and genuine shock to see a woman synonymous with laughter face the quiet gravity of mortality.

“I am so touched by it,” Szubanski says of the reaction. “It’s such a precious, beautiful thing. I don’t understand it fully. I don’t know why. Why me? I don’t really know. I don’t think you can ever. No one’s ever managed to figure out what that thing is. Part of it is just hanging around long enough.

“And it’s strange in a lot of ways because, really, I wasn’t born here. Look at my name. But that is so Australian, isn’t it? And it moves me really deeply. The response was like this tsunami of love. And I swear to god, I think that helped me. I really do. People were so lovely.

“After I had completed the chemo and I was up in Sydney, this tradie guy comes up, and says, ‘Just checking, you all right?’ Yep. ‘Good, good.’ Things like that give me goosebumps now, that people would care. And it makes me want to cry. It does make me cry, doesn’t it, clearly?

“How do you explain it,” she says, wiping away tears. “It’s such an extraordinary feeling to be on the receiving end of that. It really is. And I’m very grateful. I don’t know why. I don’t know why me. I don’t know what it is I do. But boy, am I thankful for it.”

In part, perhaps, our shared adoration stems from exactly that: that Szubanski is neither prophet nor politician. In her novel Middlemarch, author George Eliot wrote that the world was “partly dependent on unhistoric acts”, a literary genuflection to the quiet labours of those whose efforts, or sometimes mere presence, makes it easier for the rest of us.

Szubanski leaned into the same idea in the foreword of her new book, with a dedication to her mother Margaret, whom she describes as “an unhistoric woman”. But in truth, the same could apply to Szubanski herself, a woman whose contribution to the national sense of humour has kept many of us smiling for most of our lives.

“Our lives are a bit easier because of all those unhistoric men and women,” Szubanski says. “Mum was one of them, just a simple but extremely complex Scottish working-class lassie. She’d be 102 now if she was alive. I love to be able to acknowledge those people who don’t normally get credited, but who really shape so much of life.”

In a way, too, Szubanski’s most famous fictitious avatar – Sharon Strzelecki, the deeply put-upon, almost cripplingly lonely second-best friend to spoilt princess Kim Craig (née Day) in Kath & Kim – is the greatest expression of that idea. Her enthusiasm is boundless and she yearns to belong, but belonging seems to elude her. She’s all of us, in the myriad ways we try and never quite feel like we fit.

“She’s the spirit of thankless volunteerism,” Szubanski says, of the character, created when she was playing baseball and realised so many people who kept the machinery going – umpires, coaches, captains and field workers – were unpaid. “They keep the wheels turning, these people; they’re so important for society and for community,” she says.

The story of Magdalene Mary Therese Szubanski seems quintessentially Australian. Like many of us, her family came from somewhere else (she was born in Liverpool, England). And she grew up in the suburbs of Melbourne at a dinner table with a World War II Polish resistance fighter and an Irish and Scottish stoic. Family meal times? Complicated, she says, smiling.

Both of Szubanski’s parents were affected by war: her mother’s father “was a very funny, extremely traumatised man, horrendously so. By the time he was 16, he’d lost 10 brothers and sisters to poverty, and his father. And then he ended up at the Somme and Passchendaele in the First World War, where a lot of Australians were.”

As an adult, Szubanski came to understand her parents’ often hidden frailties. “Between [Mum’s] father, my father, and her own traumas, I think she tried to transcend her damage,” Szubanski says of Margaret. “She had that courage that she could look at her faults and flaws in a way with an honesty that I really admire, that not many people can, but she just couldn’t get the trajectory to get out of it because they didn’t have the tools.

“So growing up was a combination of fighting and hilarity and warmth and some cruelty thrown in there, too, and harshness and a lot of love, but just all of that. It was not straightforward. People parent very, very differently now. But also, poor bloody Mum, she got here and not a year later, my father was diagnosed with a very, very serious cancer. So she had a lot to deal with – they both did.”

At the tender age of 11, the future echo of Sharon Strzelecki was already emerging. Szubanski was a talented junior tennis player and competed in the Victorian School Boys and School Girls Championships at Kooyong. It was there that she met another competitor, Margaret Cecilia Louise – or Marg – Downey. “We met and we just clicked, we absolutely clicked,” Szubanski says.

They drifted in and out of contact and then reconnected at the University of Melbourne. “But by then, I was a radical lesbian feminist working in a women’s refuge, and she was at the Catholic college [and wearing] Laura Ashley.” Still, the foundation stones were laid for a friendship that has carried them throughout their lives. The gift with purchase for the rest of us: a string of critically acclaimed, fan-adored comedy masterpiece collaborations, including The D-Generation, Fast Forward, Big Girl’s Blouse and Kath & Kim.

I met Szubanski and Downey for the first time – along with their future Kath & Kim co-stars Jane Turner and Gina Riley – on the set of Fast Forward in the 1990s. That show was artistically significant not only because it popularised a number of Szubanski’s most memorable characters, including serial complainer Lynne Postlethwaite (imported from The D-Generation), ditzy sports reporter Pixie-Anne Wheatley and, with Downey, Chenille and Janelle, the hosts of an over-the-top morning TV advertorial show.

“She was a star in the making,” Downey says of Szubanski in that period, when Australian comedy was undergoing a bold transformation. The D-Generation itself paved a path for everyone from Rob Sitch, Santo Cilauro, Tom Gleisner, Michael Veitch and, later on radio, Jane Kennedy. And as part of the group drifted into Fast Forward, the others evolved into The Late Show, the production company Working Dog, and a range of projects from Frontline to the film The Dish.

“We just got each other’s humour,” says Downey of her friendship with Szubanski. “We could bounce off one another and we just started writing a lot of sketches together and performing them. We were from very different worlds, to be honest. In a funny kind of way, we were an odd couple, and to this day we’re a bit of an odd couple.”

In 2006, Szubanski ventured onto the stage as William Barfée in the Melbourne Theatre Company production of the hit Broadway musical, The 25th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee. The production starred Marina Prior, Tyler Coppin and David Campbell. Szubanski’s casting was bold – the role had always been played by men. The production also introduced Szubanski to Campbell, a pop and jazz recording artist who cut a swathe through musical theatre on his way to becoming a television host. Szubanski had expected him to be a “rock ‘n’ roll kind of guy”, but was immediately charmed by his easy manner. “He’s also soulful and funny and warm and loving, and he’s just a great guy,” she says.

Later, when Szubanski saw Campbell talking to British stage actor Lisa Hewitt, she decided to play matchmaker. “She was completely involved in making this happen,” Lisa – now Lisa Campbell – says. “When I returned to the UK, and said [a long-term relationship] is unrealistic, she said, ‘This is special, you need to fight for it.’ ”

Campbell and Hewitt married in 2008 – Szubanski was a bridesmaid – and the couple have three children, Leo, now 16, and twins Billy and Betty, now 11. Szubanski is Betty’s godmother; a very powerful relationship, the couple say.

Magda has “a beautiful, maternal” response whenever kids talk about an achievement, Lisa says. “Magda will always say how proud she is of that achievement but reminds them that she loves them without it.”

It is also the heart of why Szubanski is so universally beloved. “Magda makes us laugh at ourselves and her at the same time,” David Campbell says. “It was never that she was the butt of a joke. We were all the joke. And that’s a very Australian way of doing comedy. Then, after a while, the caricatures, like Kath and Kim, become real. And now there’s a generation of people who speak like that.”

At about the same time, Szubanski shifted into the realm of soft politics, becoming the face of the campaign for same-sex marriage. A 2017 national postal survey gauging support returned a result of 61.6 per cent of voters in favour of marriage equality and in December the same year, the Marriage Act was amended to allow it. But the campaign was divisive. And, at times, it seemed like Szubanski shouldered more than her fair share of the effort. “You become like an avatar,” she says. “You’re speaking on behalf of a group of people who don’t have a voice, or aren’t heard, or they can’t express themselves. So it was nerve-wracking.

“But you have to be a unifying person. I wanted to bring people along. I wanted to message it in a way that wasn’t polarising. It wasn’t politicised. It wasn’t allied particularly to a political party. It felt owned by a lot of people. When the announcement came, all I felt was relief – joy, of course, but the primary emotion was relief, [that] we hadn’t f---ed it up.”

In 2025, before Szubanski faced that life-changing diagnosis, she dealt with crippling pain and disturbing, vivid dreams that repeatedly pulled her out of sleep. “They kept waking me up in the middle of the night going, ‘There’s something really wrong.’ My body was obviously on alert,” she says. “And then a few months before [the diagnosis], the dream started saying, ‘You’re dying, you’re dying.’ ”

Szubanski pushed her doctors for more tests. When the results came in, the conversation was short and to the point. She was on her own. “There were a number of people I could have taken with me, but I don’t know, sometimes I’m quite independent,” she says. “I went in and she said, ‘Well, there is something there.’ I said, ‘Is it cancer?’ She said, ‘Yes, it’s cancer.’ ”

As Szubanski began to grasp the seriousness of her particular cancer – an incurable, relapsing lymphoma – “that it might be just a matter of ... if it wasn’t going to be months, but maybe years, not that long. I went into shock,” she says. “I immediately started texting and she’s telling me the thing and I’m texting my friends.”

And then she did what she always does in a challenging situation: she called Marg. “I just remember saying, ‘Oh no, no.’ She was just incredibly openabout it,” Downey says, “and she said, ‘Look, Marg, it’s not one of the good ones.’ And she didn’t know how long she would have or whether the treatment was going to work. I think she had to do a deep dive into how she was going to handle it and what treatment she would go with.”

Such experiences profoundly reframe a friendship. They also reshape your sense of what really matters in life. “We talk about death, we talk about dying, we talk about our thoughts about what might be beyond this life,” Downey says. “Going through something like Magda is going through has really made us discuss issues that we wouldn’t have even dreamt about when we were young or when we were at university, having to confront all sorts of pretty heavy stuff.”

Has Downey contemplated her life without Szubanski’s friendship in it? “I have,” she says. “That would be an incredibly sad time because I think Magda knows me better than most people – not every single secret, but she’s across most things – and to have that shared history since childhood is pretty special.” She would also miss the laughter. “There aren’t many people, I don’t know whether you feel this – but where you have a sort of shorthand with one another and one word can trigger hysterical laughter or a ‘remember that?’. We have so many shared memories.”

When Szubanski told the Campbells, the trio made the decision not to conceal anything from the children. “[We’ve] always been as honest as possible,” Lisa says. “The way that she’s been able to describe [the diagnosis and the treatment] to us has been so helpful for us to understand. And that clarity has been great for our kids to understand, too.”

Szubanski found her own understanding by pouring her thoughts and emotions into her manuscript. A line in the foreword notes: “writing the book will force me to look at things I don’t want to see and remember things.”

“It’s not a biography, it’s a memoir, but it’s about the sort of feelings of things,” she says. “And so there’s some stuff that I talk about, especially towards the end, that’s extremely painful. A little bit of me is like, ‘Jesus, girl, you got cancer, do you really need to make yourself feel those feelings?’ But my natural instinct is just to blab the truth, and I say that from the get-go.”

So, I ask Szubanski, where are we today? We have friends in common and I have followed, at least indirectly, her health journey in some detail. For a time, there was chemotherapy and crushing fatigue. Now, as we are talking, the sparkling, instinctively hilarious Magda we know and love is very much in the room. The same week as our interview, she is in the studio recording the audiobook. And I’m aware she’s only just fighting fit and will need to rest at some point.

The short answer is this: the median rate for relapse is four years, depending on potential treatments, and the median survival rate is about eight or nine years. “But that’s improving [and] honestly, it can change at any time. It’s definitely going to shorten my life. It could shorten it quite significantly. I don’t know. If I get to 75, I’ll be bloody thrilled, but if I get to 70, I’ll also be thrilled. But for the moment, touch wood, achieved deep remission.”

And the laughter isn’t going to stop. As we talk, our conversation shifts into my quoting old D-Generation and Fast Forward sketches, the lines of which have never left me. One sketch – about a stressed mother and daughter fighting in the kitchen during a family dinner – sends Szubanski into fits of giggles. It’s a 40-year-old sketch, and still as funny as it was back then. She wrote it, she reveals. Unsurprisingly, perhaps, tense family meals are in her wheelhouse.

One interesting effect of Szubanski’s public health journey is that people have perhaps finally met the real woman behind the punchlines, says Downey. “She has a lot of depth. She’s incredibly intelligent, but she can laugh at herself. She’s self-deprecating, but she’s a very strong person.

“She’s coming at this illness with great intelligence and great integrity and great poise and great bravery, actually. Once upon a time, people probably thought, ‘She’s hilarious, she’s funny.’ But now I feel as though the tide is turning a bit and people are beginning to realise that she’s far more than just a funny person.”

And in her inner world, Szubanski says she is happy. Single, but very happy. Which begs the question: would she like to fall in love again? “At the moment, I’m not probably quite in that headspace, but never say never,” Szubanski says, with a smile.

“I’m completely open to it, but I’m also really happy. I have a great life, which I appreciate incredibly now in the most complete and comprehensive way. I have terrific friends and family. I have a lot of love in my life, so I’m having a good time.”

I Can’t Tell You But I Will by Magda Szubanski (Text Publishing) is out September 29.

Nations League: Kylian Mbappé injured after scoring France winner in Turkey

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 21:35:43 GMT

France beat 10-man Turkey 1-0 to start Zidane era

Italy 0-2 Belgium, Georgia 0-1 Northern Ireland

Kylian Mbappé limped off with an apparent knee injury, moments after scoring France’s winner against Turkey in the Nations League on Friday.

The Real Madrid striker rifled in a low shot in the 55th minute after he was set up by Michael Olise. Soon after his record-extending 67th France goal, Mbappé sat on the ground and grimaced as he rubbed the area around his left knee.

The new France head coach, Zinedine Zidane, replaced Mbappé with Désiré Doué. In an encouraging sight, he was able to walk off the field of his own accord – but Zidane said afterwards that he expects his captain to return to Real Madrid for treatment.

“It’s not great. Unfortunately I think he [Mbappé] is going to have to go home. We don’t want to take any risks,” Zidane told French broadcaster TF1. “He overextended his knee while shooting. It’s not very encouraging.”

Jules Koundé hit the post for France before Turkey were reduced to 10 men, goalkeeper Ugurcan Cakir sent off for handling the ball outside his area after Bradley Barcola had been played through on goal.

Elsewhere in Group A2, Roberto Mancini’s second debut as the Italy head coach ended with a barrage of boos as the Azzurri were beaten 2-0 at home by Belgium.

Mika Godts marked his first competitive cap with a fine individual goal after 20 minutes at the Stadio Olimpico. Dodi Lukebakio’s powerful strike in the 69th minute put the visitors out of sight in a chastening first game for Mancini.

It was an encouraging start, though, for new Belgium coach Mark van Bommel, who succeeded Rudi Garcia following the Red Devils’ run to the World Cup quarter-finals. Belgium host France in their next match on Monday, while Italy travel to Turkey.

Earlier, Shea Charles scored a last-gasp winner after his brother Pierce saved Khvicha Kvaratskhelia’s penalty as Northern Ireland began their Nations League campaign with a dramatic 1-0 win over Georgia in Tbilisi.

Pierce Charles guessed right to keep out a poor penalty from Kvaratskhelia in the 65th minute, having already made an excellent save to keep out Georges Mikautadze’s close-range shot earlier in the second half of their Group B2 game.

At the other end, Shea Charles had spurned the visitors’ best chances to score but, in the ninth minute of time added on, he scrambled home from Trai Hume’s cross, securing a first ever away win for Northern Ireland in the Nations League.

There was a nervous VAR check for offside but eventually Shea Charles could celebrate just his second international goal. Although Northern Ireland left the pitch celebrating, there was a major blow in stoppage time as defender Dan Ballard pulled up clutching his hamstring.

Michael O’Neill had been frustrated with several decisions from the referee, Orel Grinfeeld – not least the penalty, which came after Ballard and Luka Locoshvili tussled in the box and Grinfeeld was sent to the VAR monitor. Northern Ireland’s next opponents, Hungary, lost 1-0 to Ukraine in Budapest thanks to Danylo Sikan’s goal.

In the third-tier Group C2, Milution Osmajic’s 86th-minute goal helped Montenegro fight back to beat Cyprus in Podgorica. Armenia top the group after beating Latvia 2-0 at home earlier on Friday.

Turning Point USA knew of security concerns yet insisted Charlie Kirk speak outdoors, report says

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 21:32:45 GMT

According to report, school staff recommended event move to a more secure location weeks before Kirk was fatally shot

A new report says that Turning Point USA insisted the conservative political group’s leader Charlie Kirk speak outdoors at Utah Valley University – where he was ultimately assassinated – despite security concerns raised with his team by the school’s leaders and its police chief.

The independent report with those findings was commissioned by UVU and released on Friday. The report examined security procedures leading up to the 31-year-old’s fatal shooting on 10 September 2025 during a talk at the university’s campus in Orem, Utah.

According to the 158-page report, school staff recommended Turning Point USA (TPUSA) move its event to a more secure location weeks before Kirk’s slaying. However, TPUSA “insisted upon” an outdoor location which “created significant protective operations considerations”, the report said.

It added that a face-to-face, pre-event briefing and walkthrough with UVU police chief Jeff Long and the TPUSA protection detail – including the organization’s security supervisor Dan Flood – “should also have occurred” on UVU’s campus hours prior to the event.

“Chief Long texted Dan Flood to meet on the Hall of Flags outdoor pedestrian walkway at 11[am], however, this face-to-face meeting did not occur,” the report said.

Kirk was shot and killed by a sniper that day in the early afternoon.

According to the report, the university also asked TPUSA for an estimated attendance figure. But the organization never provided one, despite saying it would control ticketing for the event, Utah’s Salt Lake Tribune newspaper reported.

“Based on our review of all available information, that at no time during the events leading up to the assassination of Charlie Kirk, or in its aftermath, did any employee or agent of UVU act in bad faith or in willful and wanton disregard for the safety of others,” the report said.

However, it also noted UVU’s having deferred to TPUSA on various event logistics. “Several key event security decisions were deferred to the TPUSA field representative even though UVU staff members raised concerns, including concerns related to holding the event in the outdoor fountain courtyard area and using TPUSA’s ticketing process,” the university’s report said.

“Those decisions placed the event in an area that was more difficult to control and limited UVU’s ability to obtain reliable, real-time information regarding anticipated attendance and crowd size.”

The report added: “UVU should have retained decision-making authority over key security-related issues, including venue selection, ticketing, access control and other conditions necessary to support campus safety.”

In response to the report, Kirk family attorney Brett Parkinson said: “UVU hosted this event, and in doing so, assumed responsibility for the safety of all in attendance, including Charlie. The buck stopped with UVU leadership and law enforcement.

“Justice for Charlie and his family requires true accountability for UVU’s fatal shortcomings that day.”

Meanwhile, a statement from Jon Anderson, UVU’s president, said the university had a responsibility to “learn from the findings of this review, and follow through on its recommendations”.

“This requires humility, an honest examination of our policies and practices, and a commitment to act on what we learn,” Anderson’s statement also said.

Anderson, who became the university’s president in August, also said in his statement that UVU had made “meaningful progress in strengthening campus safety over the past year”.

Kirk’s family is planning to sue the university. His family alleged in a 16 September legal notice presaging wrongful death litigation that UVU had placed “a politically controversial figure like Charlie Kirk in an outdoor event … surrounded by tall buildings and other elevated observation platforms” – and that the setup was like “walking him into a fishbowl”.

UVU said it was aware of the notice and said it “addresses legal matters consistent with our established processes”, according to the Tribune.

Utah resident Tyler Robinson has been charged with aggravated murder in connection with Kirk’s killing. He has pleaded not guilty, and no trial date had been set for him as of Friday.

Irwin holds nerve to sink Leeds and send Warrington to Grand Final

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 21:03:08 GMT

Leeds 12-14 Warrington

Late penalty clinches Old Trafford trip

Warrington Wolves reached their first Super League Grand Final in almost a decade after emerging through an absorbing playoff semi-final against Leeds Rhinos to move within 80 minutes of a first league title in over 70 years.

The Wire have not been at Old Trafford since 2018 and remain without a league title of any kind since 1955, one of the longest streaks in rugby league. But that streak is now one victory away from ending after Sam Burgess’ side navigated past the Rhinos on a gripping night at Headingley thanks to a dramatic late Ewan Irwin penalty.

The game was level at 12-12 before Warrington were awarded a controversial penalty after George Williams was taken out off the ball. Irwin converted it to put the visitors ahead and they showed immense defensive resolve in the closing moments to hold on and book their spot in the Grand Final. They will face either Wigan Warriors or Wakefield Trinity next Saturday.

As for Leeds, they will look back on this as a huge missed opportunity. Brad Arthur’s side lost their last two home games to surrender top spot in the table to Wigan Warriors, before falling at the first hurdle here.

Leeds’ preparations had already been stunted in the build-up with several key withdrawals but those issues were deepened further minutes before kick-off. Chris Hankinson, already deputising for the Rhinos captain Ash Handley, pulled out with an injury in the warm-up meaning Ned McCormack was drafted in for only the seventh game of his Leeds career.

He and younger brother Fergus, himself only playing in the third Leeds game of his career, due to injuries, were hugely influential in an engrossing first half which delivered a real contrast in styles. The Rhinos, as they have been for most of this season, were always threatening when Jake Connor was given the opportunity to kick the ball, while Warrington’s running game was constant.

It was the Wire who took an early lead when Matty Ashton out-jumped Ryan Hall to tee up James Bentley to open the scoring against his former club. But the hosts responded with some style, with a period of pressure on the Warrington line yielding their first points as Brodie Croft’s cut-out pass found Ryan Hall unmarked in the corner.

Connor converted superbly from the touchline before the Leeds scrum-half delivered a magical moment to haul his side ahead. It was his clever kick on halfway which caught the Warrington backline cold, allowing McCormack to collect before turning the ball back inside for a supporting Connor, who again converted. Suddenly, Leeds led by six: and Headingley was alive.

However, the resilience which has brought Warrington to this stage in the season came to the fore as half-time approached. They withstood more Leeds pressure before taking advantage with their next meaningful attack as George Williams’ pinpoint pass gave Luke Yates the time to cut through and touch down next to the posts. Irwin converted, and it was all square at the break.

But despite both sides looking threatening on multiple occasions in that first half, the potency seemed to fade after the restart and give way for an attritional contest. The Rhinos and the Wolves were both guilty of spurning gilt-edged opportunities to go back ahead, with Connor peculiarly off-target with a kick as Leeds looked to probe the Warrington line.

At the other end, Warrington found themselves in Leeds territory on multiple occasions but they were unable to unpick the Rhinos’ defensive line, with the hosts standing up well to pressure that was only set to rise further. As it entered the final quarter of a gripping semi-final, it remained all square and too close to call.

t was clear any points could now be decisive. And with 15 minutes to go, a crucial juncture arrived; Warrington were awarded a penalty after Williams was adjudged to be checked off the ball by James McDonnell. Leeds challenged the call but were overruled and from the resulting penalty, Irwin’s kick put the Wolves back ahead by two.

The drama wasn’t over though. Connor thought he had kicked a sublime 40-20 but replays showed Keenan Palasia had been tackled before offloading to the half-back. With the last kick of the game, Connor then tried to kick a penalty from 60 metres: but it fell short, and the Wolves progressed.

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 20:58:23 GMT

Northampton 59-26 Newcastle

Backs both score hat-tricks in nine-try victory

The new season is up and running and so are the defending champions. Northampton’s attacking game was wonderfully slick at times in this nine-try dismissal of Newcastle Red Balls and here was an opening night warning to all their rivals that they are serious about becoming the first club for seven years to win consecutive Prem titles.

There is a huge amount of rugby to be played, clearly, between now and next June but on this evidence their fast-moving backs are once again going to take a lot of stopping. There were a brace of hat-tricks for the classy Tommy Freeman and the exciting teenager James Pater while George Hendy also wasted no time underlining his claims for an England squad place.

Up front, Emmanuel Iyogun also had the kind of game that will further endear him to the national management. Even a stronger Newcastle outfit, with ambitions to escape the league’s basement this year, found themselves repeatedly sliced open although the Red Bulls did show more in the way of energy and ambition than has generally been the case in recent times.

Christian Wade added a couple more tries to his sizeable career collection but at no stage did his team look like overturning the early season odds. Northampton could even afford for the headline-loving Henry Pollock to have a relatively quiet night, give or take a searing second half break and a flutter of pre-game social media interest about his latest choice of hairdo.

Only those recently beamed down from Mars will be unaware that Pollock has linked up with the boxing promoter Eddie Hearn and the sight of him warming up in a headguard prior to a ‘big reveal’ of his new braided hairstyle was merely a latest attention-seeking gimmick. Rather more significant is that he delivers on the field and, fortunately for the flanker, there is no shortage of collective talent around him.

Among the more intriguing new faces is Pater, skinny as a rake but with the priceless sporting gifts of rare anticipation and vision. There was a very good reason why Saints, in the end, were prepared to bid farewell to George Furbank and here it was for all to admire on a cool, still autumn evening. The 19-year-old full-back picked a lovely delayed line for his first try on the left and was again in precisely the right place at the right time to touch down again with the Red Bulls temporarily down to 14 men.

The visitors did score a nice early try, finished by the ever-sharp Wade, but Harrison Obatoyinbo being sent to the sin-bin for a gratuitous trip coincided with the Saints locating another gear. First Hendy came thundering through the defensive line to finish a textbook strike play from a lineout and then, with the cover further stretched by Pollock and Pater, there was a juggling score for Freeman to secure a try bonus point after just 24 minutes.

When they play the angles so cutely it is almost impossible to stop last season’s title winners indefinitely, despite their relative lack of mountainous specimens up front. Archie McParland missed out on an England summer tour spot through injury but looked a seriously classy player here while, in front of him, the newly capped Iyogun made his presence felt with an excellent turnover and a thumping hit on Obatoyinbo.

To Newcastle’s credit they did at least stick at it, Wade further underlining his try poaching ability with another slick finish in the right corner. Northampton, though, are primed to strike at any moment and did so again when Fraser Dingwall put the galloping Alex Coles away to make it 31-14 at half-time.

English National Ballet: Rhythm Riot review – this triple whammy brings zing, grit and chills

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 19:00:14 GMT

Sadler’s Wells, LondonA trio of dances taking influence from Stravinsky, tap and William Blake’s poetry combine with powerful performances exuding showmanship

Damn, there was some amazing dance going on in mid-20th century New York. You had George Balanchine forging a new American ballet, all slick speed and striking angles, and in Harlem there was the Cotton Club and the Savoy, swinging dancefloors and entertainers like the legendary Nicholas Brothers, of whom Balanchine was a fan. There’s a taste of this world in English National Ballet’s latest triple bill, with a distinctly American flavour and a focus on propulsive rhythm.

Balanchine’s Symphony in Three Movements was made in 1972 as a memorial to Stravinsky, although the eponymous music is from 1945. Balanchine and Stravinsky were an absolute dream team, architects of multiple masterpieces. Here the clarity of line and stripped-back nature of the design crossed with the depth and crunchy complexity of Stravinsky’s score is a perfect balance. There’s palpable power from the pit, with the English National Ballet Philharmonic relishing the music under the baton of Maria Seletskaja.

The choreography has peppy energy as Swanice Luong arrives with a zing in a bubblegum pink leotard, bouncing into a jazzy tuck jump like a Gap advert. She, Emma Hawes and Ksenia Ovsyanick are like a trio of mean girls competing to be queen bee. Sharp of gesture and brilliant of smile, Ovsyanick is particularly aloof. It’s such a specific technique and ENB aren’t a Balanchine company, but they do it justice.

The spirit of the Nicholas Brothers arrives in a new piece, Bow Out, by American choreographer Micaela Taylor, inspired by the showstopping tap duo’s acrobatics in the 1943 film Stormy Weather. It’s an exuberant blend of classical, jazz, hip-hop, tap and Lindy hop, in soft shoes and black tailcoats, to a soundtrack of jazz, clattering tap beats, and new music by Philip Patrick Harper Bucknor, AKA Tru. Taylor bounces off the syncopation, hooking tightly into the rhythm or squeezing out the juice between the beats while the dancers snatch movements from the air. There’s precision, virtuosity and showmanship, but also something more ominous: disillusionment, farewell, a grittier texture, and showbusiness itself almost becomes its own character. An immensely enjoyable and intriguing debut from Taylor.

Another premiere comes from a choreographer who’s been working in New York for 30 years but hails from Korea, Jae Man Joo. It’s thoroughly of the now in the sense that this is a vibes piece that harnesses lots of ritualistic mass-unison movement and creates an intense, immersive world through atmospheric visuals and score. The soundtrack is two works by Latvian composer Pēteris Vasks (plus some Korean beopgogongyang drumming), outwardly emotive, strung-out strings that signify angst and melodrama, but the whole piece is so committed to its aesthetic that somehow it works.

Everything is black – costumes and artfully distressed backdrop – and Sangeun Lee is like a goth Miss Havisham in bedraggled black ballgown, a ghostly figure haunting the stage. Joo’s piece is named after the William Blake poem Auguries of Innocence, a meditation on the moral failures of man and our destruction of nature. The intricacies of Joo’s interpretation are mostly lost to a first-time viewer, but there’s plenty to get to grips with in this finale to a wildly eclectic triple bill.

At Sadler’s Wells, London, until 3 October

‘Society needs children’: Alan Johnson calls for better-paid UK paternity leave

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 18:39:28 GMT

Exclusive: Former Labour minister says working-class fathers are being shortchanged and budget should correct it

Parliament was in recess when Tony Blair called Alan Johnson up to his flat above No 11. The former prime minister was relaxed, padding around in his socks, while his son Leo played with his toys. Johnson, then the education secretary, spoke about his own son from his second marriage, who was a similar age.

“Tony said: ‘Oh you’re a father?’” recalled Johnson. “I said: ‘Tony, I had three kids by the age of 20!’ He looked at me and said: ‘So you really are working-class …’”

It may be almost a quarter of a century since Johnson introduced paid paternity leave during his time as the trade and industry secretary, but working-class fathers are still being shortchanged, the former minister has told the Guardian.

Johnson has added his name to a growing number of current and former MPs and senior Labour figures calling for six weeks of paternity leave paid at 90% of earnings, capped at £1,200 a week, with the offer extended to self-employed fathers, who are currently the only parents with no entitlement to paid leave.

The author married his first wife, Judith, when he was 18, adopting her daughter and going on to have two more children by the time he was 20. His fourth child, with his second wife, was born when he was a minister in the New Labour government in his 50s.

Johnson recalls that when his second child was born, he came home from work on a night shift in the postal service to find a note from his wife telling him she had gone to hospital to have a baby. He slept for a few hours and went back to work.

“Men were meant to go down the pub, buy everyone a drink, smoke a cigar, and leave all the kind of hard work to their partners,” he said. “By the time my fourth child was born, it was practically compulsory to be at the birth – things move on and the law has to move with it.”

Working-class fathers are still far less likely to take up the current paternity leave of £187.18 a week for two weeks, among the least generous offerings in Europe. According to analysis of HMRC data by the campaign group the Dad Shift, 90% of paternity leave in 2024-25 was claimed by fathers in the UK’s top half of earners – those who generally make more than £37,800 a year – and 95% of claims for shared parental leave were made by fathers or partners in the top 50% bracket.

Many fathers and partners would still be in the position of having to go back to work the day after the birth of a child, just like he did, added Johnson.

“The statistics about who is actually accessing paternity leave is just stunning. It shows that it’s a class issue,” he said. “It’s great that more prosperous dads are taking paternity leave, but we’ve got to do something to increase the take-up among the lower paid.”

The Joseph Rowntree Foundation estimates that introducing the new policy of six weeks at 90% of pay in the forthcoming budget would cost the government an additional £1bn, but increased tax receipts from women going back to work could reduce that cost to £220m.

Asked if the government should introduce the change in the next budget, despite the strong economic headwinds faced by the chancellor, John Healey, Johnson was in no doubt. “Absolutely. In government terms, the cost is money down the back of the sofa,” he said. “And actually if the finances are preventing couples from having children, ultimately that is bad for society. Society needs children, mankind needs to procreate. So encouraging childbirth is good for society, full stop.”

The policy would be popular, and unlikely to be opposed, he added. “If it was, in pure political terms, it’s a good dividing line for Andy Burnham and the Labour party to take,” he said. “It’s an excellent dividing line.”

The age of asterisk: Manchester City’s glittering era of success is tainted now

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 18:36:58 GMT

Friday’s verdict against Manchester City will change everything we understood about their Premier League title triumphs

Welcome, then, to the age of asterisk. Whatever punishment Manchester City and their owners receive at the end of this process, the fact remains, everything is tainted now.

Overturn the tables, scatter the gold coins. Throw your medals in the bin. You cheated to win them. Whatever that thing was, it’s done. Stolen glory, stolen income, stolen joy. Every chant, every “we won the lot”, every awkward documentary scene about the deep, throbbing heart of this empire of love. It all looks odd, sinister, cold, sloppy, but also, and this is always the best response, utterly absurd.

This is not over of course. We still work on the principle of innocent until repeatedly proven guilty, pending mega-bucks final appeals. There could yet be a dramatic reversal at the next stage. And if so, fair enough. Trust the process. So for now we must also asterisk the asterisk. It should also be pointed out that City still deny all allegations, even when proven at the first instance. They have also, in fairness, not been found guilty of all of those 100-plus charges. Maybe the club can spin this, take the positives, a vital away charge to take into the appeal.

But for now this is a good day for football. And also a good day for, of all things, the world. The Premier League may seem an unlikely revolutionary. But in the age of despotism, of endless chatter about the decline of the rules-based international order, any tribunal that finds a fund back by the one of the United Arab Emirates’ ruling families guilty of breaches of minor but still vital sporting regulations deserves its own statue outside the Royal Courts of Justice. People in wigs: not always slaves to power, or indeed the enemies of the people.

Mainly this is a great day for the Premier League, which must be commended above all for its refusal to bend. There has been frustration at the time it has taken to reach this verdict. Technically it is a full eight years since Der Spiegel published the first allegations of industrial-scale cheating. And spare a thought here too for Rui Pinto, the original whistleblower, currently in witness protection after being found guilty of information-related offences. This verdict suggest football’s greatest vigilante was also right, or right enough. Raise a glass, José Bloggs of Oporto, or whatever you go by these days.

That extreme delay is simply another consequence of taking on an entity that is willing to spend so aggressively on the world’s most energetic lawyers, to threaten to bankrupt the organisation it signed up to serve and nourish. It always seemed worrying that an accusation of not cooperating with financial reporting, a charge that on the face of it could be cleared up in half a day, should take three years to reach a verdict.

But this is testimony to the lawfare-level response. In this context, and pending a proper sanction, the entire case speaks to the basic sanctity of the rule of law, of applying the same rules to all irrespective of status, a small but high-profile rejection of the idea wealth and political heft can steamroller regulation and process.

And that punishment really is key. Because everything is on the cards here, not least the much‑trailed potential destruction of the brand. There has always been a whispered suggestion the league is taking a hammer to its own knees in this process. That thing we sold you all those years? Well, it’s not straight. The product you paid for and believed in wasn’t real.

Arguably everyone who bought a Sky Sports subscription in that period now has a legal claim against City. I signed up for sport. This was an exhibition event. But the Premier League has been rigid in the right way. What is that legacy actually worth, how much more damaged will it be, if its owners shy away from their own rules and allow the serial champions to shortcut their way to plastic success? The answer is: very little. At that point we may as well all turn off the lights and abandon the stage to the world of scripted product.

It is important in all this to spare a thought for City fans, who are innocent of anything other than wanting their team to win and believing the evidence presented to their eyes. There will be some who see conspiracy, because they want to, who choose to fight on, or pretend not to understand. We live in an age when even billionaire inherited rulers get to style themselves as victims of oppressive power structures.

But the fact is the rules do matter, even if you think they shouldn’t exist. They matter because other teams were abiding by them. Other teams didn’t buy players, lost bidding wars, lost games and league titles by fine margins during a period when one team was saying, well, thanks but no thanks. This is why cheating matters. You can disagree with the offside law and try to get it changed. But if you just ignore it and keep on hammering the ball into the net, you’ve destroyed your own sport.

City’s fans deserve sympathy generally. They don’t run the club, they simply support it. They have been loyal to their owners, even while those owners, on the basis of this decision, were turning the club into a toxic entity, a parasite on its host and on the basic idea of sport. What is the right response to this? Some will simply feel sad at the tarnishing of memories.

But there is also a legitimate suggestion it is time for those owners to sell up and move on. This has been a disgraceful episode in so many ways: the casual cheating, the refusal to mitigate or compromise, the assault on English football, the attempt to bleed the rest of the field dry.

The fact is anyone with an interest in justice, equality and abiding by universal rules, should be pleased with this result, including City fans. Although there is of course still a huge opportunity for the process to hole itself below the waterline.

Guilt followed by a minor slap on the wrist. This would asterisk the asterisk, would provide a complete reversal of all that goodwill. What would be the point of going through this only to blink at the sanctions stage? And yes, this is the job of an independent tribunal, but the league will have agency in how this is interpreted, through its submission and its evidence.

And there is very little mitigation here. Not reporting financial information might sound trivial in another sphere. But in football, where success is defined by expenditure, this is deliberate and highly effective deceit. City have continued to spend freely, to win things under this shadow, in a space where more than simply results and titles are at stake. Football is a zero-sum game. When you cheat, you’re taking money and opportunities out of the pockets of others.

Not to mention glory, happiness, life chances, things people work and bleed for all their lives. In their place you’re introducing failure, doubt, career regression, moving home, moving jobs, cutting ties, losing connections, all based on skewed results on a sports field, all based on cheating.

The list of teams that might have won league titles in those years reads: Manchester United, Liverpool, Manchester United, Liverpool, Manchester United, Liverpool, Arsenal. Perhaps these clubs will even consider suing City for compensation. The Premier League could pre-empt this by stripping titles and reallocating glory. That still feels like an overload of asterisks. But this is what happens when you cheat. You degrade the experience for everyone.

There are two final things worth saying. Last month Bloomberg reported that the UAE had been in touch with the UK government expressing concerns about the Premier League process, and potentially, it was implied, damaging the prospect of that wider relationship.

If true, and it is simply a suggestion, this would demonstrate yet another profound misunderstanding of the culture you’re buying into. The law is not supposed to bend to power and influence. Does anyone actually want to live in a world where this is the case?

But then, it is also worth remembering that skimping on some financial rules is hardly the worst thing the UAE has been accused of in those years. There are accusations of supporting the bloodshed in Sudan, as well as numerous human rights abuses, the curtailment of dissent and massive social inequality.

Whatever its ultimate outcome the entire process stands as a warning for every sport with it eyes in a spin at the offer of transformative financial investment. Look very hard at who you get into bed with. Jam today, pain tomorrow. And it never, ever comes for free.

Alarm at UN over sanctions threatened by US on international criminal court

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 18:33:54 GMT

Group calls for proper enforcement of ICC rulings as Trump administration widens attacks on court

The US threat to impose sanctions on the international criminal court (ICC) as an institution, not just its leading judges, could fundamentally disrupt its operation and needed to be resisted, a coalition of countries to defend international law heard at the United Nations on Friday.

Ronald Lamola, South Africa’s foreign minister, issued the warning at an event during the UN general assembly called to protect the system of international law from a growing array of threats, including open flouting of its tenets and rulings by Israel.

The meeting was organised by the Hague Group, of which Lamola is co-chair, and which was set up in 2025 to protect international law and to call for the proper enforcement of the rulings of its two primary bodies: the ICC and the international court of justice (ICJ).

Lamola told the gathering that the US had already sanctioned ICC judges and prosecutors, but was now planning sanctions against the ICC itself.

“If imposed, such measures could fundamentally disrupt its operations,” he said. “An independent court remains independent only if judges and officials cannot be punished for carrying out their mandates.”

The head of the ICC, Judge Tomoko Akane of Japan, was sanctioned by the US in August, along with senior trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye of Senegal, for engaging in the ICC’s efforts to “prosecute officials whose government has not consented to ICC jurisdiction”. The attack on Akane was condemned this week by the Japanese prime minister, Sanae Takaichi.

The US has admitted it seeks to dismantle the Hague-based ICC. In his address to the UN general assembly this week, Donald Trump once again criticised the “out of control” court, which he smeared as an “evil group of people” and urged other nations to reject.

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, has accused the court of being “a corrupt and fatally politicised supranational court that has maliciously abused its authority and exceeded its mandate. We will not tolerate its assault on state sovereignty.”

The next step by the US is likely to be to impose secondary sanctions on anyone who cooperates with the court, as opposed to sanctioning its senior judiciary. A designation of the whole institution would reach every European bank, insurer and technology supplier serving the court, which sits in the Netherlands.

The Dutch government, as the host of the ICC, is taking the lead in trying to warn the US away from the effective immobilisation of the court. The Dutch prime minister, Rob Jetten, told the UN general assembly: “International law either works for everyone or for no one. This court was established to protect us against impunity and it was built on the foundations of the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials. And now, with the ICC under attack, the writing is truly on the wall.

“After all, how can you possibly be opposed to prosecuting the very worst crimes? And I believe there can be only one response: to say, hands off the ICC and all those other institutions that protect the international legal order.”

William Schabas, a specialist in international law, noted to the meeting the irony that the resort to international law and courts was increasing dramatically even as the institutions were under attack. He said nations needed to strengthen the ICC, including by ensuring positions are not traded and only the highest calibre judges are elected.

Diana Buttu, the prominent Palestinian lawyer, was among many to complain of western powers’ partial resort to international law. “The greatest threat to international law is not the state that openly defies it,” she said. “The greatest threat is our selectivity – the quiet decision that is made in capitals and rooms that the rules don’t bind everybody, they only bind some. Overcrowding and racism at Manston asylum centre linked to government decisions, inquiry hears

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 18:15:31 GMT

Kent facility became dangerously overburdened after ministers halted transfers to hotels

A catalogue of failures including racism, use of force and chronic overcrowding at a Home Office processing site for people who arrive on small boat were linked to decisions made at the highest level of government, an independent inquiry has heard.

The government commissioned the Manston independent inquiry to look at problems under the Conservative government between 1 June and 22 November 2022 at the facility in Kent.

Almost 200 asylum seekers detained at Manston are participating in the inquiry along with the former home secretaries Suella Braverman and Priti Patel, several government departments including the Home Office, Treasury, Ministry of Justice and Ministry of Defence, and HM Inspectorate of Prisons and the UK Health Security Agency.

The problems began when the site became vastly overcrowded. Manston was designed to hold a maximum of 1,600 new arrivals for no more than 24 hours as there are no proper sleeping or other facilities there. But after decisions by ministers to pause transfers of many of the asylum seekers to other accommodation such as hotels the site became dangerously overcrowded.

Up to 4,000 people were accommodated there unlawfully for several weeks at the peak of the crisis, most of them sleeping on the floor in profoundly insanitary conditions.

There were outbreaks of infectious conditions including scabies and diphtheria, the latter of which can be fatal in approximately 30% of cases in unvaccinated populations. There were also reports of assaults and drug use by guards, racist abuse from guards, and the death of a man after contracting diphtheria.

The inquiry, chaired by Sophie Cartwright KC, heard that two former prime ministers, Boris Johnson and Rishi Sunak, who were both in post at different points in 2022, were involved in decision-making about the Manston site.

Laura Dubinsky KC, representing some of the participants, told the inquiry that the decision to pause sending many asylum seekers on to hotels was in line with the thinking at No 10.

“No 10 clearly did play a decision-making role,” she said. Patel has provided evidence to the inquiry that funding was deemed inadequate to address the small boats issue, including funding for Manston and onward accommodation.

The inquiry heard that events in Manston “raise very serious questions for ministers”.

Clair Dobbin KC, counsel to the inquiry, said it was taking place in a “crucible of hostility” at a time when the arrival of small boats remains a significant issue.

She added that “to put it bluntly” the inquiry would look at whether at certain points “the entire operation at Manston was outside the law”.

One senior Home Office official wrote a report saying: “To be frank, I’m struggling for words,” after observing what he said were “the worst conditions I have observed working in this environment”.

Hussein Haseeb Ahmed, 31, was taken to Manston after arriving in a small boat. He died in hospital after becoming ill with diphtheria. He was belatedly admitted for care and was kept in handcuffs as he lay dying. The handcuffs were only removed two and a half hours before he died. According to the inquiry, evidence about his death suggests “a succession of missed opportunities”.

The inquiry also heard that “very racist language was used towards detainees by some staff”.

Sixty families were crammed into 11 rooms in a barracks building with no hot water, showers or clean clothes for nine days with one toilet for 81 people, and no soap or sanitiser available.

Some used toothpaste to soothe bites and one used a croissant wrapper to dress wounds.

Questions were raised about whether some unvetted staff were working legally at Manston.

Shu Shin Luh, one of the lawyers representing participants in the inquiry, said: “Why were people treated as less than human?”

Stephanie Harrison KC, also representing some of the participants in the inquiry, accused the Home Office of presiding over “an institutional culture defined by impunity with widespread illegality and non-compliance with the law”.

Future dates for inquiry hearings have not yet been confirmed.

Thomas Tuchel has thrown Cole Palmer’s England future into major doubt by questioning whether the Chelsea attacker wants to be part of his squad.

Palmer has only 14 caps and his decision not to join up with the squad this week, because of a minor muscular injury, caused disappointment given he was left out of Tuchel’s World Cup squad after struggling with form and fitness last season.

Tuchel has put a lot of store in team spirit and is clear about wanting commitment. The German has rarely been able to work with Palmer, who had earned a high-profile recall after making a strong start to the campaign, and did not go down the diplomatic route when it was suggested the former Manchester City player does not seem desperate to play for England. “Hard to argue against what you’re saying,” Tuchel said.

The line came with a warning for Palmer. “He misses too many camps,” Tuchel said. “That’s the overall headline. We have a lot of invitations and he couldn’t make this one. It is what it is. I am not ready to focus on players who are not here. The players that are here have my full attention.

The idea of asking Palmer to join the squad to build connections did not cross Tuchel’s mind. “To bring someone and take away capacity from our physios, it’s not helpful,” he said. “This is about the guys who are here and this is where the energy goes.”

“Every case is individual and if Declan calls me and explains to me and I actually see him play v Brighton, I see straight away on TV that something is off,” Tuchel said. “He just confirmed that impression. We Manchester City fans fear relegation and losing trophies … but club are bang to rights

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 17:51:27 GMT

Despite attempts to legally filibuster the charges out of existence for the past three years, we’ve rightfully failed

It couldn’t have been more prophetic. In 2008, 15 years before Manchester City were charged with financial fraud, fans started singing “City’s going down with a billion in the bank” to the tune of Yellow Submarine. This was because the former Thailand president Thaksin Shinawatra’s 15-month ownership of City had come to an abrupt end when more than £1bn of his assets were frozen. And although Sheikh Mansour of the UAE had stepped in to save City, we were sinking fast.

Despite the UAE’s untold riches, by December we were in the relegation zone. It’s called Cityitis – shorthand for our tendency to self-destruct when things appear to be going well. In fact we won trophy after trophy. But we continued to sing the song about going down with a billion in the bank. When the financial fair play investigation was launched in 2018, the chant got louder. Then in 2023 we learned there were more than 100 charges. The chant became even louder and more cavalier. And now that our grubby, griftin’, cheatin’ chicken has come home to roost, you can bank on one thing (if banks still deal with us) – the chanting will be louder and more cavalier than ever.

After all, this is a club that believes schadenfreude starts at home. We brag about our failings. Other songs we sing include “Empty seats at home” (to the tune of the Beautiful South’s Rotterdam) because we can’t sell out our tickets and “Is This the Etihad?” (to La donna è mobile from Verdi’s Rigoletto, natch) at deathly quiet away grounds.

It’s not about tempting fate. Nor is it hubristic irony – we can’t sell out despite winning all these trophies. It’s simply an acceptance that one way or another we’ll always be City, always suffer from Cityitis, and come the day, despite our endless UAE riches, we’ll do a City.

And that day has come. We don’t know what our fate, or sentence, is yet. When I interviewed Wayne Rooney recently he suggested we would have 60 points docked, making it virtually impossible for us to avoid relegation.

It could be worse, of course. We could lose all eight trophies we won in the period (2009-10 to 2017-18) we flouted fair play, including three Premier League titles and our record-breaking centurions season when we won with 100 points in 2017-18. To me, that would be disproportionate and would in effect mean the Premier League eating itself.

But is the verdict itself unjust? City will say yes because they don’t want anything as petty as fair-play rules thwarting their bid for global domination. The lawyers will say yes because they’re paid to do so. Many fans will say yes because they’re fans. But some of us believe we’re bang to rights.

Everton and Nottingham Forest have been docked points for lesser offences, so it would be embarrassing if City had got away with it; an undeniable case of one rule for the rich. Despite City’s shocking attempts to legally filibuster the charges out of existence for the past three years, we’ve rightfully failed. Although it appears this is not the end because City intend to appeal.

Our behaviour has been pretty outrageous at Dodge City. Failing to provide accurate and up-to-date financial reports, concealing salary details and bonuses, inflating sponsorship revenues and failing to cooperate or supply requested documents during the investigation all feature on the charge sheet. We used lawyers to royally take the piss. And when it comes down to it, that is not very City. After all, this is a club founded in 1880 as St Mark’s (West Gorton) by members of St Mark’s Church of England for humanitarian and social rescue purposes to serve the deprived area of east Manchester, where Shameless was filmed a century later.

So what happens next? We may lose trophies. We will almost certainly get relegated. We almost certainly lose our best players and say ha det bra to Erling Haaland, the great Nordic God of goalscoring (having said that he may stay just to see how many he could get in a Championship season). And we start building again.

If the very worst happens, and we lose all those trophies, at least we still have our anni mirabiles when we did the unprecedented domestic quadruple (2018-19), and treble including the Champions League (2022-23). There was barely a whiff of scandal in these years. We were simply obscenely wealthy, brilliantly run and managed by the world’s numero uno Pep Guardiola.

And plenty of positives will come out of our disgrace. The biggest being that justice is done. But there is so much more. City may get to play in the Championship where we enjoyed some of our finest moments (“We’ve got Kevin Keegan 100 goals a season,” sung to the tune of Let’s All Do the Conga a mere 24 years ago). League One? Halcyon days. For City fans of a certain age and disposition, beating Gillingham in the playoff is our top footballing memory. League Two? Thrill of the unknown. The only way is up, as the song goes.

Ticket prices come down, allowing regular civilians back into the Etihad. Prices become so low that we fill the ground. Fans begin to realise Wembley visits and winning trophies are to be treasured. Pep has already gone so there’s no danger of losing him. We learn some humility and stop coming over all sullen because we’ve only won the League Cup and FA Cup in one season.

Perhaps the biggest positive is that rather than simply pulling out the chequebook and signing the world’s best, we learn to think imaginatively. I noticed the God of Bermudan goalscoring Shaun Goater this year left his job coaching Aston Villa Women. He’s only 56, never relied entirely on pace, and I bet he’s a free agent.
