He’s the mononymic designer who has been charged with rescuing Gucci from plummeting sales. So where better for Demna to stage his third catwalk show than at the forefront of commerce – a purpose-built Gucci shop.

During Milan fashion week on Friday, the designer transformed a convention centre into a sprawling retail space that mirrored the design for the brand’s new boutiques.

Amid giant stone columns and slabs of Paonazzo marble (in the show’s case, fake), guests including Romeo Beckham, Bianca Jagger, Cardi B and Edward Norton sat on plush couches surrounded by shelves displaying pieces from Demna’s previous collections. Sales assistants hovered close by, available to answer any questions but, to the disappointment of some VICs (very important clients) hoping to indulge in retail therapy, unable to carry out any actual sales.

Demna, who joined the house last July, said he had spent the first year “dedicated to understanding and formulating what Gucci stands for”. He described the show as “his complete personal vision for the brand”, explaining that his research has taught him that Gucci “is about luxury that wants to be seen”.

Until 2022, Gucci, which is owned by Kering and accounts for roughly half of its sales, was thriving. However, when Sabato de Sarno did a sharp U-turn from his predecessor Alessandro Michele’s theatrical romantic vision to minimalism, the brand plummeted. Over three years, revenue almost halved.

Demna, who during his 10 years at Balenciaga transformed it into a luxury powerhouse, has now been tasked with making Gucci relevant again.

There are hints that he is on the right path. In July, Kering reported a return to growth with the company crediting Demna’s new collections. But the pressure is mounting to accelerate a turnaround. Kering’s chief executive, Luca de Meo, who joined from Renault last year, has said it is important Gucci is “immediately recognisable and culturally pertinent”. Get that right and Gucci’s hope is queues will return to its shops.

Setting out his new vision on Friday, Demna divided the collection into three character-driven archetypes: “the rebellious aristocrat, the snob and the eccentric”, with a cast of models that captured its cross-generational appeal.

In menswear, oversized tailoring, loafers and tasselled slippers replaced the muscle tees and skinny jeans from February’s catwalk. Jeans hung low on the hips while the brand’s signature triple horse-bit belts hung even lower. Blazers featured exaggerated peaked shoulders and despite previously saying he wouldn’t do hoodies at Gucci (his signature design at Balenciaga), they did make an appearance.

For women, a “study of posh dress codes” led to both rugby tops and neat little skirt suits. Nods to the brand’s equestrian heritage came Rivals-coded with spiky-heeled, stirrup-motif riding boots and clingy white jodhpurs. There were plenty of references to bourgeois Italian ladies, now rebranded as “nonnamaxxing” by the TikTok generation, with fuzzy coats and shawls worn with wiggly pencil skirts. London’s Sloane Rangers were also acknowledged with pleated A-line skirts in Scottish tartans and Oxford shirting. Demna mentioned he liked the idea of bringing Gucci back to its roots, the Savoy hotel, where the brand’s founder, Guccio Gucci, worked as a porter during the 1890s.

There were also plenty of references to Gucci’s provocative and powerful 90s Tom Ford era. Demna described it as “nocturnal glamour” with bottom-grazing hemlines and metal-heeled stilettos. The model Alex Consani wore a long black dress with a slit from toe to bust, fastened with a bedazzled G logo at the hip, while a slinky and backless dress was loosely secured with a teardrop weight.

No general election before 2029, Andy Burnham says

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 17:06:39 GMT

Prime minister quashes speculation that Labour’s revival in the polls could prompt early contest

Andy Burnham has said he will not call a general election before 2029, after days of speculation that Labour’s revival in the polls could tempt him to call an early contest.

The prime minister was repeatedly questioned on the prospect during a round of broadcast interviews to regional media on Friday.

He initially said he was “not particularly” tempted by the idea of an early election, but later became firmer, saying he would “knock that dead” and he was “not going to do that” because he was focused on getting on with the job.

Asked by ITV Calendar whether the next election would be in 2029, Burnham said: “Well, yes, that’s when the next election will be. All of this speculation on an early election – I can knock that dead.

“You know, people want me, new in office, to be getting on with the job of delivering on the things that we’ve discussed, rather than putting self-serving politics before that, which was what I would be doing if I call an election. I’m not going to do that.”

Talk of an early election had grown during the last week after polls showed Labour pulling into the lead with support in the low 20s, and the Conservatives and Reform neck-and-neck a few points behind them.

Westminster sources said Downing Street advisers and MPs had been discussing the merits of an early poll but that even though the right was split, Labour would be at risk of losing its majority and having to form a coalition.

The Guardian revealed on Friday that Ravinder Athwal, the economist who wrote Labour’s 2024 manifesto, was taking on a senior role as an adviser to John Healey, the chancellor, to strengthen his team before the budget. This fuelled further speculation that the party’s preparations for a campaign were gathering pace.

Athwal, a Cambridge economics graduate, devised Keir Starmer’s five “missions”, which were meant to shape Labour’s approach to government.

Healey poached Athwal to be his senior special adviser from the business advisory group Flint Global, previously run by Burnham’s chief of staff, James Purnell, a Blair-era cabinet minister.

All the parties had begun increasing their preparations for a potential campaign since Burnham replaced Starmer in the summer, in case he decided to take advantage of the bounce in his popularity.

However, the prime minister has repeatedly ruled it out, both before and after taking office. In his regional interviews, he stressed his attention was on the party’s autumn conference, saying a big focus of his speech would be on setting out more details of a new model for the water industry that increases public control.

He told BBC South: “As we go into the Labour conference, we will set out more thinking about the change that we need to see in the running of water across the country. But it is clear to me that what we’ve had in the last 30 years is nowhere near good enough and is actually letting the public pay.”

During the interviews, Burnham confirmed reports that he would not be giving any exclusive interviews or articles to the Sun. The policy of declining special interviews with the newspaper has arisen from solidarity with victims of the Hillsborough disaster over the media outlet’s coverage of the 1989 tragedy that falsely blamed Liverpool fans for the deaths of supporters – for which it has since apologised.

Leading up to the conference in Liverpool, Labour members have been cheered by Burnham’s takeover, which has led to a modest recovery in the party’s popularity.

An MRP poll of more than 8,000 voters reported by the Guardian this week showed a significant shift of left-leaning voters towards Burnham’s Labour. This encouraged those in the party who have been thinking of gambling on an early election while Reform’s ratings are ebbing and while leftwing parties such as the Greens appear to be losing momentum.

Twice as many voters have returned to Labour from the left as from the right since April. The previously unreleased research, including a seat-by-seat MRP model, was conducted by Survation and the progressive activist site 38 Degrees in Burnham’s first month as prime minister.

It also showed progressive voters could push Reform UK into fourth place and put Labour within touching distance of a majority if tactical voting was widespread.

Burnham is beginning to attract a significant number of left-leaning voters back to Labour, motivated by a desire to stop Nigel Farage, the results suggest.

Israel’s match with Republic of Ireland will be an eerie occasion as political debate rages on

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 17:00:07 GMT

Despite fierce opposition to the Nations League encounters across Irish society, a boycott has not materialised

The match is being played in a neutral country and the stands are likely to be empty but Sunday’s Nations League fixture between Israel and the Republic of Ireland will nonetheless have the eyes of the world upon it.

Since February’s draw paired the sides against each other, voices across Irish society have demanded a boycott of the match. The Republic of Ireland’s government says Israel is committing genocide through its military action in Gaza, and the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) wants Israel suspended from international competition. But unless Ireland’s players decide not to take the field in the Hungarian city of Debrecen, the match will go ahead.

The debate over these two upcoming games, with Ireland to “host” Israel in a return fixture behind closed doors in the Serbian town of Backa Topola on Sunday week, has continued for months. But the temperature has risen as the first fixture approaches. Remarks made by the Ireland head coach, Heimir Hallgrímsson, that his side were “playing against genocide” prompted a stern response this week from the Israel Football Association (IFA), which accused the Icelander of “ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity”. Hallgrímsson was then backed publicly by the Taoiseach, Micheál Martin, who described the IFA’s remarks as “unacceptable” and said they should be withdrawn.

At the same time as Martin’s intervention his government faced protests by Irish fans who want the game called off. One organisation, Stop the Game, criticised the “hypocrisy” of Irish sports ministers announcing they would refuse to attend the fixture on principle, while also failing to support a boycott. Another group, Irish Sport for Palestine, published an open letter signed by more than 160 athletes calling for the players to act where their leaders wouldn’t. “Not playing the game would be the most sporting thing you could do,” the letter said. “Through your leadership and courage it would show the power of sport to unite, remind us of the shared values that connect us all, and have an impact far beyond the game.”

It is clear that all this scrutiny is being felt by Hallgrímsson’s squad. Before Thursday night’s Nations League defeat in Kosovo, Dara O’Shea said the squad had found themselves in a “difficult” and “unusual” position, and had agreed to decide a collective approach to the match in Debrecen. “It’s something that can’t be brushed over,” O’Shea said. “Whatever decision that we go through as players is taken as one and everybody’s view is respected as well.” That decision is expected to stop short of a boycott, however. The midfielder Jason Knight, speaking after Thursday’s game, said: “I don’t think the game should be going ahead but it is going ahead.”

It has been a winding road for the FAI to get to this point. Last November its general assembly voted to request that Uefa suspend Israel from its competitions for a breach of its statutes. At the same time its president, Paul Cooke, said Ireland would play Israel if drawn against them in Uefa competition. In June the FAI said Uefa had granted a request that its home fixture be played in a “neutral venue and behind closed doors” owing to the “operational challenges” of delivering a fixture against Israel on home soil. In July, at an extraordinary general meeting, FAI delegates confirmed their support for playing the fixture, voting in favour by 68% to 32%. The given justification related to concerns over “the profound impact that any non-fulfilment of Uefa fixtures would have on Irish football as a whole”.

Those calling for a boycott have pushed back on the concerns “nonfulfilment” would have had on Irish prospects, pointing to recent punishments meted out to Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia. Those three each boycotted fixtures against Belarusian teams and Uefa responded with the traditional sanction of a 3-0 walkover and, in one case, a €5,000 fine.

The Guardian view on Trump and Xi: a show of friendship, but no real attempt to address the tensions

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 16:53:49 GMT

The Chinese leader’s visit to Washington appears to have done nothing to shift the stalemate in bilateral relations

Within days, two high-profile Chinese visitors will arrive in the US – envoys of friendship, as Xi Jinping described them when he met Donald Trump at the White House this week. The giant pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, will be hosted at Atlanta zoo. Beijing dispatched the first panda pair to the US in 1972 following President Richard Nixon’s landmark visit to China. It uses the animals to indicate satisfaction or displeasure with other nations. But it also charges heftily for their lease: reportedly, around $1m a year per pair. Americans’ views of China have warmed from a pandemic nadir, but are unlikely to be shifted much by two animals, however charming. These days they are more of a token gesture than a striking symbol.

It is telling that the announcement was one of the main takeaways of Mr Xi’s visit to Washington. Expectations were low after May’s stalemate summit in Beijing, but this meeting still struggled to meet them. The US president gave Mr Xi a lavish welcome – unusually, travelling to meet the “strong, vibrant and fit” Chinese leader off the plane. He insisted that they had “never gotten along better”.

In a sense that is not surprising. Mr Trump admires and envies authoritarians with untrammelled powers. Chinese state media were welcome at the White House, unlike CNN, MS Now and Politico. Since he rarely pays even lip service to human rights, the treatment of Uyghurs or jailed Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong – facing another lengthy sentence for his international advocacy – were never likely to figure large, whatever the hopes of protesters outside.

Mr Trump told Mr Xi that any Chinese help for Iran is unacceptable; Mr Xi said that the US should adhere to the “correct position” of opposing Taiwanese independence. Beijing wants Washington to shift from the long-held stance of “not supporting” it. That would be a grave mistake, but Mr Trump has given worryingly mixed messages on Taiwan.

It is striking how little of consequence has emerged from the summit given that this is arguably the most consequential diplomatic relationship in the world. A two-month extension of the trade war truce was announced as Mr Xi arrived in the US. China’s curb of rare earth exports has checked Mr Trump’s appetite for an economic offensive; Beijing is anxious about its struggling economy. But if they are more wary of the fallout, they are also more fearful of the other side gaining ground. AI is central to this battle. Mr Trump has resisted all calls to restrain development because “Whoever wins AI, wins.” Mr Xi said it had to be managed responsibly, but Beijing has attacked “threat narratives”, fearing that the US wants to prevent it catching up.

CNN last week highlighted the dangers: the US military reportedly prepared to intercept a Chinese ship in the Middle East after an intelligence report said it was carrying nuclear weapons components – only for officials to realise that the partially AI-generated analysis had misidentified the cargo. Controls on development are desperately needed, but neither side is willing to accept them. Even the limited AI dialogue and “notification hotline” for AI safety proposed by Scott Bessent, treasury secretary, seem to be rather less than meets the eye. This summit should be viewed with alarm not because it saw substantive developments – but because it illustrates the dangers of drift.

The Guardian view on the 2026 Booker shortlist: what it takes to be a man

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 16:52:33 GMT

All the contenders for this year’s prize are a reflection of the crisis in masculinity

Jarvis Cocker, one of the judges for this year’s Booker prize, has expressed surprise that the shortlist, announced this week, contains four male authors and only two female writers, because, “generally speaking, the male-written books weren’t as good as the ones written by women”.

The Pulp frontman might be on to something. Over the past 10 years, however, seven Booker winners have been men; the number of women boosted to four by the controversial joint win between Bernardine Evaristo and Margaret Atwood in 2019. The 2024 Booker shortlist was the first to have five female authors in the prize’s history. Last year’s winner Flesh, by British-Hungarian author David Szalay, stripped what being a man means down to its bones.

This year’s contenders all approach the same question through wildly different forms: historical, domestic, dystopian and comic fiction. The novels by female authors both have male protagonists: a reluctant medieval monarch in Rebecca Perry’s May We Feed the King and a 57-year-old history teacher in contemporary Massachusetts in The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout.

The Disappearers by Marlon James and John of John by Douglas Stuart, both previous Booker winners, show young men confronting their sexuality in the repressive climates of late 20th-century Jamaica and the Outer Hebrides, respectively. In The End of Everything from science-fiction giant M John Harrison, the central character is trying to survive in a post-apocalyptic Britain under invasion from ambiguous entities (AI is never explicitly mentioned). In Black Bag, by Luke Kennard, an out-of-work actor lands a job in which he has to wear a black bag all the time, based on a 1967 social psychology experiment in which a student was asked to wear a big black bag for a whole semester. “It’s a statement about being a man,” one character says of the eponymous bag. “There’s a whole contingent of men who are lost and dissatisfied.”

All the male characters in these novels are walking around in metaphorical black bags, flailing awkwardly in the dark, unknowable to those closest to them. Whether set in medieval times, Donald Trump’s America or a nightmarish near future, the 2026 shortlist is a reflection of current anxieties about masculinity.

Publishing is just catching up. Thanks to the so-called Sally Rooney phenomenon, the book world (if not the Booker) has been dominated by novels written by and about young women, a long overdue pushback against generations of swaggering fiction by men. The male gaze has finally shifted. As Szalay has said, “you can’t write like Martin Amis or Norman Mailer or Philip Roth now”. Notable exceptions such as Szalay and Ben Lerner, whose novel Transcription was a surprise omission from the longlist, have been steadily chronicling 21st-century manhood. But some feared that male writers and stories were being overlooked altogether. Last year, the independent publisher, Conduit Books, was set up exclusively for male authors.

The shortlist shows a renewed confidence in narratives about men. Here are fathers and sons, husbands and lovers, kings and losers, none of whom conform to male stereotypes. All of the novels are about a longing for purpose and connection. In a world where the strongman myth is mighty, the characters show vulnerability and uncertainty. As the lyrics of a 1998 Pulp song have it, they make us “start to wonder what it takes to be a man”.

How Labour can reform Britain’s pensions triple lock

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 16:37:08 GMT

Readers offer solutions to the thorny problem facing the government, in response to an article by Gaby Hinsliff

Gaby Hinsliff (Britain needs cash and everyone knows we should break the pensions triple lock. Where is the courage?, 22 September) is right that public policy should not subsidise wealth without limit, but breaking the triple lock is a poor way to target affluent pensioners. Most pensioners are not affluent. Indeed, a quarter of pensioners require benefits in addition to the state pension just to survive and keep a roof over their heads.

If the aim is to stop subsidising wealth, a more direct target is the generous tax treatment of private pension savings. A taxpayer contributing £100 to a pension can receive £40 or £45 in tax relief if they pay higher- or additional-rate tax, compared with £20 for the basic rate. Tax and national insurance contributions relief on private pensions costs the government a staggering £84bn a year.

Most of this money (almost three-quarters) goes to the wealthiest 20% taxpayers because they can afford to save the most and receive the highest rate of relief. Instead, a flat 20% rate of tax relief on private pensions would preserve the incentive for basic-rate taxpayers while reducing the additional subsidy concentrated among higher earners. It’s also fair because when pensions are drawn down, much less tax is recovered by the Treasury, making the net cost of this relief over £50bn a year.

This could raise billions more than breaking the triple lock. The triple lock’s 2.5% floor was only significant during the period when both earnings growth and inflation were close to zero. When inflation and earnings growth are above 2%, as they are now and are expected to be over the coming years, the difference between the triple lock and a conventional uprating mechanism becomes irrelevant.

The policy challenge therefore is to avoid the economically irrelevant, politically damaging and socially divisive red herring that is breaking the triple lock and instead reform the far more regressive support given to large private pension pots. Stephen RichardsonGrange-over-Sands, Cumbria

Gaby Hinsliff makes the point that retirees of the future are likely to have smaller cushions to fall back on than baby boomers. But it is precisely this that justifies maintaining the triple lock as a bulwark against poverty. Young and middle‑aged workers do indeed face the prospect of an impoverished old age. As highlighted in the Pensions Commission interim report, according to 2025 figures, 43% of working-age people are undersaving for retirement, with just 25% of Bangladeshis and Pakistanis of working age participating in a pension scheme.

The pensions crisis is likely to grow, given the rise in the numbers of self-employed people – the group least likely to be saving for a pension. Millions of workers in their 40s and 50s face the prospect of poverty in retirement, given the rise of precarious working and continuing age discrimination in employment.

We do need a new deal to achieve generational fairness, but breaking the lock will leave millions facing poverty. The alternative must be keeping the lock, but tackling the reasons that justify its existence – low incomes, insecure employment and the high cost of housing. Chris PhillipsonEmeritus professor of sociology and social gerontology, University of Manchester

There is a simple tweak that would improve the affordability of the triple lock. The goal of the triple lock is to ensure that the value of the pension keeps up with both price inflation and wage inflation. But the way it has been implemented allows pensioners to do much better than this.

Between 2011 and 2026, prices rose by 60% and earnings rose by 66%, but pensions rose by 89%. This happens because in some years prices rise more than wages, but in other years wages rise more. So the pension does better than both of them.

The fix is to smooth out the earnings link. Instead of looking at wages growth over the last year, we should look at growth over the past five years, for example. Pensioners would still be protected against price rises, and would maintain their current position in the wages league table. But they would no longer rise up it. Bob VickersTwickenham, London

Gaby Hinsliff claims that “Every serious party needs billions of pounds to fund their promises, and everyone knows there’s an obvious place to find the money, but nobody wants to be the first to say so. And so a deferential silence shrouds the pension triple lock.” The problem is that everybody might think they know this, but that does not mean it is right.

If we do need to find money, it is within the government’s power to create it. And if it refuses to use that power, it can look elsewhere within the pension system for funds. For example, the pension tax relief given to the highest-earning people in this country, at rates above the basic level of income tax, costs at least £15bn a year – vastly more than costs attributed to the triple lock.

We have a cost of living crisis and a pension poverty crisis. So why is everyone looking at punishing some of the most vulnerable people in our society when the rich continue to have their ever-increasing wealth subsidised by the state at a cost of many billions of pounds a year?Richard MurphyEmeritus professor of accounting practice, Sheffield University

Along with my state pension, I receive two small pensions from the Ministry of Defence and the NHS. If my husband should die before me, I don’t know how I would survive financially. We have a small cottage and downsizing wouldn’t result in a significant profit.

My “inheritance” from my parents disappeared when my mother had to go into care with Alzheimer’s; her house had to be sold to pay for her care.

In a week when the billionaire tax avoider Jim Ratcliffe badmouths the country, Gaby Hinsliff makes no reference to the tax system and how the very rich can get away with paying very little.

She also makes no reference to why the UK is doing so badly financially or why young people are struggling – my son can’t afford a house – after a decade of Tory misrule, a decade of Brexit wilderness and the legacy of Thatcherism. Removing the triple lock won’t solve the now endemic financial challenges the UK is facing. Ingrid MarshNewton Abbot, Devon

Gaby Hinsliff is right about the triple lock: it has done its work in raising the ratio between the state retirement pension and average earnings from 18% in 2010 to about 30% now. Two problems remain: what should replace it and how to stop an opportunist opposition from playing politics with the issue?

There is no need to decide this matter now. Far better to announce the end of the triple lock in the forthcoming budget and refer the question of a replacement to a time-limited, cross-party commission. The state pension should not become a political football or part of a short-term fiscal fix. David PurdyCausewayhead, Stirling

Arts Council England doesn’t need ‘swagger’, it needs reform

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 16:34:28 GMT

Reader Chris Hodgkins proposes a dual‑pillar system that safeguards national institutions while establishing a dedicated body for grassroots arts and music

The interview with the new chair of Arts Council England (ACE), who says she wants the organisation to “get its swagger back”, misdiagnoses the crisis facing England’s cultural system (‘I want us to be loud’: Arts Council England’s new chair aims to reconnect young people with culture, 18 September). Swagger is not what is missing. What is required is contrition, honesty and structural reform.

Eighty years after its creation, Arts Council England remains built on a 1946 architecture that privileges opera and classical institutions while systematically marginalising jazz, folk, world, brass, choral and grassroots arts and music. This is not a matter of confidence or energy; it is a matter of structural imbalance. The Review of Jazz in England (2025), Margaret Hodge’s review (2025), and ACE/Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport’s 2026 responses all identify bureaucracy, mistrust and inconsistent decision‑making – yet none confront the deeper failures: lottery funding misuse, national portfolio organisation dominance, regional inequity, governance opacity, and the collapse of grassroots infrastructure. These problems are not recent. Every major review confirms the same pattern: ACE’s centralised model reproduces historical privilege and suppresses contemporary cultural practice.

International evidence shows that modern cultural systems – in Scandinavia, Ireland and Australia – are built on devolved delivery, direct investment in artists, touring infrastructure, and integrated cultural‑education policy. England has none of these. ACE’s legacy architecture cannot deliver the government’s growth agenda, cannot support regional cultural economies, and cannot unlock the high‑growth potential of grassroots arts and music.

What is needed now is not swagger but a new organisation. I propose a dual‑pillar system that safeguards national institutions while establishing a dedicated body for grassroots arts and music, with transparent allocation formulas, restored lottery funding, art form‑specific policy and a national touring infrastructure. Swagger will not fix England’s cultural system. Structural reform will. Chris HodgkinsEaling, London

New map projections don’t make the Mercator wrong

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 16:31:30 GMT

The transverse Mercator projection was created for European sailors – and it worked for their world, writes Paul Harwood

The subject of projections is incredibly complicated and you did a good job of navigating the discussion (‘A map is never neutral’: meet the cartographers who took on centuries of western bias, 18 September).

However, suggesting that transverse Mercator is inherently biased is not fair (if it is possible to be unfair to an equation) to both the projection and the cartographers.

Mercator et al just did the job of creating maps that were useful for the European sailors they were working for. The fact that everyone carried on using it was our laziness and not their bias.

The Equal Earth projection is a much better representation for what we use maps for now, but that does not make the Mercator wrong.

You say “A London-centric worldview has long dominated how world maps are presented.” But I can think of almost no maps that have London at the centre. The international coordinate system (ie latitude-longitude, which is unchanged by this resolution) is based for arbitrary historical reasons on a meridian drawn through Greenwich.

However, the “centre” of this coordinate system is not London but a point in the sea off west Africa. No map or representation has to use this as the centre and the current best practice – called UTM – has 60 different zones (thus 60 centres) to represent all parts of the globe.

Even the UK Ordnance Survey mapping system is not “centred” on London. As far as you can say it has a centre, it would be somewhere in Lancashire. Paul Harwood London

Why Ed Miliband has embraced his ‘awkward dad’ image in viral TikTok video

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 16:22:55 GMT

About 1.5 million people have watched footage of foreign secretary that capitalises on social media’s love of a cringe moment

It sparked delight among the diehard Milifans and a begrudging smile from those less keen on the foreign secretary, but a viral video of Ed Miliband has – possibly – confirmed his status as the internet’s awkward dad.

About 1.5 million people have viewed an interaction between Miliband and the TikTok personality Feroz Khan on the streets of New York, during which the digital content creator asks Miliband a series of questions including his name, job and his top piece of advice.

Following the same formula employed by Khan in every video, Miliband is stopped in a seemingly – though of course not at all – impromptu manner by the influencer who says: “You’re very well dressed, what do you do for a living?”

When Miliband, in New York for the UN general assembly, explains that he is the foreign secretary (adding that he is the UK equivalent of Marco Rubio when Khan claims not to know what that is), the influencer asks: “What makes your work so special?” Miliband gushes that he is “trying to make the world a better place”.

So far, so soft serve. But it is when Miliband is asked about any challenges he has faced and, with the charm of an ingenue, replies – “Oh wow! I ran to be prime minister of Britain. It didn’t go so well … but I kept going!” – that it is clear his media team have fully capitalised on social media’s love of the cringe moment.

Miliband has been on a journey since May 2014, when the then Labour leader was photographed ineptly eating a bacon roll during a campaign visit in New Malden. It was an image that launched a thousand memes and, occasionally, if daftly, was pointed to as a reason that Labour lost the 2015 general election.

Freed of the shackles of leadership – and embraced by a generation that frames mortifying incidents as unifying moments – Miliband is now free to take pleasure in the delights of a vegan fruity flapjack, safe in the knowledge that the video of him doing so will probably bolster his particular internet aura rather than damage it.

While Reform UK’s Lee Anderson wrote thunderously of the video, “Our Foreign Secretary! Putin will be quaking in his boots!”, his team were perhaps notching up the hits and watching Miliband’s expanding online presence.

The PR consultant Mark Borkowski said: “Ed Miliband has finally worked out that the awkward dad thing isn’t a reputational defect. It’s his brand. In an age of politicians desperately trying to manufacture authenticity, the slight cringe actually makes him feel human. He’s not trying to be cool, he’s letting the socials enjoy the fact that he isn’t.”

While the video nods to content consumers being in on the joke, some observers have pointed out that it is clearly staged rather than spontaneous, because Miliband’s aides do not stop when the foreign secretary starts speaking with a “stranger” and his answers seem rehearsed.

A government source agreed that it may well indeed have been a remarkable coincidence if Miliband had just bumped into an internet celebrity who also just happens to bump into famous people including Jennifer Lopez, Sydney Sweeney and Bradley Cooper.

“This isn’t Ed trying to hoodwink anyone. This is how these videos work – it’s really exciting working with content creators, but you have to outsource editorial control,” they said. “The vast majority of people who watch a video like this understand that the tone is native to the format.”

With the clock of views ticking up, the video had clearly reached a lot of people who may have been unfamiliar with Miliband’s early oeuvre. But Borkowski said there was potential for the knowing nod about Miliband’s maladroit moments to backfire.

“The danger comes when the choreography becomes visible,” he said. “Awkwardness works because it feels accidental. Once people think the ‘dad dancing’ has been Blackfriars Road focus-grouped, the joke shrivels.”

The makers of the 7 Up series set out to prove a point about class. What they achieved is far more profound

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 16:10:14 GMT

The epic documentary series reveals much about the shifting social attitudes of the last 60 years – and much more about the quiet mystery of human life

For an hour or two this week, I’ve been in the company of people whose lives I’ve seen unfold, almost from the beginning, almost to the end. They are people whom, with one exception, I’ve never met. And yet I’ve shared in their triumphs and disappointments for decades.

They are the group who, in 1964, when they were seven years old, were the subjects of what was initially a single, 40-minute ITV documentary, but which flowered into a work that is quite magical. Returning to those same boys and girls every seven years, watching as they turned first into shy and awkward teenagers, then into husbands and wives, then into parents and grandparents, the 7 Up series has become a document of our times – but also something larger and far more revealing. This week the broadcaster aired what it says will be the final chapter: the seven-year-olds are now 70.

The original aim of the show, made under the World in Action banner, was sociological and transparently political. It wanted to expose the entrenched nature of the British class system. And so it watched a trio of pre-prep school boys singing verses in Latin, contrasting them with the cheeky East End kids living just a few miles and a world away. While the posh trio could name, even then, the specific Oxbridge colleges their parents had in mind for them, Paul, raised in a children’s home, asked: “What does university mean?”

Sure enough, we have seen how those born into money keep it, while those with less have less – though what the programme missed was the huge and expanding group in between. By focusing either on foxhunting John at one end or cabbie Tony at the other, it largely left out what would turn out to be the story of these decades, namely the sprawling growth of the middle class.

Indeed, it’s the programme’s early assumptions that often turn out to illuminate most sharply how much society has changed. In 1964, the researchers only thought to include one child who wasn’t white: Symon. In a later episode, we hear the director, the late Michael Apted, ask him about being “illegitimate”, until Symon gently sets him straight: “We’re living in different times.” Apted is also admonished for his sexism: why, says Jackie, does he always ask the women about marrying and settling down, but not the men?

We get glimpses of the politics of these years. Lynn was a devoted children’s librarian, until successive rounds of budget cuts hacked away at the service to which she had given much of her life. We hear Tony complain about immigrants enjoying easy access to benefits, including housing – except that footage is from the 1970s, a reminder that the current debates are anything but new. We see that Bruce, who as a seven-year-old aspired to be a missionary in Africa in order to help the neediest, is now a lifeboat volunteer for the RNLI. Aware of the recent assaults on that organisation, we suspect he’s still doing God’s work.

Perhaps most striking is the shifting view of mental illness. When 28 Up aired in 1984, much of the nation was shocked by the fate of Neil, who as a wide-eyed seven-year-old had dreamed of being an astronaut, and who was now found lonely, wandering and homeless. There is vague talk of a “nervous complaint” and Apted asks him, “Can you lick it?”, as if a stiff upper lip and cold shower might do the trick. Now, Neil speaks directly of a lifelong battle with depression, naming it at last.

It’s not wrong to speak of “much of the nation”, by the way. 7 Up came of age in the era of terrestrial, limited-choice TV when the audiences were enormous and major programmes were collective experiences. The medium had weight and a kind of patience, so that a six-decades-long project like this one was at least conceivable. In the age of YouTube Shorts and Instagram Reels, there won’t be another. (Though before we romanticise the olden days too much, 70 Up self-critically notes that the children’s parents never gave anything that we would recognise as consent.)

Still, it’s not here – in the charting of shifts in society or broadcasting – that the magic lies. If the original ambition was to examine class in modern Britain, the series very soon transcended that to becomebigger, to become, like the best works of art, both timeless and universal. As Peter, now retired from teaching, says, “It’s a film about living a human life.”

We see the compromises that real people in real situations have to make. Bruce was once “the only socialist in the village” who, on principle, taught maths at an inner London school to kids who had none of the privileges he had known as a boy. At 49, we found him in a master’s gown at a public school, facing accusations from old friends that he had sold out. But life, we realise, is not political theory. Sometimes it just takes a different course. There are events you cannot plan for, including, of course, the lottery of health and the random intrusions of mortality. You know it’s coming, but it stops you all the same: two of the seven-year-olds of 1964 are dead.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Those who remain are very clear on what matters. One after another, they say they now understand the centrality of family. At 70 and a retired lawyer, Andrew offers an age-old lament when he wonders if, perhaps, he should have forsaken those extra hours in the office that seemed so important at the time, and gone instead to his children’s school play or sports day. Apted overlooked this dimension, too, often asking his subjects about their career disappointments or the apparent modesty of their achievements, failing to see what he eventually recognised as the “power” of the families they had built.

We hardly need to be told that, because we see it for ourselves. We see again and again how these people were shaped, yes, by class but also by the family situations they were born into, and especially by what was missing. So many of them devoted themselves to avoiding the mistakes of their parents, to ensuring their own children enjoyed the stability they had lacked.

Perhaps the most vivid example is Symon. At seven he was in care; now aged 70, it still gnaws at him that he never knew his father. In the 1964 film, the kids visited an adventure playground: Symon and Paul, both raised in the same children’s home, immediately set about moving planks and bricks. They were trying to build a house. In the latest film, we learn that Symon and his wife became foster parents, not just once or twice but, over the decades, to a staggering 130 children. As Symon said of his own children when he was 28, “They’ve got everything. They’ve got a father.” The animating premise of each of the Up films was the old Jesuit saying: “Give me a child until he is seven, and I will give you the man.” There turns out to be great truth in that, a truth far more profound than the political point the film-makers first set out to prove.

As Nick, a boy who dreamed of exploring the moon and went on to become a nuclear physicist, says, we are moved when we see time-lapse photography of a single flower, watching it “blossom and then fade away”. How breathtaking then to see the full span of a human life, several of them at once – the quiet, ordinary mystery of it. How breathtaking and how beautiful.

70 Up is available on ITVX

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

Trump faces tough choices as Iran dangles deal to reopen Hormuz before US midterms

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 15:43:59 GMT

Iran’s seven-day timetable would restart nuclear talks, but will the US be willing to deliver on terms that include reining in Israel in Lebanon?

Iran’s seven-day timetable to reopen the strait of Hormuz and start talks on its nuclear programme has been pitched as a deal that could rapidly extricate Donald Trump from a political crisis but requires the US president to make difficult concessions.

In the five days left before the proposed reopening of the strait, which is expected to relieve pressure on global energy markets, Trump would need to lift Iranian asset freezes, permit Iran to export its oil and, probably most difficult of all, order Benjamin Netanyahu to end Israel’s attacks on Hezbollah in Lebanon, thus achieving the “ceasefire on all fronts”.

Iranian diplomats in New York said they thought a three-hour meeting earlier this week with the US envoy Steve Witkoff in which they laid out the seven-day plan was productive, but were doubtful the US would deliver.

Iran nevertheless feels it has done the diplomatic spadework, taking the proposal to China for endorsement and ensuring that Oman, located on the south side of the strait, was also on board.

The foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, explained that the idea was to take the elements of the Iran-US memorandum of understanding that Trump signed in June and repackage and accelerate the process since, as they understood it, Trump had come to hate the MoU.

“The conditions we have asked the US to meet is nothing new, nothing more than what was already in the Islamabad agreement, which was signed by the US president,” Araghchi said. But what is new is the speed.

In the first four to five days under this timetable, the US would have to lift the naval blockade on Iran’s oil ports, restore the waiver that lifted sanctions on Iran’s oil exports, end the war on all fronts and permit the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets.

On the sixth day, the strait of Hormuz would be reopened by Iran, with ships using a new route designated by Oman and Iran. And on the next day, negotiations would start on the future of Iran’s civil nuclear programme, including a protocol to allow UN nuclear inspectors back in to look at Iran’s damaged sites and the stockpile of highly enriched uranium. This accelerates the point at which nuclear talks would begin, from 60 days in the June agreement to seven.

Those talks could, of course, take a long time, but from Trump’s perspective, the strait of Hormuz would be reopened before the midterm elections, a point in the political calendar that the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, says has never been a factor in Iranian thinking. Trump had claimed Iran was waiting until after the vote to offer a deal.

Iran, Araghchi argued at a largely off-the-record briefing with reporters – at which Pezeshkian was also present – had every reason not to negotiate with the US.

In particular, he admitted to being sceptical that Witkoff could deliver. He recounted how he had twice held talks with Trump’s special envoy, after which Witkoff had described them as “productive and good”, only for the US to bomb Iran the next day. Other Iranian diplomats say Trump’s willingness to rein in Netanyahu in Lebanon remains key. If he could do that, a deal would be feasible.

It is a difficult deal for Trump to swallow since the strait would reopen largely on Iran’s terms, with the new route predominantly going through Iranian waters. Saudi Arabia is also concerned that the route deal is bilateral between Iran and Oman, and not with the Gulf states as joint signatories.

Trump says he has a choice to make between the annihilation of Iran and engagement – an engagement that, he says with typical hyperbole, could make Iran one of the great countries of the world. In reality, the judgment he has to make is more prosaic. Is he prepared to go back to war with Iran after the midterms and, if not, does he believe the US can squeeze the Iranian economy so hard that the leadership will succumb.

Pezeshkian, who handed all questions about the talks to Araghchi, admitted Iranians wanted the war to end and did not deny the economic pressure, but said the public had withstood sanctions for 45 years.

He also insisted Iran’s decision-making machinery was functioning. The reclusive supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, was completely healthy, he claimed, a testimony based on spending seven hours in his presence. He did not explain why, apart from security, Khamenei had not issued a voice recording, photograph or video as proof of life.

Manchester City found guilty of breaking Premier League’s financial fair play rules

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 15:35:49 GMT

City face sanctions after more than 100 rule breaches

Club insist on innocence and are expected to appeal

Manchester City have been found guilty of the vast majority of more than a hundred charges related to breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules, throwing English football into turmoil.

The serial champions now face the possibility of being relegated from the Premier League, or expelled from the competition altogether, after a verdict in the biggest disciplinary case in the history of the sport was finally delivered.

Neither party was willing to publicly confirm the outcome on Friday with an appeal process expected to be pursued imminently by City. Two years after the hearings first began, however, there is now some clarity as to the scale of City’s rule-breaking.

The 134 charges made against City cover the seasons 2009-10 to 2022-23 and cover a number of areas, with the most serious relating to claims that the club failed to provide “accurate financial information” to the league during this time. From season 2009-10 to 2022-23 inclusive City won seven Premier League titles, a Champions League, three FA Cups and six League Cups.

A City spokesperson said: “The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the club’s statement of February 2023.

“The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.”

The Premier League did not comment, citing the confidential nature of the case. Club executives are understood to have learned about the outcome following a shareholders’ meeting in central London on Thursday and subsequently signed non-disclosure agreements.

In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.

If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.

If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.

Andy Burnham was asked about the news on Friday evening. The prime minister told ITV Granada Reports: “I’ve only just been made aware of it – I think these are reports at this stage. But if they’re confirmed, obviously I will want to look at the report of the independent commission.

“People shouldn’t jump to those kind of conclusions. I know, this has been a long process between the club and the Premier League. I think quite a contested process. So I don’t think it’s as simple as jumping to conclusions. I think we would all need to study the independent commission’s report in some considerable detail before reaching any conclusions.”

The verdict was reached more than three and a half years after the 134 charges were first brought and more than two years since disciplinary hearings began. According to the Premier League rulebook, the appeal process has a stricter time frame, whereby any party who wishes to appeal a decision by a judicial panel must do so by email within 14 days of a decision being announced. Under rule W.86 any hearing should conclude no longer than 12 weeks after the first appeal is submitted. Any decision by the appeal board must also be published, alongside full written reasons, within 30 days of the conclusion of the hearing.

Should City fail in their appeal, the judicial panel would then be expected to produce its verdict on the level of sanction applied to the club. Premier League rule W.64 describes the list of punishments available to a panel. Alongside levying a fine, any disciplinary committee could first suspend a club from competition, or levy a points deduction, or in the most extreme circumstances expel a club from competition altogether.

Such is the scale of the charges brought against City that there is no direct comparison to be made with other disciplinary cases. The recent case involving Chelsea, who were found to have breached the FA’s rules on agents on 74 occasions, resulted only in a cash fine of £10m but Chelsea were adjudged not to have gained significant sporting advantage from their actions and were praised for self-reporting the misdemeanours, which had occurred under the ownership of Roman Abramovich. Neither of these factors would appear to apply in the City case, given the systemic claims of financial misreporting and the fact that a majority of the charges related to a failure to comply with league rules.

The unprecedented catalogue of charges related to five distinct areas of alleged rule-breaking. More than 80 charges related to a club’s obligation to act in “the utmost good faith” when relaying information to the Premier League and to give complete disclosure of any information requested. These claims pointed towards the league’s belief that City had given an inaccurate picture of the club’s financial situation and withheld documents that might have cast greater light on it.

The rest of the charges related to alleged breaches of profitability and sustainability rules (PSR) and the related Uefa financial fair play regulations. Finally, 20 charges related to the club’s obligation to provide “full details of … remuneration”, with breaches being claimed in the rules relating to the payment of players and managers.

The extent of the charge sheet reflected a process that had been a decade in the making. Uefa found City in breach of FFP in 2014, a decision which resulted in City paying a €20m fine. The Football Leaks affair, in which millions of private documents relating to football clubs and players were hacked and made public in 2015, led to reporting on City’s affairs and a new investigation from Uefa. By 2020, Uefa had suspended City from the Champions League for “overstating its sponsorship revenue in its accounts”. This suspension was overturned by City on appeal to the court of arbitration for sport.

In December 2018 the Premier League began its own investigation into City. A highly secretive inquiry, which required legal action by the Mail on Sunday to prove it was taking place, it is believed to have been inspired by the Football Leaks revelations and resulted, four years later, in City being charged.

From shocking cruelty to the reason Claudia hid in a bush: 10 things you need to know about The Celebrity Traitors

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 15:00:10 GMT

Meltdowns, more contestants, Ross Kemp being ‘the daddy’: read on for our guide to the return of TV’s best reality gameshow

Prepare to become obsessed with famous people backstabbing and betraying one another in a Scottish castle. Yes, autumn is upon us, meaning the return of last year’s TV sensation, The Celebrity Traitors.

The inaugural VIP version of the BBC’s reality gameshow proved a runaway hit and broke ratings records as Alan Carr chaotically schemed and sobbed his way to victory. The second series promises to be bigger, better and more murderous with extra episodes, shock twists and an even starrier lineup.

The cloaks are freshly laundered. Poisoned chalices have been polished. Claudia Winkleman has fluffed her pet owl’s feathers. With less than a week to go, here’s everything you need to know …

This year’s contest has an expanded field of 21, up from 19, and has attracted what has been hailed as “one of the most high-profile casts ever assembled for a reality show”. Filming took place from late May to early June in the now-familiar surroundings of Ardross Castle in the Scottish Highlands. The cast stayed 30 miles away at Inverness Airport’s Courtyard by Marriott hotel.

The headline names – “Big Dogs”, in Traitors parlance – are the actors Richard E Grant and Michael Sheen, the supermodel Jerry Hall and the comedian Miranda Hart, making a welcome TV comeback after years out of the spotlight due to chronic illness. They’re joined by the singers James Blunt and Leigh-Anne Pinnock, formerly of girlband Little Mix, alongside soap royalty Ross Kemp (AKA EastEnders’ Grant Mitchell) and Julie Hesmondhalgh (AKA Coronation Street’s Hayley Cropper).

There are boffins in the mathematician Prof Hannah Fry and University Challenge quizmaster Amol Rajan, plus half a dozen relative youngsters: the actors Bella Ramsey, Myha’la, Sebastian Croft and Sharon Rooney, plus the Love Island presenter Maya Jama and the content creator King Kenny. The cast is rounded out by slightly too many comedians: Joanne McNally, Rob Beckett, Romesh Ranganathan, Joe Lycett and James Acaster.

She might have bowed out of Strictly Come Dancing but fear not, Winkleman still presides over this contest, sporting her trademark fringe and talking-point wardrobe. “It goes a little Artful Dodger for this series,” she admits. The presenter also confessed to corpsing regularly, adding: “Rob Beckett said something that made me hide in a bush until I composed myself.”

Richard Osman caused a kerfuffle three weeks ago by letting slip the embargoed launch date. During a live edition of The Rest Is Entertainment podcast, he let slip that the series would start on 23 September. Cue sighs of relief at Traitors HQ because Osman was wrong.

The mind games actually begin on Thursday 1 October at 8pm on BBC One, kicking off with an extended 75-minute opener. There’s also a one-off bonus show, Traitor or Faithful? Claudia Decides, exclusive to BBC iPlayer and revealing how La Winkle chooses her cloaked conspirators.

The series will air two nights each week, on Thursday and Friday. Last year’s run had nine episodes but the BBC has realised it’s on to a winner and added one to make 10. Each will be directly followed by spin-off show Celebrity Traitors: Uncloaked, the “vizpod” (visualised podcast) helmed by comedian Ed Gamble.

McNally and Ramsey are bookies’ favourites to win, followed by Blunt and Sheen. Ramsey is predicted to be a strategic player, after revealing they have been playing a similar board game for the past 12 years.

Jama and Acaster are also hotly tipped. King Kenny is the rank outsider, with Rajan just behind. Your starter for 10: will he be first out?

Two trailers have been released so far and fans have been scrutinising them for clues. Ramsey is shown suppressing a devilish smirk, suggesting they might be a Traitor. Thespy elders Sheen and Grant look as if they’re relishing the action. Blunt and Jama appear equally thrilled.

Rajan gives an annoying wink at the Round Table, which could be pride before a fall. There’s also eager anticipation of how Myha’la’s name might be misspelt on the slates. Hart seems endearingly excited but hard man Kemp looks terrified. Perhaps he’s seen the ghost of Paloma Faith.

The “toxically competitive” Fry says she used statistical analysis and Alan Turing’s codebreaking strategies to give her an edge. Action man Kemp apparently emerges as “the Daddy” in the early stages, leading the group on their first mission.

Grant admits to being surprised by the game’s “cruelty”. On a more lavatorial note, Lycett confessed that he spent his entire castle stint “trying not to fart”.

The debut series was a smash hit, dominating the pop cultural conversation for weeks. It averaged 14.9 million viewers, peaking at 15.4 million for the final. This made it the year’s most-watched show and the top-rated entertainment programme since 2016. Can the follow-up hit the same heights?

An intriguing rumour is that a third of the contestants, ie seven, end up as Traitors, presumably meaning plenty of recruitment to the turret. Gamble promises a “wildly different game”, while Ed Havard, the BBC’s director of entertainment, says: “Things happen that you didn’t think could happen on Traitors and have never seen before.”

The Guardian’s own Marina Hyde has promised “some real meltdowns – mainly from the men”. Osman added that it’s “intense”, while tabloids have teased “an epic sequel”, full of “plot twists and paranoia”.

Celebrities have also been complaining about their official headshots. Beckett wrote on Instagram: “I think there’s a Traitor in the Photoshop department. What the fuck has happened to my face?” Jama was quick to reply, adding: “They did us all dirty tbh.”

There’s been speculation that showrunners want the Faithful to win. After all, Traitors have triumphed in the last two UK series – Carr in the celebrity spin-off, Stephen Libby and Rachel Duffy in this year’s civilian edition. Does this mean producers will tip the game to favour the Faithful?

This year’s extensive cohort of comedians have grumbled that the “Alan Carr factor” means they will automatically be mistrusted, making it harder for them to win. Some have taken this to mean none of Hart, McNally, Beckett, Lycett, Acaster nor Ranganathan survive until the later stages.

However, McNally let slip on her podcast that she knows who wins. Only players who get close to the endgame know this, hinting that McNally is among them.

The Celebrity Traitors is on BBC One on 1 October

This article was amended on 25 September 2026 to use the correct pronouns for Bella Ramsey.

Our lives and identities have moved online – and it’s driving us insane

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 15:00:09 GMT

People have become servants to social media. The ultimate flex is to walk back to real life

Think of your online life as a garden. At first it’s just a few seeds here or there – a Facebook profile where you created entire albums from a night at the pub, or maybe a Tumblr or a Myspace page listing your favourite bands. It is fun – something just for you and your friends to enjoy.

Then the garden grows. You get an Instagram account and document moments from each day on Stories, use LinkedIn for networking and sharing career triumphs, and check your X/Twitter hyper-vigilantly in case you wrote something that just got you cancelled.

Your online garden grows more sprawling and complex; now it’s no longer just a fun project for yourself on weekends and weeknights. As it grows, you start to view it through the eyes of others.

How will this garden be seen? Will people like it? What can I plant in this garden that will make more people like it?

A few more years pass. And now, instead of working on the garden here and there, you’re in there all the time. You have discovered if your garden is really enticing, you can make money off it. You want – then need – big numbers coming in there. You look at other people’s gardens all the time and you get jealous. They have better gardens.

When you’re not in your garden, you’re still somehow tending to it – looking at the number of people coming in, and comparing them with what it used to be, and being worried that maybe you didn’t plant the right things. But people will tell you if you’re doing it wrong. They’ll spray paint all over the garden walls how much your garden sucks, how you’re a loser, how ugly it all is.

And with all this activity going on you hardly notice how, over time, the world outside your garden has shrunk, until soon there is no outside world. The garden is your home now.

When this current moment ends and a more enlightened time kicks in, descendants looking back will see that millions (or is it billions?) of us have spent the last 10 years or more migrating our lives and identities, and our political, communal and social selves, to a digital realm that has sent many of us insane.

The (digital) signal that we are living a better life has been imbued with more energy and importance than living a better life itself.

Those descendants will see what we can’t really see now – a massive serf culture has emerged, where people have become servants to these gardens.

They’ll see how truly unfree so many of us are – allowing the rich, real, tactile world to recede, while the digital gardens have sprawled to take up all our time and energy (the average user spends about 2 hours and 39 minutes a day on social media.)

And it will become apparent that the real elite won’t be the people with the most popular digital gardens. They’ll be the people who never had gardens. Or people who had small private gardens, where they only let a few friends in.

Brand strategists and trend forecasters are saying that, in 2026, the true measure of status is privacy and a low or no digital footprint.

This is a different way of living off-grid.

You experience a rich and interesting life in the real world and don’t feel the need to post about it.

Sign up to Five Great Reads

Each week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morning

after newsletter promotion

Your sense of self worth is not linked to how many people see that you’ve been somewhere, hung out with someone or worn something.

Your income, status and financial security is not dependent on your social media account.

Your attention span has not been corrupted or shortened by chronic social media consumption and AI use – and this gives you almost superhuman powers such as the ability to read long, difficult novels, think critically, and retain information in your head.

Your emotional stability is not dependent on how your content is performing.

You have not internalised the digital panopticon where everything you do is with an eye to how it is perceived.

You have a healthy social life in the real world, meaning you have less time or inclination to post.

Brand strategist Eugene Healey in his Substack wrote a recent series on “post-luxury status symbols” and said “the greatest privilege is to be chronically offline” and “in this culture of overexposure – it’s only natural that it becomes desirable to opt out”.

The ultimate flex is not needing social media, walking away from your digital garden and back into your real life.

Brigid Delaney is the author of five books, including The Seeker and the Sage

‘We will get stuff done’: Burnham seeks to banish ghosts of Starmerism at Labour conference

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 14:25:25 GMT

The PM returns to Liverpool, where he was mocked last year, with a promise that no one will be left wondering what he’s trying to do

UK politics live – latest updates

Andy Burnham was not even in the audience for the prime minister’s speech at the Labour party conference this time last year. As Keir Starmer made the case for continuity to his restive party, Burnham was spotted slipping out over the bridge towards Liverpool’s Albert Dock.

The then Greater Manchester mayor had been vying for the spotlight throughout the party’s annual gathering, presenting the argument for change. But even he could not have envisaged the schism that would take place in the ensuing 12 months and would put him on the main stage as prime minister at this year’s conference, beginning in Merseyside on Sunday.

At the time, Starmer retained a tentative grip on the party, while Burnham was mocked for leaving Liverpool with his tail between his legs, awkward and abashed, especially over his controversial comments about the government being too “in hock” to the bond markets.

But below the surface, disquiet was starting to take shape in the party. Several cabinet ministers confided privately in Liverpool last year that they believed Burnham would ultimately be seen as the party’s Cassandra: comically ham-fisted, but nonetheless telling hard truths about the party’s problems.

After he succeeded Starmer in the top job in July, Burnham has made “Hope again” his conference slogan, with No 10 strategists pitching this year’s event as a definitive break with the past.

Burnham has been promising to defy the political and economic consensus of the last 40 years since he was elected as MP for Makerfield in a byelection that proved to be the final domino for Starmer’s faltering leadership, and he will use this conference to set out how he aims to do this.

It will also attempt to break old habits in the Labour party’s way of doing business, which has often been hindered by pessimism, fear and factionalism. Cynics in the party will wonder if this effort can withstand current economic pressures, given soaring borrowing costs.

Hayden Munro, Burnham’s new political director, has told cabinet ministers and special advisers they must defy such cynics, and every message they send must be about how there is renewed faith in Britain.

Munro, a former strategist for Jacinda Ardern, who colleagues say is the “in-house hype man”, told them the theme of conference would be how help was coming for ordinary working people.

Burnham’s government would put care of people as the first consideration, he told them, restoring “the right values” – a nod to the widespread fears in Labour about the rise of overt racism across the political sphere.

Ministers have been tasked with announcing policies that deliver immediate breathing room for families, but also long-term plans and investment to make everyday life easier and more affordable, with a particular focus on public control of essential services. Burnham will emphasise again that he intends to deliver the biggest change to Britain in 40 years.

But the other theme of the conference will be courage, that this will finally be a government that will fix problems long been thought to be intractable: rough sleeping, social care, and youth inactivity.

“‘It’s too hard’ will no longer be used as a justification for not acting,” Munro wrote in his note to advisers. “We will get stuff done.”

Addressing the Labour conference in Liverpool is a kind of homecoming for Burnham, even though he is most closely associated with Manchester. He was born in its suburbs, it is where he had his formative political awakening on the Hillsborough injustice, and the area where he returned just a fortnight ago in tragic circumstances, after his father’s death from Alzheimer’s.

Burnham writes all of his own speeches and has spent the last few weeks, in between meetings and travelling by train between London and Manchester, working through his ideas. He told reporters at the UN general assembly in New York this week that his conference speech would be his own political philosophy spelled out in primary colours.

“I keep saying: ‘Nobody won’t know what I’m trying to do.’ People will know, you can make your judgment on whether it’s right or wrong. But people are going to know the direction I want to take this country in,” he said.

This approach marks a definitive break with Starmerism. One Labour strategist said: “If we achieve one thing at this conference, it will be that no one will ever say about Andy Burnham what they said about Keir Starmer. You can never say ‘we don’t know what he stands for’.”

Burnham is the beneficiary of a gentler political landscape than Starmer was a year ago, when Reform and the rapid rise of far-right demonstrations had dominated the summer. Labour had been sinking in the polls even before the scandal-fuelled resignations of Angela Rayner and Peter Mandelson just weeks before the event.

Going into conference now, Labour is in the lead with all pollsters for the first time since October 2024, partly thanks to Burnham’s own bounce but also as a result of declining trust in Reform after a series of scandals.

There is very little appetite for rebellion among the Labour rank and file who have often made it awkward for Labour leaders with votes on the conference floor. “It is going to be very boring,” one senior party figure said. “Everyone is desperate to make it work.”

after newsletter promotion

Activists will be pushing for conference to commit to a commission on electoral reform, which Burnham has said he will put in Labour’s next manifesto but which strategists do not want to make a major topic of his first months in office. At least three dozen local parties have submitted motions on the subject, more than on any single policy issue since conference rules were tightened in 2023, making it likely it will be one of the priority topics for debate.

The only other unwelcome surprise would be an emergency motion on Israel and Palestine. Ministers had hoped Ed Miliband’s announcement of sweeping sanctions against West Bank settlements would be an answer to calls for Labour to take a much more robust position on Israel.

But party staff believe something more could come when emergency motions are tabled this weekend. “There is always another demand, and conference will always vote for almost anything put in front of it on this,” another senior figure said. “The unions have very left policy mandates.”

Most of the exiled former cabinet ministers and Starmer loyalists are swerving conference this year – the exception being Darren Jones, the former chief secretary to the prime minister, who will take part in some keenly watched fringes. But few have his inclination. One ex-minister said he did not feel welcome.

“No one wants a spectre at the feast,” he said. “Any appearance is going to attract some unwelcome attention. I do think more of us will start to speak out, whether on oil and gas, on the economy, maybe on Europe, but frankly doing that at conference is too unhelpful – even if it’s the kind of tactic that Andy himself has been doing for years.”

Many said they saw it as a chance for a break. One former minister close to Starmer compared himself to Arsenal’s Declan Rice, who played more minutes last season than any other English footballer but who will now sit out England’s matches over the international break. “I haven’t had a rest in about six years. I think it makes sense to miss the first Labour conference in about 15 years,” he said.

There will be time for interventions – helpful or otherwise – in the coming months. Conference is the first of four phases that No 10 views as opportunities for Burnham to seize public attention and set direction. After that will be the budget, his 10-year plan expected later in the autumn, and then the spending review next year.

But if conference gives Burnham another poll boost, it will add to the chatter in Westminster that he could decide to call a general election sooner rather than later.

“Conference could be make-or-break for that decision,” one MP said. “If the left looks united, if the polls continue as they are – and if we then beat [the Greens’ Zack] Polanski in Holborn and St Pancras then there will never be a better time.”

Most cabinet ministers are wary. “Why are we here if not to use this majority we have got to improve the country?” one said. “If we are saying we are here to get things done, then let’s do them now.”

For now, Burnham seems to agree. Speaking to broadcasters before the conference, he said he was “not particularly” tempted to call an election. “I see all the speculation and it just races ahead,” he told BBC West’s political editor, Paul Barltrop.

“The time has come: draw a line, get the country looking forward, pulling together, people feeling a bit of hope in their lives again. That’s what I’m trying to do, and I hope to take it further in the coming period rather than putting people back into an election cycle.”
