Game, set … match? Can a dating coach help you win at love?

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 14:00:08 GMT

Would you pay thousands to meet the love of your life? In an age of app fatigue, many singles are hiring coaches to help them find partners. But are they chancers preying on the lovelorn, or do they hold the key to true romance?

Modern dating is a hellscape. Just ask any single person, who will probably regale you with stories of endless swiping, ghosting, cringe Hinge dates and unfulfilling “situationships”. But what if there was a way to escape all this and put yourself on a fast track to finding The One?

That very aim is driving the rise of dating coaches – people who make money from helping their clients to find a partner. According to the New York Times, now is a better time than ever to be a relationship coach, with the widespread dissatisfaction with dating apps and a growing sense of “heteropessimism” fuelling their popularity. In 2023, Shirley Williams, a then 37‑year‑old from New York, went viral when she posted a video sharing that she spent $10,000 on a dating coach, and got engaged within a year. Her post sparked intense debate between people who thought it was a ridiculous expense, and others who wondered why this was so much more controversial than, say, investing in education, travel and work.

Dating coaches shouldn’t be confused with matchmakers, who aim to fast-track things by setting their clients up with people. Instead, most coaches follow a programme of self-care and confidence exercises, alongside elements of manifestation – the very unscientific practice of visualising your life goals. My instinctive reaction was to assume that they’re simply the latest way for my generation of millennials to outsource our problems. And after speaking to coaches and their clients, I’m still sceptical that they’re the key to finding love, but I’ve learned that there’s much more to it. In fact, if you want to form a better relationship with dating, or figure out where you’ve been going wrong, then a dating coach may be just what you need.

My introduction to dating coaches happened at a party, when I got talking to Izzy, who excitedly told me how hiring one had changed her life. At 30, Izzy had never been in a relationship. “At one point, I was the only one in a female friendship group of 15 who was single, so I found that really alienating,” she says. “It makes you feel like you’ve done something wrong – like there’s a missing piece in the puzzle.” It got so bad that Izzy had begun to internalise the belief that she was uniquely unworthy of love. But that started to change when her brother introduced her to dating coach Lucy Yarrow. A year after completing the 12-week Love With Lucy programme, Izzy is nine months into her first serious relationship – and she couldn’t be happier.

How did the coaching actually work? Yarrow’s programme was based around identifying Izzy’s “limiting beliefs” about herself – for example, that she was “going to be single for ever” – and challenging the ways they were holding her back from finding love. The first step was delving into her romantic past, all the way back to her first kiss, to find the origin of her insecurities. “Through that, so many things surfaced – some of the terrible, awful horror stories I hadn’t really shared or picked up on, even from being a teenager,” Izzy remembers. “Obviously, that shapes who we are now. So we did a full retrospective.”

Once they had identified the core issues, Izzy was given “empowering beliefs” to counter negative thoughts about herself. (Including slides featuring daily tasks, with written affirmations to read out loud.) Yarrow also set her homework, like asking herself a specific set of questions after a date, such as, “What side of me did they bring out?” and “Did I feel valued and attractive in their company?”

In fact, one of the biggest hurdles Izzy had to overcome was learning to focus on her own experience. She realised she was so preoccupied by wondering what men were thinking on dates that she forgot to even consider whether she was enjoying herself. “I’d always go to these negative spaces like, ‘What if he doesn’t want another date? What if he ghosts me?’” she explains. “I think that’s a pattern a lot of women probably fall into, because we’re conditioned to be that way. But Lucy would say: ‘Izzy, you also have autonomy and power here. What is it that you want?’”

It’s important to note that, while many dating coaches have some life coaching qualifications, they don’t have to undergo any official training. Unlike professionally regulated titles, such as psychiatrist, anybody can call themselves a coach (or a therapist, because many therapist titles aren’t protected either). Ian MacRae, a psychologist and member of the British Psychological Society’s research board, says dating coaches are essentially left to self-regulate and are not bound by the same rules as his peers, such as patient confidentiality. This is what allows so many life and dating coaches to double as content creators on Instagram and TikTok (or appear as “experts” on reality shows such as Married at First Sight).

Even so, MacRae says this doesn’t mean they’re all bad: “Most people who do it are probably well meaning, but a subsection of them are actually good at it, so it’s about doing the research to figure out who is both well-meaning and good at it.”

Many coaches have completed some form of training. Yarrow, who coached Izzy, studied at The Clique Academy (now known as She Leads) – an online programme that specialises in training women to be life coaches. She tells me that the vast majority of her clients are heterosexual women in their 30s, and that the most crucial part of the process is zoning in on what they actually want. “A lot of people want a partner, but it’s about really homing in on what those top priorities are. I want to be in a relationship and feel ‘X, Y, Z’ with someone who is ‘X, Y, Z’.”

How much does all of this cost? As with therapists, the prices of dating coaches can vary immensely. Some have huge social followings and charge thousands for their guidance. Yarrow costs about £85 a session, depending on the length, with clients usually requiring between eight and 12 weekly meetings to cover her programme.

The rise of dating coaches, plus the fact that they seem to be largely a heterosexual phenomenon, points to a growing dissonance in straight dating culture. In her 2025 book, Love in Exile, the writer Shon Faye describes this as a “crisis of expectation”. In previous generations, the primary goal was for men to be a provider, but today women want someone who can be a best friend, a therapist, a soulmate, with whom they share emotional intelligence and a physical connection – a list that most straight men aren’t yet being socialised to fulfil.

Laurence Houde, who is based in New York City, has been working as a men’s dating coach for two and a half years. She realised that, although we’re used to hearing about the so-called “dating crisis” from women, men are equally unhappy with the romantic experiences they’re having. She usually starts with a 90-minute session, priced at $397. This features a “love life audit” of previous partners, and includes a week of follow-up support, including messages and voice notes.

Sign up to Inside Saturday

The only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.

after newsletter promotion

Houde splits her clients into two categories. The first are men who are “a little bit more emotionally prepared to invest in a relationship” and have already done some of the “groundwork” on their own, often with the help of a therapist. The second category don’t quite understand what’s not working yet and wonder what they’re doing wrong. These men, she says, can be prime targets for manosphere influencers, who cynically use their insecurities as a gateway to extreme, misogynistic content online. Instead, she takes the opposite approach. “Usually, I find that expressing their emotions doesn’t come as easily for them,” she says. “Often, it’s a fear of being seen, so we look at that fear and dig into why it’s there, and then I give them exercises to overcome it.”

Perhaps the most interesting thing about the rise of dating coaches is how they normalise the idea of changing yourself to find love. When millennials like me were growing up, romcoms promoted the fantasy of being loved for being totally yourself, flaws and all. (At the end of Bridget Jones’s Diary, Mark Darcy tells the clumsy, expletive-loving, cigarette-puffing heroine: “I like you very much just as you are.”) This summer, The Project – the debut novel by British Vogue dating columnist Annie Lord – suggested that the dating zeitgeist has shifted. In the book, Daisy and her best friend, Maya, essentially act as coaches (in all but name) to James – a friend from university who they think has so much potential if he could learn to open up about his emotions and dress a little better. When romantic feelings start to develop between James and Daisy, she realises it’s not just James who needs to change, because she’s got a lot of deep-rooted patterns that are holding her back, too.

Lord tells me that when she was writing the book she started therapy and began to unpack some of the reasons why she has been single for so long. (These included being attracted to men who weren’t interested in her, and suspicious of those who were.) “I poured a lot of that into Daisy’s character, which is why she probably goes through a bigger change than James by the end,” she says. “And change can be good. Right now, we’re treating people so disposably that we don’t allow the space for them to change. We’re not patient enough.”

If you’re thinking about hiring a dating coach, it’s advisable to be sceptical of anyone demanding thousands for their services – particularly those who make unrealistic promises about finding Happily Ever After, or suggest you can “manifest” your way to love by carrying crystals, lighting candles and chanting. “My advice,” MacRae says, “whether you’re seeing a psychologist, a psychiatrist, a therapist or a dating coach, is taking everything with a grain of salt.”

But if you can find the right coach, with a reasonably priced programme that works for you? Then there is potential for personal growth – and, yes, love. “My goal was to find a partner, but it wasn’t really about that,” Izzy says. “I needed to feel happy, confident and good at being single and exploring romance. I needed to do the work to be in a better place myself.”

I love a drink in the stands, but Burnham’s beer proposal feels out of step with modern football

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 14:00:08 GMT

Focusing on the right to drink at your seat is an odd place to start when discrimination in the game runs much deeper

Andy Burnham is right that football fans have historically been treated differently from other sports fans. But if we’re going to talk about discrimination in football, the ban on drinking at your seat feels like a strange place to start.

The rule may have its roots in a very different era of football, but for many fans today, being able to take a pint to your seat may not be top of their list of changes they’d like to see in the game. Especially at a time when discrimination is very much present elsewhere in football.

The legislation, introduced under Margaret Thatcher in the 1980s as part of a crackdown on football hooliganism, was rooted in the idea that football fans needed to be treated differently from the supposedly better-behaved crowds at rugby and cricket – which smacks of classism and the stereotyping of working-class fans. But football has changed since then, and so has drinking culture. Fans have adapted to the restrictions and built a matchday ritual around them. A good fan concourse pint is up there with an airport pint or a beer-garden pint on the first day of summer.

Fans have got used to this routine, and one of the biggest concerns of lifting this ban now seems to be the Boxpark-ification of football: the dreaded performative beer throw when anything good happens.

Even when it’s not performative, it does raise a problem of logistics. With no cup holders, when a 95th-minute winner goes in and you’re suddenly off your seat with your limbs in the air, a pint is unlikely to remain where you left it. There will be people walking back and forth from the concourse during the game for another pint or the toilet, too. It used to happen before, of course, but it would still be a new irritation that fans would have to adapt to. And, most importantly, it isn’t a change many fans seem to have been asking for.

As a fan of both men’s and women’s football, I’ve experienced the Women’s Super League’s successful trial of beer at your seats, as well as drinking at non-league games, and it was a nice change. It has even become a distinct part of the matchday experience in leagues where the atmosphere is different and the crowds are smaller. But the women’s game is not simply the men’s game with fewer people in the stands. The matchday experience is different – and that’s important when we talk about what works.

Watching Everton Women with a beer in hand can be lovely. So can spending a long day at the cricket with a pint. But I was also at the game in which Chloe Kelly scored the winner for England against Germany at Euro 2022, and was immediately swallowed up in the chaos of the celebrations, being thrown around by the people around me. Having a pint in my hand in that moment would have been less than ideal. Beer and football can clearly coexist, but what works at one level of the game, or in one kind of crowd, doesn’t necessarily translate neatly to another.

But this is where Burnham’s argument starts to feel out of step with the reality of football now. At a time when working-class fans are being priced out of their season tickets, racist, sexist, homophobic online abuse is ever-present, and figures at the very top of the game – such as Jim Ratcliffe – use their platform to push deeply divisive politics, it feels out of touch to make the right to drink a pint in your seat a headline example of football discrimination.

And that’s not to deny discrimination of working-class fans, but this is a problem that runs much deeper in the game. And if the old assumption is that football fans are uniquely likely to cause trouble when alcohol is involved, lifting the ban doesn’t automatically remove that belief. It’s possible these biases will show up in how games are policed, with a heavy pre-emptive police and security presence.

If the ban is lifted, there’ll be teething problems, there will be beer showers, complaints and no doubt a bunch of stories in the press making an example of any issues of violence held up as evidence that football fans can’t be trusted with a pint. Eventually, though, fans will adapt, security will relax and, for the most part, it will probably become normal.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

But that’s precisely why Burnham’s argument feels like such an odd intervention. There are serious questions about class and access in football that deserve to be scrutinised as discrimination. If Burnham wants to tackle the ways football fans are treated unfairly, there are plenty of other places to start.

Football fans have every right to drink their beer wherever the rules allow. But sometimes a pint is just a pint – and football has bigger battles to fight.

Marva Kreel is a broadcaster and football content creator

Jeffrey Donaldson, the former leader of the Democratic Unionist party in Northern Ireland, could be sent to prison for more than 10 years over the sexual assault of two women when they were children, a court heard on Friday.

Donaldson, 63, who is planning to appeal, sat stony-faced throughout the 70-minute pre-sentencing hearing in Newry courthouse.

In a statement, they said: “Noah was a happy, cheeky, playful three-year-old boy who loved to laugh, loved to giggle and who brought joy wherever he went. He was part of a loving and caring family, living with his mummy, daddy and his little baby brother. He was at the centre of our world.

“Noah was being assessed for autism, although he had not received a diagnosis. He also had mild hearing loss and was speech delayed.

He said they walked to an under-fives play area and CCTV footage in the park “showed Noah playing with his relative”. He said the relative, who was not named at the hearing, had provided a statement to police. Noah was found by a Met police diver “approximately 5 metres from the bank and within submerged tree roots”. The depth was estimated at 1.8 metres at that point, he added.

A postmortem examination at Addenbrooke’s hospital mortuary in Cambridge recorded his medical cause of death as pending further investigation, Connick said.

The Suffolk assistant coroner Jyoti Gill said at the outset of the hearing, which was not attended by the boy’s family: “I would like to express my deepest condolences to Noah’s family and friends and all those affected by Noah’s death.”

She said at the end of the six-minute hearing: “The inquest is adjourned to a date to be fixed in due course.”

Noah’s father, Rhys Woods, had paid tribute to his son in a message shared on a community Facebook group last week. He described Noah as the “sweetest and most innocent little boy, with nothing but love to give”, and added: “We are going to miss him so very much.”

Football players paid tribute to Noah during Everton’s home match against Ipswich Town on Saturday by wearing black armbands.

For all his youth, such has been Kimi Antonelli’s consummate control this season he has barely put a foot wrong. In qualifying for the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, however, he was given a salutary reminder that the full-on commitment that makes him so engrossing to watch can still bite.

Antonelli’s error was uncharacteristic and, he conceded, unnecessary. He knows his lead in the championship – 81 points over Russell – is such that he need take no chances, especially at a track where Mercedes enjoy such a huge advantage over their rivals. Russell’s pole, an immense lap of the street circuit in Baku, was eight-tenths clear of Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc in second, the largest margin to pole of the season.

Antonelli has been a revelation in only his second season in F1 with eight victories so far but on Friday in Baku he was sat disconsolately trackside after only 11 minutes of running. A little too eager into the 90-degree left-handed turn one, he clipped the barrier.

He took damage to the track rod and a puncture and while he attempted to bring the car home, he was told to park up by a race engineer Pete Bonnington. “We can’t fix this, mate,” Bonnington said. The 20-year-old’s time was enough to see him through to Q2, in which he took no part. Finishing in 16th and angry with himself he held his hands up to the error, caught out as the grip ramped up.

“I turned in and suddenly I had a lot more front end than the lap before and touched the wall,” he said. “Mistake from my side, very unnecessary. I’m very mad about it and we’ll try to do better tomorrow. We’ll try our best to recover as many places as possible.”

The mistake is Antonelli’s only serious error this year since he crashed in final practice at the season-opening Australian Grand Prix and he was understandably crestfallen, aware a fractional misjudgment had been enormously costly.

Russell in is every position to take advantage and to try to claw back some of the points he desperately needs to keep the title fight alive but Antonelli knows that the race is far from a write-off.

At Monza he came back from 19th to take victory and Baku, with its long straights, has similarly generous opportunities for overtaking. But he cannot afford to be caught in incidents in the midfield.

“Race smart in the early stages tomorrow and I am sure he has the pace to climb his way back up the field,” said the Mercedes deputy team principal, Bradley Lord.

The prosecutor Kevin Lucie, outlining the basis of the criminal damage charge, alleged Thomas slashed an adrift boat with a knife.

He told the court: “On 22 September, around 4.30pm, the defendant on his social platform livestreamed himself from a boat on the English Channel. He broadcast to a significant number of people a boat of migrants being supported by the RNLI in the English Channel. It was a single Rib [rigid inflatable boat] which was adrift.

“He armed himself with a knife. He slashed the boat.”

Lucie said Thomas was arrested at a BP service station and taken into custody, where his mobile phone was seized but he allegedly refused to provide the pin code.

When asked about the boat, Lucie confirmed he was unsure if the damage was worth more or less than £5,000, and said: “Unfortunately, it is the case that it did go back to France. We have asked for the cost of the damage.”

Thomas, also known as Danny Tommo, was refused bail. The father of four, described as a professional roofer, was seen dabbing his eyes with a tissue at one point during the hearing.

He appeared for the hearing via video link, wearing a black top and grey coat, and spoke only to confirm his name and date of birth. He was supported in court by his teenage son, as well as fellow far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, also known as Tommy Robinson. Other supporters were placed in a separate room to watch a live stream from the court, a routine measure when interest in a case outstrips the space available in a courtroom.

There was a visible police presence, with an officer in the public gallery of the courtroom, another at the courtroom door and third in the seated waiting area outside the courtroom.

On Thursday evening, several hundred people, many wearing black, gathered outside a police investigation centre in Basingstoke, apparently in the belief Thomas was inside. Dozens of police officers could be seen monitoring the group as the protest continued for several hours.

Thomas has said he would like a crown court trial. A hearing will take place in Portsmouth crown court on Tuesday 29 September.

His lawyer, Simon Pentol KC, said: “This defendant is not charged with an offence of political activism, whether you agree with it or not, that is not the issue. He has elected crown court trial over criminal damage simpliciter and nothing more, and for not acquiescing to a notice requiring him to provide a pin number.”

He added: “I invite this court to bear in mind it’s dealing with a 37-year-old man who lives with his long-standing partner and their four children, all aged between 18 and three, his partner is pregnant once again, four months. She is a full-time mother, he is the full-time provider, or breadwinner, as they used to say.

“He is a professional roofer by trade. He is, therefore, having to look after his family who, through his political activism, have been under huge threat and due to publication of his mother’s home address, she has had to move home.”

What are the Lib Dems for? They must champion localism to stay relevant in an age of single-issue politics

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 13:02:14 GMT

Ed Davey’s party are the obvious candidates to push for the deeper local democracy the public is crying out for

September is the cruellest month for political commentators because it is when something has to be said about the Liberal Democrats. They are a play without a plot, a chorus line of seemingly endless “don’t knows”. Their leader, Ed Davey, recently warned that “we’re in the fight of our lives” to defend the values of liberty and equality. Really? How can this be when Davey is becoming about as relevant as Count Binface?

The Lib Dems’ central predicament has remained unchanged for a century, ever since the decline of David Lloyd George and the rise of the Labour party. There is simply no space in Britain for a centrist party when so little divides the big parties and they broadly stick to the prevailing ecomomic orthodoxy.

But there is now a ray of hope. One of the newer developments in British politics is the rise of single-issue parties. In Scotland and Wales, the Scottish National party and Plaid Cymru demand independence from the UK, while in England the Reform party has dedicated itself to curbing immigration.

A lack of a clarifying message could partly explain why the Lib Dems have suffered heavy defeats at recent byelections, and slipped to fourth or fifth place in many national opinion polls, regularly trailing the Greens and Reform.

In order to improve their electoral fortunes, the Lib Dems need an equally straightforward cause, one that should have broad appeal and identify an area neglected by the other parties. That cause is now glaring: the devolution of government authority.

Time and again in national league tables, England ranks as having one of the most concentrated central governments in Europe, and by some measures in the world. English citizens’ ability to participate in local democracy is extremely weak compared to other countries such as France, Germany and those in Scandinavia.

Welfare comparisons show the UK’s local services fare poorly and inequitably compared with those, for instance, in localised Scandinavia. The authority of Britain’s central executive over local government is overbearing, with ever more disappointing outcomes for citizens.

Localism is the issue and one that has featured prominently in political debate for decades. New Labour even proposed a “new localism”. The result was just 12 elected mayors in England and Wales between 2001 and 2005.

In 2010, David Cameron pledged a “radical shift in power from central government to neighbourhoods”. He then did the opposite through enforced housing targets and a fierce programme of austerity. Similarly, in 2024 Keir Starmer promised to “deepen democracy by … devolving power to communities”. Yet one of his first moves was to overrule local discretion in planning approvals, describing councils as “blockers and nimbys”.

Over the years, the phrase “shifting power locally” became an almost ritualistic election chant, clearly based on polling data. No government really meant it. Ever since Margaret Thatcher, the centre has taken ever more control of local taxation, education, housing, care services and planning. The job of a British local council today is in effect to do what the centre tells it. It has not much money nor power for anything else. It is therefore no wonder that local democracy is subject to ridicule: see, for instance, the recent “independence” vote in the Oxfordshire village of Piddington.

Unquestionably the most headline-grabbing of Westminster’s pseudo-localists is Andy Burnham. Does he mean it? His innovation of a cohort of metro mayors – introduced under the Conservatives – inserts a new level of regional bureaucracy between central and local government. Their role will primarily be to enforce national targets of housebuilding and energy investment, and presumably to override decisions of local councils beneath them.

Burnham’s announcement that mayors in England will be able to keep a share of income tax and business rates was cited as proof of his commitment to his so-called devolution agenda. But the extent to which mayors will be able to wield these powers remains to be seen.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

The prime minister’s moving of parts of the No 10 operation to Manchester hardly reduces the power of the centre. It merely relocates it, temporarily. Here, surely, is a Liberal Democrat cause.

Significantly, the one area in which the Lib Dems have flourished is local government. At last May’s local elections, the party took their control of councils up to 76, establishing them as a major political force across local government. This was a major achievement. There are now more Liberal Democrat council leaders in Britain than the 71 Lib Dem MPs. As such, their impact on the actual government of the country is substantial.

This cries out for revolution and the Lib Dems have every reason to be its champions. The party should go flat out for democratic, truly local self-government. Models of appropriate tiers and functions can be found across Europe. The cause is now aided by mountainous evidence that Britain’s centrist model – the famous “Rolls-Royce” of Whitehall – is now a clapped out jalopy. Every week the headlines cry that nothing seems to work.

This is the all-consuming challenge for the Lib Dems to make their own. Propose a major constitutional reform. The party’s 76 local councils can list the powers they want restored to them. It is these council leaders who must stand on stage at their conference, not Westminster’s indolent parliamentarians. Liberal Democrats should become the party of local Britain and restore the government of the people to the people.

Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

The woman’s current lawyer, James Blair Newman Jr, said: “Our client maintains that she was a victim of sexual assault, but she was entirely mistaken in her allegations identifying Mr Carter.”

Continuing her statement, the woman said memories of sexual assault were triggered by seeing an advertisement calling for victims of Combs to come forward. ‘Birdwatching is close to rapture’: Margaret Atwood on why she has given C$1m to avian research

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 13:00:50 GMT

Award-winning novelist celebrates late partner’s love of birds with gift to establish the Graeme Gibson chair in avian biology

If she could be any bird, Margaret Atwood would transform into a raven. “They’re very smart. They’re social, playful and just a very successful bird,” she says while seated in a corner of a bird observatory in the Lake Erie Islands archipelago. “They’re quite an intelligent problem solver.”

The observatory, which she set up with her late partner, Graeme Gibson, is located on the west shore of Pelee Island – the southernmost community in Canada – and is so new that there are no lightbulbs in a handful of lamps.

Pelee sits at the nexus of two important migration routes, making it a destination for birds travelling thousands of kilometres each year. Ravens are not among its regular visitors – only one was spotted in recent memory, in 2023 – but Atwood likes the old Inuit joke about them.

A hunter arrives at a place he has never camped before, and asks a raven where to spend the night. “The raven says, ‘The base of that hill is a good place,’ and so he sets up his little tent there,” says Atwood.

“In the middle of the night, a boulder rolls down the hill and crushes him. And the raven, as he’s enjoying the feast, says, ‘Works every time.’”

The bestselling Canadian author, whose prophetic works of speculative fiction have won countless awards, has blurred the lines that separate humans and birds both in her work and, at times, in her life.

She and Gibson, also a novelist, once dressed up for a party as Odin’s ravens, Thought and Memory. They wore black gloves and fashioned beaks from black construction paper.

Gibson died in 2019. In his final years, vascular dementia overtook his ability to journal about the birds. Still, he would watch them daily.

“Our back yard feeder and our birdbath were attracting only sparrows and robins and grackles and the occasional pigeon, but he didn’t care: every bird was worthy of attention,” Atwood wrote in a foreword to Gibson’s book, The Bedside Book of Birds. “‘I no longer know their names,’ he told a friend of ours. ‘But then, they don’t know my name either.’”

Now, Gibson’s legacy is about to help expand humanity’s understanding of birds. On Friday Western University, in London, Ontario, announced that Atwood had donated C$1m (£540,000) to celebrate her late partner’s love of birds.

The gift will create the Graeme Gibson chair in avian biology, with the goal of better understanding the fundamental processes that shape how birds move, adapt and behave in an environment undergoing profound transformation.

Atwood has championed many causes, including Indigenous education and human rights, but environmental protection is at the forefront of them.

“I have what they call a platform,” she says. “And I also had what they call extra money.”

Behind the deadpan is a longstanding belief in the power of science to answer deceptively simple questions about the natural world. How do birds navigate thousands of kilometres? How do they sense magnetic fields? How do they know where to go?

“Look at navigation,” says Chris Guglielmo, the co-director of the advanced facility for avian research at Western University, which received Atwood’s gift.

“We have a lot of descriptive understanding of what happens when we manipulate the magnetic fields, for example, the bird changes its orientation. We know they have these senses. But how they actually work is still a big mystery, and very exciting for people to try to study.”

The university has emerged as a global leader in avian research, developing the world’s first hypobaric climatic wind tunnel for bird flight in order to better study how they move through different types of air.

Guglielmo and his team have also made significant contributions to understanding how migratory birds fuel themselves, travel and survive long-distance journeys. But even the leading minds remain stumped by many of the mysteries that still surround the lives – and minds – of birds.

“Our new graduate students sometimes struggle to come up with a scientific question,” Guglielmo says. “And we tell them, there’s a million questions we don’t know the answer to. I have a whiteboard covered with potential questions. I just don’t have enough funding, people and time to even begin answering them.”

That’s why when he received the call about the gift, he was told to sit down first.

“It made me feel so good that we’re not only reaching and having impact in the scientific community, but that more broadly in the public sphere,” he says, adding that the gift was a “validation” of work done by the university’s scientists.

Weeks before the gift was announced, Atwood celebrated the opening of the Atwood-Gibson Bird Centre on Pelee Island. Resembling a towel hung loosely from a clothesline, Pelee Island is a rare enclave that blends Carolinian forest, dunes and marshes. Sitting at the intersection of the Atlantic and Mississippi migration routes, each spring it welcomes more than 200 species, not to mention thousands of serious birders.

At the event, she was simultaneously treated as literary royalty – attenders queued nervously for a chance to speak to her and pose for photographs – and as Peggy, the no-nonsense islander who often spends months at her cottage there and is woven into the community of 235 full-time residents.

The new building expands the footprint of the Pelee Island Bird Observatory, which the couple co-founded more than two decades ago to study the transcontinental movement of birds. It is also a refuge from Atwood’s nemesis: chiggers.

“You don’t know about chiggers?” she says of the six-legged larval mites hiding in the grass around the building. “Once you learn about their bite – and the itching that never stops – you never forget.”

While Atwood was exposed to birds – and chiggers – during a youth spent in the Ontario hinterlands with her forest entomologist father, Gibson became a bird lover later in life, with the zeal of a born-again religious convert.

“At its heightened moments, birdwatching can encourage a state of being close to rapture,” he wrote in his book. “It is an ecstasy that is said to accompany the writing of poetry; sometimes it comes when we’re listening to music.”

His “spark bird” – the name birders give to the particular species that triggers a lifelong love of the pursuit – was the red-tailed hawk, which is spotted frequently on the island.

Others, including the blackpoll warbler, are declining rapidly. The warbler breeds in the northern boreal forest, as far north as the Arctic, before embarking on a nonstop journey of almost 1,800 miles over open water to South America. Its population has dropped more than 80% in the last five decades, making it the fastest declining songbird.

Canada and the US have lost nearly 3bn birds since 1970. While certain species, including ducks and birds of prey, have surged in number, birds that travel thousands of miles each year have dropped in population by nearly 30%.

The declines, expected to increase further with the climate emergency, matter profoundly for a place such as Canada, where many bird species are migratory.

Atwood says the four biggest threats to birds – windows, cats, toxic pollution and environmental destruction of their habitats – are all things humans can help stop.

The first two are easier to address, but the latter are more challenging.

“People think: we can cut down this forest, and we’ll just make another forest over there. It’s not going to be the same. Birds have specific habitats that they need, so it’s not like spreading butter on a piece of toast.”

Atwood, who has spent much of her career imagining dystopian futures, is nonetheless optimistic about a future that has not yet been decided.

“Let’s say hope is a built-in human characteristic. Unless you’re deeply depressed, you wake up every morning thinking, what will this day bring? Maybe it will be a chocolate bar. Maybe there’ll be some surprises. If our ancestors didn’t have that, we probably wouldn’t be here,” she says.

“All of us trust this possibility that the doors are not locked. Yes, you may open door A and fall down a flight of stairs, but you may open door B and there will be a chocolate bar.”

She points to how young people, especially children, appear hardwired to engage deeply with nature.

“The passion is built in. They’re very interested in anything that moves, anything outside, and unless some grown-up teaches them to be afraid of such things, that interest will continue,” she says. “We are part of the natural world. It’s your choice of how to be in it.”

More than 11 years ago, Atwood and others signed a letter of outrage after the Oxford Junior Dictionary dropped a number of nature-themed words – including raven – in favour of a technology-heavy vernacular.

The writer Robert Macfarlane and the children’s book illustrator Jackie Morris released an elegy to youthful wonder in response to Oxford’s decision. But against the odds, birding is surging in interest among young people.

“If there’s no young people interested in a thing, whatever that thing is, it will die out. The fact that it’s not dying out, but it’s going in the other direction, is quite hopeful,” says Atwood. “I was talking to some booksellers recently, and I said, ‘What are young people buying?’ They said, ‘They’re buying great big fat Victorian novels.’ Who would have thought that?”

Birding can nevertheless appear to be a rather niche interest. To those who do not quite grasp the appeal: “I don’t think it’s a question of what birders are seeing that you’re not. It’s a question of what they’re feeling that you’re not,” she says.

“So maybe you should take some magic mushrooms. Because it all comes down to passion. Most of what we do in our lives we think it’s reason; we think it’s something that you can put into an argument. But everything begins with emotion.”

Atwood has spent much of her career examining the implications of societies that allow their freedoms and ecosystems to erode. But she is also a critic of those who neglect the relationship between humans and the natural world, cautioning that neglecting one can have dire consequences for the other.

“It’s easy, for example, to raise money for kidneys. Because people think: ‘Everybody’s got kidneys. I’ve got kidneys. If anything happened to my kidneys, I would want there to be a kidney facility for me,” she says.

“But people don’t make that immediate connection between their bodies and the natural world. There’s so much research that shows just how beneficial it is for our bodies to spend time in nature.”

Indeed, Atwood’s writing has long contained a warning that societies can allow the systems that sustain them to erode, often recognising only too late what was lost.

“Utopia is impossible, but if you don’t believe in the ability to attain something better, you will inevitably end up in a dystopia. Because dystopia is quite possible,” she says.

“Or to put it another way, we’re much better at creating hell than we are at creating heaven. Although I also think heaven would be quite boring.”

It’s not hypothetical: the dangers of AI are already here

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 12:00:50 GMT

Israel and the US have used AI to kill in Gaza and Iran, while law enforcement uses it in surveillance and arrests. The future is here

In recent weeks, concerns about AI have forged unlikely alliances in the tech and policy worlds. Tech moguls such as Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Demis Hassabis joined Dario Amodei, Satya Nadella and Bill Gates in sounding the alarm about the dangers of AI and called for a slowdown of the technology’s development despite years of racing for dominance. The senator Bernie Sanders teamed up with Steve Bannon to urge Congress to regulate AI, which has become one of the very few issues to unite Americans across the political spectrum.

The latest moves were sparked in part by the AI researcher Jacob Coxon’s warnings on Twitter/X that AI companies are “gambling with our lives” and believe that the technology “could kill us all by the end of the decade”.

The reality is, we don’t have to wait to see how AI will bring about unprecedented death and destruction, because we’ve already witnessed its unleashing.

Bill Gates’s nearly 6,000-word essay in late August warning about AI and its potential harms to humanity doesn’t come as a surprise. One of us has been a Microsoft employee for nearly a decade, witnessing all the dangers unfold in real time. Together, we’ve spent the past two years organizing with other Microsoft employees and activists to uncover the company’s role in the genocide of Palestinians in Gaza. We have collectively called on Microsoft to cut ties with the Israeli military.

But it’s not just Microsoft that is involved in AI-driven destruction.

Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza was a testing ground for the use of AI in warfare and the results were deeply disturbing. Israel’s military used AI to identify people to kill, with 12,000 targets generated and bombed in the first month alone. This was done with little to no meaningful human oversight, as documented in an investigation by Oscar-winning Israeli journalist Yuval Abraham, whose latest film NAZA, a Guardian-produced film, includes chilling testimonials by the soldiers involved.

Earlier this year in Iran, the US military launched an AI-involved airstrike that hit Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab, Iran, killing 156 children, teachers and other civilians. The strike that caused what is almost certainly the worst incident of civilian casualties in the war was, most likely, the result of a “targeting mistake” that relied on faulty data.

The horrors wrought by AI aren’t limited to people overseas – they’re already being felt by vulnerable communities in the US The Department of Homeland Security is using AI tools – including Microsoft’s Azure – to monitor, arrest and deport immigrants at a massive scale. Law enforcement agencies nationwide are deploying facial recognition technology despite evidence of algorithmic bias that has led to the wrongful arrest and incarceration of Latino and Black Americans. The NYPD also partnered with Microsoft to build its Domain Awareness System, using Azure to connect to 18,000 security cameras, according to the New York Daily News, creating a mass surveillance system that has expanded to Georgia and other parts of the world, including Brazil and Singapore. Datacenters that power AI are being built in rural and low-income neighborhoods throughout the US where many are living under the poverty line and are now facing significant health threats from air pollution caused by these facilities.

Though many of these harms have been documented over the years, rightwing government leaders are continuing to shut down dissent through dishonest and draconian measures. Donald Trump has called AI risks a “hoax” and said any attempts to limit the power of the technology were part of a “sick conspiracy”. House Republicans have dismissed the public’s concerns about AI, blaming Chinese government disinformation for public opposition to datacenters. Israel’s culture minister, Miki Zohar, has threatened to revoke the citizenship of NAZA film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, accusing them of “treason against the state”.

One thing is clear: the dangerous future that Gates, Amodei, and others are warning us about is already here, and we must act now to prevent further harm. Those of us with families in Gaza, Lebanon, Iran and US neighborhoods terrorized by ICE already know people living through the nightmare.

In the last few weeks, we’ve seen promising efforts from US policymakers attempting to curtail the potential harms of AI technology. The House recently proposed the Frontier Act to embed third-party evaluators within tech companies to conduct safety assessments, and earlier this month, Sanders and the representative Greg Casar introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act to stop tech leaders from building and developing technologies that humans cannot control.

These bills are a good starting point. But they could take years to pass and don’t address the devastation already being caused. Frontier AI companies and governments must act now to ban the selling and use of AI technologies in military targeting, autonomous weapons systems, and mass surveillance. This is what employees from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind are calling for.

We are living through a precious and fleeting moment when we can still confront the harms AI has already caused to the most vulnerable and course-correct before they become irreversible, spreading into more communities. We need to establish clear guardrails right now and shape the future of AI so that it protects everyone, not just a privileged few.

Mohamed Hussein organizes with No Azure for Apartheid, an employee-led movement calling on Microsoft to end its involvement with the Israeli military. He is also a leader in Palestinians and Allies at Microsoft, an internal employee group.

Granate Kim works with No Azure for Apartheid and is the Campaigns Director at MPower Change, an organization that mobilizes Muslim communities in defense of human rights.

‘I’d strip for £100!’ Dominic West and Sienna Miller on nudity, narcissism and their juicy new show War

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 12:00:49 GMT

The stars are no strangers to public scrutiny of their most intimate relationships – but they’ve never experienced anything like this. They talk about playing a famous divorcing couple, and how money makes things revolting

In a London hotel room, Dominic West is weighing up how much he would accept to strip to his socks. In the new series War, West plays a social media billionaire who is supposed to be fairly decent, though there’s one excruciating scene – goading someone to strip for money – that reveals he’s definitely also a bit of a git. “That, I suppose, is the kick billionaires must get: that people would do anything for money,” he says. He wonders what his price would be. His co-star Sienna Miller laughs and says he’d do it “for the lols”, and West grins and says: “No, I’d want three figures. A hundred quid.”

War is a juicy eight-part legal drama, where Miller and West are a divorcing couple – she a narcissistic film star, he said billionaire – so just about all their scenes together are suppurating with contempt, which is fun, but also a bit of a shame because they have such good chemistry. They first worked together 21 years ago in the West End production of Shakespeare’s As You Like It. “So we had a history, which was great,” says Miller. There have been many times she’s gone into jobs where “on the first day you’re married to someone and you don’t know them. It’s helpful to have some sort of rapport.”

West was cast first – he had worked with the creator George Kay previously on the classy BBC drama The Hour, and Kay had written the role of Morgan Henderson, a tech entrepreneur, with him in mind. Miller plays Carla Duval, a Hollywood star who wants half of her philandering ex’s wealth – with the help of her formidable legal team. Neither Carla nor Morgan have much to recommend them. Miller struggled, she says with a laugh, to “find the more human aspects of her, until I realised it was really fun not to. I decided to have fun leaning into the unappealing qualities of Carla, which was quite uncomfortable for somebody who errs on the side of people-pleasing. To not be invested in other people’s reactions or responses. To be narcissistic, basically.”

For West, it must have been just as tricky finding his way into playing a “benign billionaire”. Do they exist? The BBC podcast Good Bad Billionaire came in useful, he says. Only a handful of the billionaires covered could be considered “good”. “Basically they’re the ones who give away all the money … It was intriguing to me, the idea of a benign billionaire.” But Morgan obviously has a ruthless side – the hardball divorce negotiations, and that strip scene. “And you go, oh, now we see why he’s a billionaire. But other than that, I was doing what Sienna was avoiding, and I do all the time, which is desperately try to make people like me.”

Was the high-profile divorce based on real-life cases? No, says Kay when we speak. Only one scene was inspired by real events – when the actor and director Olivia Wilde was served custody papers at a public event on behalf of Ted Lasso star Jason Sudeikis. “It was one of our most emotional days [on set],” says Kay, “because it’s such a horrible thing to do.”

The show was inspired by a conversation Kay overheard in a queue in an airport lounge. “This woman screamed ‘Yes!’ into her phone. I turned around, because I’m quite nosy, and said: ‘Can I ask what has made you so happy?’” She told him her husband had finally signed the papers after a four-year divorce battle. The more Kay looked into high-stakes, high-end divorces, the more he realised it was filled with drama – the prenups, the affairs, the property – and ideal for the kind of glossy legal shows he’d grown up watching. “I’m a kid of the 90s,” he says. He loved the big law shows such as Ally McBeal, and later The Good Wife, and The West Wing was inspiration as a workplace-based drama. “I loved the humour. I wanted to do something with the sort of zip and repartee of those shows.” It’s the reason the cast of War is so comedian-heavy, including Miles Jupp and Nick Mohammed as solicitors at rival firms. “People [who] are just super-sharp on the cues because if anyone slows down, it dies on its feet.” (Extra fun fact: Mohammed and Celia Imrie, who plays a barrister, were also filming The Celebrity Traitors at the same time. “They were so tight-lipped!” says Kay.)

He had previously worked with writer Abi Morgan on her show The Hour; Morgan’s series The Split also features glossy divorce lawyers, but Kay says his were “all American references”. There’s already a second series with the rival law firms taking on a defamation case. Expect more juice.

A public divorce brings wild scrutiny of the private lives of the people going through it, and when it’s a celebrity couple – as Morgan and Carla discover – it’s on a different scale altogether. Miller and West both have experience of this, though not in divorces. West had a brief period of what might politely be called “marital scrutiny” (in late 2020, photographers camped outside his house after photographs were published of him with his The Pursuit of Love co-star Lily James) but Miller had years of intense hounding during her relationship with the actor Jude Law. A victim of phone hacking by the News of the World, she won damages in 2011, gave evidence to the Leveson inquiry, and settled with News Group Newspapers in 2021 over alleged hacking.

“They [the paparazzi] were hounding you, weren’t they?” says West, remembering scenes outside the London theatre where they worked in 2005. Yes, says Miller, “but it feels like another life and another world. It’s now almost, from a kind of sociological perspective, interesting to look back on what the culture was like then.”

What is curious, though, is why Miller seems so willing to put herself through it in her work: in War, as in Netflix’s Anatomy of a Scandal, she’s harassed by paps and dealing with an unfaithful husband. Having only got the later scripts after signing on, she didn’t know what Carla would be dealing with. She laughs and says maybe directors instantly think of her for “that kind of storyline, which is something I’ll now avoid”. But does it stir up difficult memories, or is there a catharsis in playing it? “Maybe that’s it. Maybe it is kind of reframing it for myself – to pretend at it, and to then remember how crazy that was as a way of living.” Separately, Kay says his stars’ personal experiences didn’t influence the casting or writing. “One of the things we did quite quickly was we resisted any of that meta-referencing, because they are incredibly good actors, and these parts are different from their own experiences.”

West has had plenty of accolades, but Miller has always been underrated; she has said that the emphasis on her personal life probably derailed her career. She puts in a wonderful performance in War, as she has in other roles such as the weighty 2018 film American Woman. “I feel less like I have to prove something, and I’m not sure whether that’s because I don’t have anything to prove, or I just don’t care about proving myself any more,” she says.

There are also a few better roles now for older women. “I remember speaking to actresses who were like: ‘You’re so lucky that you’re turning 40 now, because we were obsolete when that happened.’ But I still wish I’d played Juliet.” She remembers speaking to a theatre heavyweight not so long ago and asking if he thought she could still play Juliet. She laughs as she remembers: “He said, ‘I just think people will struggle to see you as a virgin.’” West adds with a laugh, “You just need an old Romeo.”

Has this show put them off ever getting divorced? “Of course!” says West (married since 2010). “I think that’s the big takeaway. I was talking to a guy who was rich and getting a divorce, and he backed up everything in the show. The interesting thing, and George anatomises it so well, is how two people who loved each other can descend into warfare. That’s where the drama is: that knife edge between love and hate. You get it in any relationship, when you’re arguing or whatever, but this is in a wildly expensive public arena. Like a battle in any commercial situation, with big lawyers, your marriage becomes that.” A commodity, says Miller (she’s engaged to the actor Oli Green), “to be bartered with, and the more acrimonious, the more money [for the lawyers]”.

The stress and vitriol unleashed by this divorce, arguing over numbers so big they’re almost meaningless, seems barely worth it. I’d have settled for a lot less to avoid it (I’d be a terrible divorce lawyer). “I imagine that kind of money to be incredibly corrosive,” says Miller. “I have been in proximity to people who have a huge amount of money, and I just don’t see them as happier. I mean, it’s a revolting amount of money.” West has given billionaires more thought recently than he’d probably like to. “If you’ve got several hundred billion, and you’re not solving the climate crisis, then really something’s deeply wrong.”

War is on Sky Atlantic on Friday 2 October at 9pm.

Meryl Streep’s casting as Aslan has angered the Christian right. Don’t they have more pressing issues?

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 11:50:46 GMT

The Oscar-winner is voicing Narnia’s wise lion in Greta Gerwig’s adaptation of The Magician’s Nephew, leading to roars of fury from US evangelical commentators

It is a confusing time to be alive, given how often these days Hollywood indulges in revisionism. Who knew that the Wicked Witch of the West was the heroine after all, that Cruella de Vil simply had a difficult childhood, or that Mufasa was adopted? Now it turns out that Aslan, CS Lewis’s messiah with a mane, is a lioness – or at least, may sound like one in Greta Gerwig’s upcoming adaptation of The Magician’s Nephew, because Meryl Streep is providing the voice.

News that the Oscar-winner might be portraying Narnia’s Christ-like big cat first surfaced in April last year, prompting a flurry of complaints from conservative Christians. This week, the naysayers were back after Empire published a first look at the film, along with an interview with Gerwig in which the director confirmed the casting and explained her choice of actor. Streep, it turns out, was hired not because the Barbie director desperately fancied stoking the flames of controversy, but because she needed someone over 70 who could convey both wisdom and childlike wonder.

“I wanted someone who was profound but not pretentious, who had gravitas but not morose self-seriousness,” Gerwig said. She also explained she wanted one of the finest actors working today, adding: “That list is not a long one.”

Some American evangelical commentators have already made up their minds that this new version of Narnia comes from from the seventh circle of hell. Radio host Jenna Ellis accused Gerwig of “profaning Christ with the divine feminine”, while Texas preacher David Fairchild called the casting “creative vandalism”. The Daily Wire’s Isabel Brown said the decision to cast Streep was offensive because “CS Lewis literally intended Aslan to be the incarnation of Christ inside the world of Narnia”. She pointed to the end of Lewis’s novel The Voyage of the Dawn Treader, in which Aslan tells Lucy and Edmund they will come to know him by another name in their own world. For Brown, casting Streep was a “deliberate mockery of Christianity”.

There has been no confirmation from Gerwig that this new Aslan is in fact female. And not everyone agrees that casting Streep is a problem: Christian writer Mary Pezzulo has pointed out the irony that some evangelicals think it’s perfectly all right for Jesus to be portrayed as an animal yet draw the line when he’s given a woman’s voice. “Very Online conservative Christians really think that portraying Christ as a lion, a carnivorous beast with notoriously smelly urine who sleeps 23 hours a day and steals meat from hyaenas, is beautiful sacred art,” she wrote. “But having Christ portrayed by a woman is sacrilege.”

However you view this one, it’s weird that a film adaptation of one of the least known books in the Narnia series now feels like the subject of an emergency reconvening of the Council of Nicaea. Also, Gerwig has said she plans to reimagine the fantasy world through a rock opera prism: the great lion king’s eyes have been coloured like David Bowie’s mismatched peepers in publicity shots, and the creation of Narnia is apparently designed to look and sound as if Genesis is being staged by the Spiders from Mars. Daniel Craig is playing the deeply suspect sorcerer of the title, while Emma Mackey steps into Tilda Swinton’s shoes as the White Witch, Jadis. But all anyone can think about is that Aslan now sounds remarkably similar to Miranda Priestly, Julia Child and Mrs Thatcher.

That’s actually a shame, because The Magician’s Nephew has enough going on that it shouldn’t require a culture war to make a splash. Its story sees two children discover a wood full of pools leading to other worlds; one takes them to a dead city beneath a dying sun, where they wake the queen who exterminated its entire population and accidentally bring her back to London. The book has a sense of madcap wonder about it that occasionally makes all the waiting for Aslan to turn up in The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe, only for him to immediately sacrifice himself, feel like a glacially paced, religiously didactic slog by way of comparison.

Remember when Barbie went from a potentially cheesy movie about an anatomically unlikely child’s doll to the most talked about film of the year? Something similar could happen here. And then again, Streep might just be playing a lion in a children’s film. Either way, it seems remarkable that an actor whose voice nobody has yet heard in the movie has apparently displaced the White Witch herself – or perhaps even some of her famously addictive turkish delight – as Narnia’s most devious and malign influence.

‘You learn more from the losses and the draws’: Red Roses relishing clash with revitalised Black Ferns

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 11:26:33 GMT

A week after Canada ended their winning run, England’s World Cup winners face a New Zealand team aiming to inflict more pain at Twickenham

A wounded animal is the most dangerous. The Red Roses might not have lost to Canada last Saturday but they did not win either, for the first time since 2022. England’s 40-game unbeaten streak continues with a blemish and when things do not go to plan they usually respond with a dominant swing.

Despite adding defence specialist Shaun Edwards as a coaching consultant earlier this week, the Tests do not get easier. This Saturday they face the team who last made them taste defeat in the World Cup final four years ago, the Black Ferns.

In recent years England have had their number, winning the three Tests they have played against each other in the past three years. But the nations have not played one another in two years and the Black Ferns are revitalised under the new head coach, Whitney Hansen, who has not yet lost since taking over the job in December of last year.

Panic buttons will not be grasped for by the hosts; the match against Canada was a thrilling and close Test which deservedly came out as a draw. On-field battles like that can help the Red Roses get better, according to the England back-row Abi Burton.

“I am not scared of losing any more, I am scared that we will become stagnant,” Burton said. “I don’t think we are at that point because we constantly look to get better in training and push each other from a selection point of view. But ultimately you don’t know what you don’t know and if we are at the point of we don’t feel like we are potentially progressing … you do need that ‘they are actually here now, they are on our tails, we were fighting before but we need to fight even more now’. You learn more from the losses and the draws than you do the wins.”

The discourse has been about their non-win but the biggest news out of the England camp this week is Edwards’s arrival. The head coach, John Mitchell, has said the 59-year-old is already forming good relationships with the players and Burton echoes that sentiment, saying they bonded over their rugby league backgrounds. Burton comes from a rugby league family with her father, Danny, playing for clubs such as Bradford Bulls.

“We got to have that moment of connection to have a chat about that, it felt really cool and special to share that with such a legend of the game,” she said. “It helps you connect and learn about each other.”

The general consensus from camp is that Edwards has slotted in seamlessly and has given the players defensive areas to work on this Saturday. Burton added the coach has an aura about him and has brought a new energy.

“That is something we haven’t had in a while,” she said. “Obviously Scaz [Emily Scarratt] went into her coaching role but she has been a constant. I think that aura is so powerful and it makes us want to step up because it is like this man is legendary. You don’t want to let him down, you want to step up. You don’t realise you have another gear to give until you get put in that situation. I think it is super exciting that he has joined us and he will be a real asset to the squad.”

The game will be played in front of almost 60,000 at Allianz Stadium almost a year to the day since the Rugby World Cup final, a game the Red Roses won after beating Canada. Prior to the tournament many had believed the showpiece in 2025 would have been between England and New Zealand. The Black Ferns did play on that final day but won the bronze medal after Canada beat them in the semi-final.

The New Zealand lock, Maiakawanakaulani Roos, says downing the Red Roses is their target and having several players compete in England’s PWR last season has aided their preparation. Roos herself played for Trailfinders, as did the captain Georgia Ponsonby with others like Liana Mikaele-Tu’u competing for Harlequins.

“We haven’t played them in two years and our game has grown so much and they have just gone from strength to strength,” Roos said. “I am really excited to see how we go and turn up for the challenge that is the Red Roses.

“I think we have seen how each other trains, seen the habits that we hold and it is so competitive. I really cannot wait to play them just because we know how they train now and how they do things. I think that is a bit of a point of difference that the girls who have played in the PWR have been able to help our team understand.”

England’s goal this weekend will be to start a new winning streak, while New Zealand’s will be to make sure the Red Roses head to Canada in October with their world record firmly in the rear view.

‘We skate on the rooftops of damaged buildings’: a day in the life of a skateboarder in Gaza

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 11:00:47 GMT

As the war in Gaza approaches its fourth year, the Guardian follows five ordinary Palestinians as they go about their lives. Each tells the story of their day, revealing the terrible toll of the conflict. Rajab al-Reefi teaches children to skate to ‘bring some joy’, but finding boards and safe spaces is a daily challenge

Rajab al-Reefi remembers the day the club’s last skateboard broke. Those pastry-thin layers of maple, carefully pressed into a curve, had carried child after child up and down the homemade ramps of the skatepark. Having endured years beyond their typical lifespan, the board’s layers buckled, cracked and finally snapped.

At 30, Rajab is a leader of the Gaza skate club, a group that has spent the past decade teaching girls and boys to skate. But Israel’s siege of Gaza blocks a vast array of ordinary household goods from entering the territory, with the Israelis claiming they could be used by Hamas. One of the banned items is a skateboard.

Rajab is a skater in Gaza, a place with almost no boards left. This is what a day in his life looks like.

double quotation markI wake up early in the morning, and the first thing I do is go to get water for the house and bring drinking water.

Water trucks stopped reaching our area because drivers are afraid to come this close, due to the risks. We have been living about 30 metres away from the yellow line [a border line controlled by Israel]. As a result, I have to travel to other areas – water for daily use is even harder to obtain, as it arrives only once a week and at a specific time.

After I get the water, my wife prepares breakfast and we have it together. I take my children to kindergarten, then return home, get dressed, prepare my equipment and head to work. Before the war, all of my work revolved around skateboarding and working with children. But now, with skateboarding activities mostly suspended, I work as a photographer whenever opportunities arise, so that I can support my family. I also spend time posting on social media to bring attention to our cause.

double quotation markAfter I finish work, I go home and prepare myself to go to skateboard practice with the kids, so we can do the things we dream about.

Getting the boards we have now was extraordinarily difficult. When the war began, I had to leave all our skateboards with some of the children I train, because I couldn’t take them with me. Our area is near the [yellow line] border, and I was afraid that something might happen to the houses we had left there, and that I would lose whatever equipment remained. In the end we lost them – some of the houses were bombed with the boards inside. Only a very small amount remained.

In Gaza, we always try to repair and reuse whatever we can. We have even managed to produce fuel from old car tyres. So of course we tried every possible way to repair our skateboards and keep going. But eventually we reached a point where repairs were no longer possible because of heavy wear and the lack of spare parts.

When the last board broke a few months ago, honestly, we felt hopeless. But we started contacting the children who we’d left skate equipment with during the war, asking if it was still in their destroyed homes. Some said yes – so we searched under the rubble to retrieve these boards. Honestly, while we were digging, we were working with our bare hands. We knew we might encounter unexploded ordnance. We were in great danger, but we found some equipment there, and now we have a few repaired boards.

In the sun outside the YMCA, a group of about 40 children have gathered. They stand in an orderly line against the fences and watch two small girls wearing matching pink trousers, white T-shirts and long ponytails run a few steps, drop the boards and jump on. They bounce over the uneven ground, attempting a body aerial – where you jump 180 degrees and land back on the board. Neither quite lands it, but when they turn at the edge of the court, both are grinning.

double quotation markIn the afternoon, it is time for skateboarding. I walk with my son past streets full of rubble, go to the YMCA and we practise skating until sunset and the call to prayer.

There used to be a whole skate park that we built here with the help of friends overseas, but it has all been demolished to make way for tents. For training spaces now we can use the courtyard of the YMCA, the remaining open areas along the seaport, or even the rooftops of damaged buildings. We do tricks in the rubble – sometimes on empty missile casings – and post them online.

Today, we try to skate using simple moves, just to bring some joy to the children. Let them do simple moves, just so they feel that skateboarding still exists in Gaza.

Losing children whom we had trained was one of the hardest tragedies we experienced. We also lost the places – like our homes and the skate park – we had dreamed of for years and worked tirelessly to build. As soon as those dreams became reality, the war came and destroyed everything.

When we had no boards, the absence of skateboarding completely changed my life. I have become more irritable and less able to cope with what is happening around me. Still, I continue reaching out to many people in the hope of finding a solution.

I find it astonishing that in 2026 no one is able to bring in a simple wooden skateboard – something that harms no one and could bring happiness to hundreds of children.

double quotation markAfter the skating is over, I make my way back home. In the evening, we often feel anxious because the bombing has not stopped.

Sometimes we cannot fall asleep straight away, and we spend the whole night feeling anxious because of the sound of aircraft. Since I have children, I try to calm and reassure them. I tell them, “Don’t worry, the bombing is far away. We are safe, and nothing will happen to us.” I do not do anything in the evening apart from spend time with my children and my wife.

My main goal is to help children release the negative emotions caused by everything they have witnessed and endured during the war, while also ensuring that skateboarding continues to exist in Gaza.

Digested week: I had Nigella down as tradwife burlesque but her Bake Off debut won me over

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 10:44:14 GMT

Plus, Prince Harry spreads his love of Marmite to his kids, and Dolly Parton’s nephew turns out to be fairly unusual

It was a big week at the UN, Buckingham Palace and the White House, but for all sentient people of Britain, the top story this week was that Bake Off is back and we need to talk about Nigella. (“Isn’t that the thing you use on cold sores?” said my gen Alpha child, as yet uninitiated into the lifestyle icons of our age. “That’s Bonjela,” I said.) I went into the opener of the show’s 17th season crankily resenting the departure of Prue Leith, who I love, and who offers, apart from anything else, a corrective to all the women on TV at the moment lecturing us about how to age from behind Maga-style glow-ups. (Youth on HBO anyone? No thanks!)

And in the first half of the show, Nigella did indeed seem to struggle. She was quiet, watchful and seemingly unsure of herself in the face of the wide array of personality types on the show, who were also struggling to adapt to new surroundings. This isn’t working at all, I thought, and then halfway through the show she clicked, or possibly I did.

I should say that going back I was never a big Nigella person. I bought her first cookery book a million years ago and loved the excess of all that butter and cheese. But over the years, as her brand grew and refined, I just assumed she was part of the large cohort of women who aren’t really for me – broadly speaking, who commit themselves to a kind of tradwife burlesque that, even at ironic remove, seethes with the conventionality of the thing it’s critiquing.

Anyway so much for that. As Bake Off unfolded, I crumbled like a flapjack in biscuit week (don’t email; per UK tax law, a flapjack is, indeed, a biscuit). It is so rare to watch someone of Nigella’s star power comport themselves on telly in such pensive style, so that even when she’s trying to be saucy, it seems to me, her natural state is one of anxious enthusiasm and a depth of feeling that comes out in odd places. “May I just say, I love salt,” she said, with the mad emphasis of someone correcting a widely held but incorrect assumption about themselves and instantly, of course, I loved her.

While the rest of the House of Windsor wrestled with the fallout from Tuesday’s publication of Charles Spencer’s book, Prince Harry – surely closer to his uncle in thought and style than anyone else in the family – gave us some benign royal news in the form of an update on his children’s eating habits.

Since moving from the US to the UK last month, the prince said his two children were enjoying Marmite for the first time – and I’m going to have to run the quotes in full here, for their jolliness and mild strangeness. “Is that a British thing?” said Harry to Hello! magazine at the WellChild awards this week, referring to Marmite. “Because it’s always been in my life, and now the kids are eating Marmite on crumpets, which is big for me.” I mean, what’s that about? Of course he knows it’s British; perhaps he feels in brand competition with the iconic British spread. Anyway, on he went: “They used to diss me for having Marmite in the house, and now they’re in the UK it’s like that’s kind of like water under the bridge, so it’s good.”

That’s nice; I mean it. I was happy when one of my two accepted that Marmite was the only way, although I’ve never had much success with any of the other British staples and nor has Harry, who said his attempt to put his kids on to beans on toast “hadn’t gone down very well”. I’d watch a full series on this, in which Harry puts toad in the hole, yorkshire pudding and the full English (“is that a British thing?”) in front of his kids – but no one tell Brooklyn Beckham or he’ll be round with his cookbook.

Disappointing news from the Dolly Parton estate, where that very nice-seeming nephew of hers who broke the news of her death in a video statement last month has turned out, judging by court papers filed by the Parton estate in Tennessee this week, to be – how to put this? – fairly unusual.

Bryan Seaver, who Parton employed for more than two decades as her head of security, is alleged to have sent Danny Nozell, Parton’s manager who runs the late singer’s estate, a series of communications, including the lines, “I’m a killer” and, “I’m literally an international arms dealer and mercenary. All I do is warfare. Everyone needs to be worried about what I might do.” Meanwhile, in trying to explain himself to TMZ this week, Seaver apparently made things worse with the explanation: “I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments. I am a security professional and I am a killer. However, nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by.” So that’s OK.

To be fair to Seaver, “all I do is warfare” is a great line I will be trying to work into my own conversations from now on. One wonders what this scene was like while Parton was alive. Famously, the singer employed large numbers of her family at Dollywood and elsewhere, and one has to assume kept any awkward characters in check. Now the queen is dead, can the centre hold?

News of the one-in-a-thousand-year El Niño coming down the pike is so grim, let’s cling to the odd bit of cheer from the climate frontline. This week in West Bengal, news of a baby elephant calf, separated from its mother and drowning in flood water, was rescued by two heroic fishers who spotted its trunk, waving out of the water like a periscope, and after following it for 3 miles into shallow water, managed to fish it out of the murk.

The calf, which was a few days old, had lost its mum and the rest of the herd at the Teesta River and, improbably, after wrestling it on to the boat, the fishers managed to find the herd and reunite it with its mum, who got in such a frenzy at the sight of her missing baby that onlookers fleetingly worried she’d kill it. Instead, she wrapped her trunk around its body, splashed its head with water and flapped her ears with abandon, making witnesses on the bank hold themselves in at the beauty of it all.

Week two of trying to change mobile phone providers comes to a close without success and what have I learned? That the phrase “I know it’s not your fault” followed by a giant rage spiral doesn’t achieve the desired outcome. That the phrases “why are you like this?” and “what is wrong with your company?” equally have little to no effect. And that inserting “literally” into the sentence “we’re talking about a £10-a-month contract, literally what’s wrong with you?” doesn’t provide the needle-moving emphasis I’d hoped. Time for a lie down and a rethink.
